THE " Maiden Circuits" that maidens long ior—

Wedding rings. TEE night that is as black as your hat bath a darkness that may be felt. THE grocer puts sand in his sugar, thinking he may thereby put rocks in his pocket. WHEN is a wall like a set of good fellows I—When It is composed of a lot of "bricks." IF bank officials seem to be going it pretty fast, depositors have it in their power to draw a check
on-them. IN spite of the rule ssserting it, two of a kind do zot make a pair, always. Do two apples make a
pear THE hilarity of the season extends even to the feathered tribe, and many a turkey loses its head in

the holiday time. CANON FARRAR came to America for rest. He took back 25,000d05. of our money, and did not,, luckily for us, get the rest. "JEMIMA SUSAN, did you get my letter? "es, Sambo." "I sent it in de hope of raisin' a fi'sme." "Sambo, you succeeded, for 11, lit de gas." ABOUT THE DAiFODIL.—The daffodil's a lovely flower, though not much of a smeller: The. florists call it "Baby-flower" because it's such a yeller. A SEASIDE visitor went to the circulating library and asked if they had the letters of Jane Welsh Carlyle. She received the reply:: "you will get 'em at the post-office." "MoTnEn," asked 'little Felix, "do the Indians own the railroads?' "No, my child." "Well, they've got something to de with them, I known, 'cos papa said he bought his ticket of a 'scalper." A MAN !recently went on board a ship lying in harbour, and meeting the cook asked him if he was the mate of the vessel. "No, faith; but I'm the man that cooks the mate," was the reply. A rs.m.sois disputing with Peter Pindar, said, in great heat, that he did not like to be thought a scoundrel. "I wish," replied Peter, "that you had as great a dislike to being a scoundrel." Cons sai.—" So far as you saw, she was doing her ordinary household duty." Witness —" should say se. She was talking." 44 WHAT is your fweetheart by trade' Lizzie 7" "A miller." *So as my last one; but missus always saw him standing in our dark pantry, and so now I've got a chimney sweet." "Marriage," says John Seldon, "is a desperate thing; the frogs in lEsop were .extremely wise; they had a great mind to some water, but they would not leap into the well, because they 'could sioA get out again." •SAYS Moore in his diary :—Shee told me a bon 'not of Rogers's the other day. On somebody remarking that Payne Knight had got very deaf, 4' It is from want of practice," says B.; Knight being a very bad listener. ARCHBISHOP WHATELY used to tell the story -of a traveller who, finding himself and his dog in a wild country, and destitute of provisions, cut. off his dog's tail and boiled it for his own supper, giving the dog the bone! AUNT—" Has any one been at these preserves ?" Dead silence. Have you touched them, Jimmy?" Jimmy (with the utmost deliberation)" Pa never 'lows me to talk at dinner." "My DEAR," said a mother, annoyed at some incautious remarks of her little girl, "why can't you keep a secret?" "Because," said Little Mis- chief, demurely, "two of my front teeth are gone, mamma?' LADY (at an intelligence office, about to engage a new servant)—" Now, Bridget, in regard to going out visiting, I—" Bridget (interrupting)—" 0, mum, you kin go out whiniver ye plase. You'll not find Bridget Lannigan hard, mum, nor dicta- torial like!" SOMEBODY out West recently sang the well- known air, which was correctly printed in the pro- grammes, "Piano, piano—Weber." The audience were up in arms, declaring they did not pay their money to listen to a puff of the Weber piano. AT the club. Z. has just returned from the Con- tinent, and is very Natl. X.—" Glad to see you back. Did you go to Italy I" Z.—" Yes." X.—"Go to Venice ?" Z.—" Yes." X.—" See the Lion of St. . Mark Z —"Oh, yes—saw him fed!" MRB. BROWN—" You told me that if I left my tablecloth out all night the fruit stains would dis- appear. Well, I put it out last night." Mr. Jones— "Of course the stains were gone in the morning?" Mrs. Brown—" Yes, so was the tablecloth." Is the earth round or flat ?" asked a member of a school committee of a candidate for a position as teacher. "Well," answered the candidate, "I'm not particular about that. Some likes it round, and some likes it flat, and some Others likes it square. I teach it any way that suits." HE continually played on the cornet, "Sweet Spirit, Hear My Prayer." The maiden lady next door sent word, with compliments, that she heard his prayer, and would pay a month's lodging for him in advance if he'd move to another part of the town. "GENTLEMEN of the jury," said a counsel in a suit about a herd of hogs, "there were just thirty- six hogs • just exactly three times as many as there are in that jury box, gentlemen." That lawyer did not win his case, and he thought the jurors were very pig-headed. "I SHALL teach you to speak properly, and then to write as you speak," said a teacher in the public schools. "Poor Billy Wilcox!" said a little voice,' apparently involuntarily. "What about Billy?" asked the teacher. "Please, ma'am, he speaks through his nose—he will have to write through his nose." THE Prince of Conti, finding as he grew old that his attentions to the fair sex were not so well received as formerly, remarked—" It is time for me to retire. Formerly my civilities 'were taken for declarations of love, butnow my declarations of love are taken only for civilities." "I AM going to buy a light coat to match these trousers," he remarked to his wife the other day, "and a light pair of gloves to match the coat, and a light soft hat to match—" "Your head, I suppose," interrupted the spouse gently; and the household knew no harmony that day. "War (asked Whatley) does the operation of hanging kill a man?" A physiologist gravely re- plied, "Because inspiration is checked, circulation stopped, and blood suffuses and congests the brain.* "Bosh!" cried Whately, "it is because the rope is not long enough to let his feet touch the ground." A LABOURER from Skye having applied to a gentleman for employment, the gentleman asked him his age. "She'll be forty years." "What sort of work can you do 7" "Oh, she was twelve years a whale-fish, ten years a wheel-barrow, six years a pleach-field, and fifteen Tears a stor.e-brak. So hersel' can do everything." FRIEND (to young author)—" How are you suc- ceeding in your literary work." Young author (hopefully)—" Well, comparatively speaking, I am doing well." Friend—" What is 'comparatively speaking?" Young author—" One of the greatest of modern writers wrote for twenty years before he had a single MS. 4accepted. I have only been writing fire years. Compared with him, I flatter myself that I am doing well." "ISAAC, my ownest own, what would you do if I should die ?" asked a wife of her husband, as she laid her fair, white arms around his neck. "Well, really, my love, I hadn't thought of it," he answered abstractedly; "but I presume I'd bury you, and then tell that red-headed widow across the street, who is always winking at me, that nothing in this world would ever induce me to mai ry again." Then she tore himself from him, plucked the flowers he had just given her from her heaving bosom, called him a knock-kneed sneak, went into hysterics, and screamed f6r her ma till the old lady came. Then wasn't there a rumpus! AT a religious meeting in America, a number of females stood upon the benches, notwithstanding they were desired not to do so. A venerable raster then quietly arose, and said—" I think, if these ladies knew they had holes in their stockings, they would sit down Upon which there was great fldgetting among the ladies, and an immediate sink- ing into their seats. A young minister, who stood behind the venerable gentleman, blushing up to the temples, said—" Oh, brother, how could you say that ?" "Say that I" replied the. old man. "Why, It must be a fact • if they had not got holes in their stockings, I should like to know how they could get them on."
She—" You attended my child in its last illness, did you not, Doctor Sharpe?" " Yes " "And my first husband also ? ' "Yes." "Well, my second is ill now, and I wish you'd come and see him through."

A large number of 'Aiembers of the House of Comb mons have already paired for the session, and left town. Mr. Chamb eriain will leave town in a few days. He is goir 4on a prolonged visit to German.y, Austria, and the, Tyrol,

In the late, tutumn of last year Prince George 'of Greece contamplated a visit to ails country. It was postponed, pending his journey to India and Japan with the Ciezarewitch. The Prince has now arranged to fulfil. the engtigement on his way home through the Thailbed States. He will be in London probably at tl"..e end of this month.

A sad case of sudden death from excessive joy is 7.eported from Dusseldorf. A girl of fourteen had been promised a visit to the Siebengebirge, which is considered one of the most delightful of Rhine excursions. The prospects filled her with so much joy that the excitement produced a strain upon the heart's action, and she fell to the floor and died.

The delightfully staif allusion of the Emperor William to his " graudmamma," in his reply to the Windsor Corporation, reminds me of a story that was current some years ago when the young Prince, still quite a lad, spent a week or two with the Queen at Windsor Castle. Some kind friend (one of his uncles, I believe) took him a trip to town,and the boy's gratitude was immense. "It was not at all gay," he said, at grandmamma'sl

By a curious coincidence it is, within a day, ex- actly thirty-five years since the last occasion when a member of the House of Commons was ordered to attend in his place, warrants having been issued for his apprehension on a criminal charge. Mr. Smith on Monday night fixed Thursday, the 23rd of July, as the date on which Mr. De Cobain, member for East Belfast, should be ordered to attend in his place. It was on Thursday, the 24th of July, 1856, that James Sadlier, member for Tipperary, was ordered to appear, and, failing to submit to the order, was subsequently expelled.

The announcement that Prince George of Wales is coming home to receive a dukedom is premature and unauthorised. It is‘quite as safe to say he will be made a duke as to say he will be promoted in the Navy—some day. The mistake is in fixing the de- finite period. The Prince comes home principally on a matrimonial errand. The dukedom will fol- low, not precede, his success at the court of love. I imagine that Prince George will not have to woo for long or in vain. He is a splendid *Pllovv, and there we plenty ,of fine girls of the highest rank who would trust themselves to his care.

A workman in a tobacco manufactory at Ohlau, in Prussian Silesia, named Opens, has suddenly be- come an opulent man. Som€ fifteen years ago he received information that a rich relative had died in Peris,leaving him a large estate in Silesia. Opeus it appears, treated this as a very good joke, and heard 'nothing further of the matter. The incident faded from his memory until a few days ago,when he received intelligence that he was indeed the possessor of a legacy of 54,000 marks, and that this sum will be further increased by the intereat which had increased during the past fifteen years.

The Education Bill was read a third time in the House of Commons on Wednesday afternoon, with- out a division. Mr. Bartley, who has consistently opposed it, and has done something to improve his position in the House, made one more speech, through which he somewhat determinedly dragged the Trojan horse. It is not expected that there will be any trouble with the Education Bill in the House of Lords. Lord Salisbury probably does not like it any more than Mr. Bartley,but he recognises the situation, and is not disposed to reopen the controversy in the Commons. The Bill will be through all its stages in the Lords in the course of a wee,k.

The 'German Emperor has presented to the Queen a very elaborate oil painting of himself, in the fu/1 uniform of an admiral of the British Fleet. The picture, which is life-size, and a fine portrait of our imperial visitor, was painted at the com- mand of the Kaiser, especially as a gift to the Queen. It is in a handsome gold frame, together with which it is about 7ft. in height. The Emperor stands as a commander en the bridge of a vessel. lie has a large telescope in the right hand, and ap- pears to be gazing ahead as though looking at some distant object on the ocean. Her Majesty expressed her gratification with the present, and it will be immediately hung in a prominent place in the Royal Portrait Gallery.

There recently died in Rixdorf, in Germany, a widow, named Albert, who was considered to be rich. Her relatives were wirprised to learn, how- ever, that though she owned a flourishing hostelry no hard cash could be discovered. In realising her estate an old sofa fell, by lottery, into the handt, of a restaurateur in the neigbourhood, and in the framework of this bit of furniture were secteted 5.500 marks in gold and obligations. One of the co-heirs was present when the discovery was made, and the owner gave him 500 marks. But the other co-heirs demanded their share, This the restaura- teur refused ; for, said be, the heirloom, sofa, money box, or whatever the deceased might have styled it had come into his possession legitimateiy, and he would maintain his right to it. Legal proceedings are pending to recover the treasure.

WORK AT HOME. I quitted work the day before Christmas Day, and am now working round at home. We cut down a large fir-tree which stood at the back door. It was a shade in summer, being about two feet thick with dense foliage. We had a nest of bluebirds hatched under the roof last year, and these came each even- ing to roost in the tree. It happened to be about five o'clock in the afternoon when we got it down, and those little birds that were in it came down along with it. The next night they came flying forward to find their roost but it was gone for ever. I took it down to fix up a summer kitchen so that lwe could do in the room without a fire. I have dug out a cellar for dairy purposes; it is cooler in sum- mer and does not freeze in winter. We have planted out about 240 prunes, peaches and grapes, and we are taking out a lot of stumps to clear the land. You will see from this that there is lots of hard work about the place, and not much apparent return for it. We have six men in the wood cutting down trees for cordwood, or fire lumber. All day long one can hear the ring of the woodman's axe, and now and again a blasting as they split up a rugged old butt,too tough for the axe. I contracted with them to cut down 100 cords at a dollar per cord, and next summer we can sell the red fir for three dollars. and the white fir for two dollars. It pays for hauling to town, and brings a little re- turn by filling up an idle time for our team when they cannot work on the land. We are having fine weather, sunshine bright and clear in the day, and then frost at night. We have had considerable wet but not more than was needful. THE WESTERN LOAFER. January 25th : There is not much work at Salem just now. Every place is shut down. It is sur- prising how these western towns go dormant in the winter months. It just takes a carpenter all his time to earn enough in the summer to keep him through the winter. However, they do not, seem to mind it at all—they just go "bumming" round the saloons and stores, smoking and spitting round stoves. I wonder sometimes how you would like the way these loafers do out here. Two or three walk into a grocery store, perhaps get a plug of tobacco, and then walk straight to the stove, appro- priate the seats, place their feet up, and then spurt tobacco juice over everything. In many stores they keep a supply of wooden pokers, and these fellows actually pull out their jack-knives and whittle away at the pokers as though that were the only thing in life. I can tell you I have felt a lot disgusted with them sometimes.

Lady Laura Ridding has come forward to ex- plain the objects of the new "Woman's League," which has, she assures us, nothing akin to Land Leagues, or Primorose Leagues still less, as we gather, to women's leagues of the class which afford so much entertainment to spectators of "Husbands and Wives," the new piece at the Comedy Theatre, it has affinity, we are told, rather with the German Women's League which in the time of the Thirty years' War successfully maintained the right of the women to all opinions of their own in religious matters. In brief, it is formed to combat" the lawlessness which treats the sacredness of marriage and the reticence of modesty as obsolete tyrannical customs." It will also wage war with the greed which stints female labour of its fair reward, and the sloth which smothers the divine instinct of motherly guardian- ship over child and servant. All these aims it holds can only be accomplished by co-operation with agencies already at work. The hon. secretary of the League is Miss C. Gladstone. of 28, Eccleston-street..

Universal sympathyk. is felt with Mr. and Mrs Gladstone in the loss they have sustained by the death of their eldest son. He had been for two years in a delicate state, and though it was not expected that he would ever again be in robust health, an early or sudden termination to his life was not anticipated. Mr. W. H. Gladstone never took a very active part in politics, and his health in later years withdrew him almost entirely from public life. Though he sat for many years in Par- liament he only once or twice spoke in the House wf Commons. He was a man of cultivated and ar- tistic tastes, and of music especially he had a wide knowledge, and much of his time was devoted to its practice and cultivation. In sacred music he was deeply interested, and he composed several hymn tunes which are weekly sung in many con- gregations who do not know their author. It was to Mr. W. H. Gladstone that the Hawarden pro- perty was left, subject to the life interest of his mother. The management of the property has for many years been entirely in his hands, and it will now pass to his eldest son.

Coleridge's cottage at Clevedon, Somerset, is re- ported to be still "in good preservation," and much visited by literary enthusiasts who have read the romantic story of how the poet brought hither his young bride now hard upon a century ago. Unfortunately, however, there is no guaran- tee that it will be saved from the common fate of ordinary dwellings. Coleridge's description of it ought to pTotect it.

LOW v;as our pretty cot; our tallest rose Peeped at the chamber window. We could hear At silent noon and eve and early morn The sea's faint murmur. In the open air Our myrtles blossomed, and across the porch - Thick jasmines twined. The little village, since grown into a pleasure re- sort,on the shore of the Bristol Channel,is favoured in its literary associations. Here, in his mother's native place, lies buried Arthur Hallam, whose name, enshrined in Lord Tennyson's "In Memo- riam," can never fade from ti-e memory of English- men. It is to Clevedon that the poet refers in that pathetic and beautiful lyric—
Break. break, break, On thy cold grey stones, 0 sea!

THE EXAMINFR, SATURDAY, 9 JULY 11 IR9I. WARRINGTONIANS IN AMERICA. LETTERS FROM MR. JAMES WINSTANLEY. Mr. John Gandy, of Church-st., Warrington, has again furnished us with several interesting extracts from letters which he has received from Mr . James Winstanley, a well-known Warringtonian, who emigrated to Salem, Oregon, a few years ago. Below we give a number of these extracts, and others will be given next week. A " POISON " OAK. Writing in October last, Mr. Winstanley says: I had a walk through the woods this morning, and I wish you could see the many colours of the leaves, from the deepest crimson to the brightest yellow, with all shades of brown and dark green, the whole forming a very pretty picture. I send you a leaf or two of the "poison" oak. I do not ihink they will harm you, although I would not rub them on my face, Some people do not need to tench them to get poisoned; for I know a young lady, who, after simply walking near a bush, with the wind blowing towards her, was dreadfully bad for a week or more. In connection with this allusion to the " poison " oak, Mr. Gandy also mentions that, in a letter sent from San Francisco in April,Mr. Whitham says that one of his children, Ruby, had just recovered from the effects of the baleful tree. She had looked just like a case of small-pox, her body and face having been one mass of running sores. "The poor lass,' Mr. Whitham adds," cannot go near the park or brushwood without catching it, aud her head swells to almost twice its natural size." CHRISTMAS IN THE FAR WEST. On January llth,Mr. Winstantly writes : Another Christmas in the Far West, quiet and happy. Edith spent the day in town and the boys went shooting until dinner. Then we hauled some logs to the river, and turned them over the bank. Thus was our Christmas Day spent. There was Christmas Day at each of the schools, and most of the families hang their presents to each other on the tree, and it you wish to give to a friend it is a nice oppor- tunity to surprise them. The families subscribe 50 cents, or one dollar each, for candies. It is put in sacks with their names on them, and that is a" there is of Christmas.

div.head: REMINISCENCES.
div.p: REMINISCENCES.

February 9th : This time last year we were in a flood. There is at present no sign of anything of that sort, and, I assure you, it is not wanted at all. Once in a life time is plenty of that sort of ' thing. We had a little snow this morning----just sprinkling. It is the only snow we have had this winter, and I think it is getting too late y have much now. ,Still there seems to be plenty on the 1 mountains, and if warm weather comes we shall have plenty of water in the river. February 22nd: I have been very sick for two weeks, but am glad to say I am all right now, though not quite so strong ae,l ought to be. All the rest of our little flock are in good health; al- though we are having some dreary weather. February is undoubtedly the worst month in the year. I was led to some curious thoughts by your reminding me that the place that knows us now will shortly know us no more, and that for ever. Poor I My thoughts weht back to school ' days, and travelled along while some might-have- beens kept cropping up each now and again. There is no sympathy out here for anyone: everybody haa to rustle' as they call it, and he who can rustle most gets most dollars. However, as I said before, lam content; and if I did not live in Ore- gon, well, I should want to.

div.head: ROYAL WEDDING AT WINDSOR.
div.p: THE ROYAL WEDDING AT WINDSOR.

The marriage of Prince Aribert, youngest son of the Duke and Duchess of Anhalt, and Princess Louise of Schleswig-Holstein, younger daughter of the Prince and ?rincess Christian, was solemnized on Monday afternoon it St. Georges's Chapel, Windsor Castle, in the presence of her Majesty the Queen, the Emperor and Empress of Germany, the Prince and Princess of Wales, and many other members of the Royal family. Several hours be- fore the time fixed for the ceremony immense crowds had collected in the Windsor streets eager to catch a glimse of the Royal personages as they passed on their way from the Castle to the Chapel. The Archbishop of Canterbury officiated.
CARLOW ELECTION.-NATIONALIST VICTORiC.

The polling of Carlow commenced at eight o'clock on Tuesday morning. There were 17 voting stations for nine districts. namely :—Bagnalstown Borris, Carlow, Fanagh, Nuphall, Tullow, Rathvilly, and Clonegal. The three chief districts are Carlow, Bagnalstown,and Borris. There were three polling stations in each. Four hundred extra police were doing duty. Mr. Hammond and Mr. Kettle, the latter accotppanied by Mr. Yarnell, made a tour of the constituency. _ -
The ballot boxes were brought to Carlow on Tuesday night.
The countihg of the voted took place on'-Wednesday at the Courthouse, Carlow, and the result was declared as follows :
Mr. Hammond (Nationalist) Mr. Kettle (Parnellite)

Nationalist majority The announcement was received with great cheering. Mr. Parnell, speaking subsequently at Mi.. Kettle's cen- tral committee rooms, said he should raise the issue at every by-election, and at the general election, and if beaten he should form his Carlow, Kilkenny, and Sligo supporters into a solid rallyine, square. There was some disturbance at the railway station on his departure for Dublin. - •

The last contested election was in 1885 when the 6.ie Mr. Edward Dwyer Gray, proprietor of the "Freeman's Journal" was elected. The figttros on that occasion were: —E. D. Gray 4,801 ; Sir Thomas P. Butler, Bart, (C.), 751 ; majority,4,oso. At a by-election in 1687 The O'Gorman Mahon (N.), the late member, was returned unopposed.

div.head: ACROSS THE ATLANTIC (No. 5.) !LETITIA THORNTON.
div.p: ACROSS THE ATLANTIC (No. 5.) !LETITIA THORNTON.
BY "TOWNSMAN." ON THE CARS. (Concluded.)
THE SCENERY-A GREAT MANUFACTURING DIS- TRICT - DIXIE'S LAND - THE UNITED STATES AGAIN-INCIDENTS OF THE JOURNEY-DINING EN
ROUTE - JUVENILE TRAVELLERS - THE ENGINES
ANT) CARS.

On we go at a speed of about 30 miles an hour, through open country, through cities of all sizes, across rivers, up mountain sides, along ravines. It is rather early in the year for agriculture, as the winter has been a hard and long one, and although it is the month of May the farmers in the State of Massachusetts are only just beginning to drag their ploughs into the light of day, and to drive them through the earth. It is a fear- fully stoney State, and one wonders how the farmers scratch a living out of such soil. On enquiry you learn it is not much of a farming State, and you are not sur- prised at it. We are travelling on the West Shore Rail- road, and after about four hours running from Boston we dash into the Hoosac tunnel, cut through a gigantic mountain for a distance of five miles. It is lighted , throughout its length by electricity, and as you sit in the rear car and look down its length, at the countless electric lights, the effect is exceedingly weird and pictur- esque. Formerly travellers had to cross the mountain in buggies, and the distance over it was some 13 miles. On emerging from the tunnel, the train runs for miles along; the serpentine course of a broad shallow river, past im- mense cle,arings,and through lumbering districts where the steam saws are making short work of forest giants. But the scenery is not such as to call for remark, perhaps the only prettily situated city on a long run being Little Falls, a city which romantically rears its head amid num- erous tall crags that jut out of a hill side and a river bed. As we speed west we run thorough a GREAT MANUFACTURING DISTRICT. Firptly comes Frankfort with its iron-works, Utica with its cotton and woollen mills, Syracuse with its im- mense salt works that cover hundreds of acres, Roches- ter noted for its boots and shoes, and Buffalo renowned for a diversity of industries and as a trading centre. Some of these cities cover great areas, and vary in population from 50,000 to 150,000. Many of them have a great number of Germans in their midst, andsßuffalo is espec- ially remarkable in this respect. This city has developed wonderfully of late. Situated at the head of Lake Erie, it does an immense carrying trade, is a home of the lum- bering industry, and will be a great distributing centre. Already it has surprising railway interests, and acres upon acres are covered with rolling stock, that show the im- portance of the city as a general commercial centre. On leaving Buffalo we sweep along the river to Niagara. catch a glimpse of the world-renowned cataract, and glide into Suspension Bridge Station. Here we change cars, and enter a train of the Canadian Grand Trunk Railway, in which we continue to our destination. No such recklessness, however, as characterised the immor- tal Eliza Harris, as she leaped into the Land of Liberty is now permissible, for the connecting links between the American States and Canada is a fragile looking structure known as the Suspension Bridge. It is a great height over the surging waters beneath, and trains just crawl across it at snail's pace—seemingly like an elephant which, fearful of treacherous ground, puts out his foot to test the road before advancing another step. But at length we are over the slender-looking bridge; and enter- ing once again the Queen's dominions find ourselves in Canada,

div.head: BY LOUISA BIOG. AUTHOR OF " CLARE WELSMAN," ETO.
div.p: BY LOUISA BIOG. AUTHOR OF " CLARE WELSMAN," ETO.
CHAPTER I.

One cold winter evening Mary Preston was sit- ting by her cottage fire busily NA orkiug. It was a rough night, and the wind rattled the easements, and slmok the outer door as if it would force its way in, despite bolts and locks. A light sleet was falling and struck the panes of glass as if some fairy host was storming the cottage with volleys of tiny artillery. But Mary sat unmoved amid the clamour and smiled from time to time as she arranged and re-arranged her work, and looked critically at it, tirst ftom one side and then from the other. It was a long white garment of extra- ordinary proportions; so small was the body and so long the skirt that it seemed designed for a being with a most extravagant length of limb. There was one sleeve to be put in, and then it would be finished, and Mary stitched away with redoubled energy as she heard the clock strike seven. What a cheerful sound the clock had, and what a bright cottage it was. I can guess the , image that will rise to some of my readers' minds at the word cottage—it wil: bring before them a dirty floor ; foul odours ; a line aeross the room, with damp clothes hanging from it; a table slopped with tea, and greasy with unnumbered meals ; chairs that the visitor dares not sit down upon; a universal muddle and waste; the whole establishment fitted up as special purveyor to the public house. There are, indeed, a pestilent array of such cottages as these, but they are as different to Nlary Preston's as purgatory to para- dise. Her floor was spotlessly clean with a bright rug stretched before the fire; her old oaken press,_ and high-backed chairs shone with frequent rub- bing ; her large deal table was white as scrubbing brush could make it; and there was as perceptible an air of comfort over all as there could be in the costliest of dining-rooms. A woman's hand was evident On all sides, and there were not wanting artistic touches here and there in the shape of a branch of red leaves and berries on the window sid, another on the oak press, and a few pictures on the wall. One of the latter represented a young lady in a straw hat and white bodice, with a neck- lace of amber beads twined round her throat, and Mary considered it very much like Miss Lwtitia Thornton, the heiress at the large house close at hand, and'had given it the place of hoLour by the old el,,ck. _ _

Nary was holding out before her the mysterious garment, now completed, with dainty trimming at tie neck and sleeves, and imagining the empty arm-holes filled with little arms, when she heard a footstep coming along the path. Her tender fancy had flied her eyes with tears, and she hastily wiped them away, hid her work in a large basket, and ran to open the door. "Here's a rough night, lass," cried a cheery voice out cf the darkness, and in a moment the speaker appeared in sight with his brown whiskers white with the sleet, and a rosy colour, while Bob, his sedate sheep-dog followed in his wake.

"Why how quick the time has gone," said Mary, "I couldn't have believed it was half-past seven I haven't got supper anything like ready, and you must be hungry, Tom !" "And what have you been doing, missis, that you have forgotten Bob and me !" asked the young shephe•d. Mary vouchsafed no direct answer, but laughed and blushed, and began to be very busy making Bob wipe his broad wet feet, and pretending to scold him for marking her floor. "You shall rub them clean, Bob," she cried, " or else I'll shut you up in the empty pig-sty ;" and Bob submitted with the air of a dog who was conscious of being off duty, ant so able to humour the caprices of his mistress without undue loss of dignity. The Prime Ministet sometimes permits himself to joke, and Bob felt that even the most responsible sheep-dog may unbend occasionally in his leisure moments. Tom Preston settled down by his fireside and began warming his hands over the red blaze, while Bob laid himself on the rts!, his hors_ st face beam. ing with satisfaction, and would have wagged his tail, had he not been deprived of that useful appendage in his early youth. The tabby cat, who has been sitting on a wooden stool, now descended, and began running round her master's legs, and Mary bustled about the room preparing supper foi the family party. She was in the act of setting a smoking slew on the table, when a knock at the door made her start and almost drop the dish. " Who tnAn that be?" she cried, and without waiting for her slower husband to stir, she ran out! and opened the door, with a chill dread that some messsnger of evil stood outside, so unasual was a call at the cottage at that late hour. A man was sf amling on the doorstep ! " Can you tell me the way to the Firs ? " he nsiced, and Mary who was still rather flurried, called her husband out, though in her ordinary state of mind she could have given the necessary direct ion with perfect case. 'You must go along the lane at the back and cross Brook's meadow, and then you'll be in the road as leads straight to the house, said Tom. " Oh, of course," said the stranger coming into the light, "I remember now ; it was Brook's meal() sr that bothered me, and I have been wan- dering up and down the lane for ever so long with- out being able to get out. I thought I knew the way, though I have not been here for ten years, and in the daylight I should have known. Thank, you, I shall be all right now." Won t.yo t walk in and rest, sir?" asked Tom with the simple politeness and hospitality of his class, for he saw by the stranger's muddy and damp clothes that he had made a long journey on foot. "Thank you very much," said he, "I must not wait, though you look very comfortable, and smell very comfortable, too," he added, laughingly eye- ing.the savoury stew. "They will think at the Firs that I am lost, which is not far from the truth, so goed-night." " I do believe," said Mary when the door closed behind him, "that it is Miss Lwtitias cousin come from foreign parts. "Is he a soldier„ then !" said Tom, "he does favour them in his looks." ,
"No," answered Mary, "Bridget at the Firs told me about him; he isn't a suldier, but he ho.s something to do with the wars."

div.head: CHAPTER H.
div.p: CHAPTER H.

Mary Preston was right in her conjecture. It was Robert Dillon, the grandson of old Mr. Ililion, Who used to live in Hampton, Mid second cousin to Miss Letitia Thornton, wao lived at the Firs. There had been some coolness between the families, and he had not seen his cousins since Ltetitia was a a child. Now he had resolved to look up his old relatives, and had run clown from London on pur- pose to see the Thorntons, but with a vague idea of what he should find on his arrival. "I used not to care much about Cousin Priscy when I was EC boy,' he soliloquised as he made his way across Brook's meadow. "She was so confoundedly pre- cise, but Ltitia ought to have grown up a pretty girl; she had a sweet little face and yellow hair when I saw her last, and now she must be—let me see—ten and twelve—she must be two-and- twenty." It was such a dark night that Dillon almost ran , ao.iinst the pillars of the portico, before he realised that he had arrived at the Firs, and the servant who answered the ring told him that the ladies had iven him up for the night and had begun dinner. Telling her not to disturb them, he asked to go' at once to his room, where he hastily pulled otf his muddy garments, and in an incredibly short spite of time emerged in trim evening cosLume. The fact is that during the last five years he had made his toilet under such strange and divers cir- cumstances, and often with such enforced rapidity that he might have sustained "character part " with considerable credit now that he was again in England. on entering the dinin7-room he was conscious of a flood of soft, light, of the glow and perfume of flowers, of a glitter of silver, and glass and white linen, and oat the presence of an elderly lady, a young lady, and a entleman whom he could not account for, but who headed the table and seemed quite at home. , "how do you do, Robert," said Miss Priscilla, "we are glad to see you at the Firs " you will remember your cousin—LaAitia—our friend Mr. Delatield." L.Ttitia looked shyly and pleasantly at the young man, and Mr. Delafield bowed rather stiffly and looked as if he could have dispensed very well with this addition to the party, though he was a good looking young fellow enough, whom most people thought it a pleasure to look at. "What a long time it is since we saw you," said Priscillia, who was a little single lady of about fifty who had lived with L.Ttitia ever since she was a child of seven. "We have all got older since we met last." "I am sure you - have not," said Dillon, "you have haven't altered a bit, cousin Priscy ; I am twenty sears older with_ knocking about

the world and getting trozen and burnt by turn.- " And Lwtitia is altered," said Priscy, "snould you have known her?" "Oh, yes, I should have known her anywhere." "She is not quite so pretty as I expected," he thought to himself, "but it is a face to remember, and 1 like the look of her." " We were afraid you had lost your way," said Ltetitia. " I did ; but I was rescued by a kindly couple in a cottage just below your grounds. "Oh, that must have been the Prestons," said Miss Priseilla,, "I do not know much of them, for they are too well off to need any help, but they seem very tidy people." " Have you been long in England ?" asked Mr. Delafield of Dillon. " I think Miss Thornton said you went through the late war " Yes ; I am on the Chronicle, and have been out for them three times." "We are to have some fighting in Afghanistan, they say, so I suppose you will he obliged to be off again," said Mr. Delafield. He was a gentlemanly man of middle height, with close dark hair and regular features without much expression; the kind of man whom you may meet any day in a railway train, where you probably would exchange, bland commonplaces with iim about the weather and the crops and then forget all about him. "No, I think not; I have had about enough of it,' answered Dillon, his face clouding. "It must be exciting work," said Miss Priscilla; "But is it not very uncomfortable?" "At times very," he said, laughing. "I believe I have slept on every bed that was ever invented, and often on no bed at all, and once or twice I have been in places where horseflesh was a luxury and dogs at a premium." When dinner was ended, they all rose from the table and went into the. drawing-room. Mr. Dela- field followed L.Ttitia to the piano, and they were soon deep in the examination of some new songs which had come home that morning, leaving Dillon to the care of Miss Priscilla. "Mr. Delafield is one of Lvetitia's trustees," she volunteered to Dillon, "and he often comes over to see us, and is very kind in advising us; he lives _- about two miles off, at Wingate House." "Oh, indeed." "Do not you think it would be a very suitable connection ?" whispered Priscilla, in an unusual burst of confidence, for she was pleased with Dillon, and had at once adopted him as a relation. "I really cannot judge, said Dillon a little coolly ; "did I understand you then, that Mr. Delafield—that Lzetitia—" "Oh no, there is nothing settled, nothing at all, and you must not mention it for the world, only between ourselves, I think it extremely probable.' And Miss Priscilla began to busy herself with the tea-cups while Dillon waited on her, discreetly leaving the other couple to their own devices. But the speech set him thinking about Lwtitia more than he would otherwise have done. There was some music, including some Russian Folkslieder from Dillon and a few pages of Beethoven from La3titia, who vowed she had a cold and could not sing, and then Mr. Delafield went away. The others sat chatting for some time over the fire, till Miss Priscilla declared that it was bedtime and ordered up the candles. "We have breakfast at half-past eight, Robert. I hope that will not be too early for you ?" said she. "All times suit me," he answered. "What an accommodating disposition," said Lmtitia., laughing, and handing him a candle;. "you are used to savages and are just the person to come to us on a visit, for you see we have no gas and are very primitive in our habits." " What a shame that she should be thrown away on that old fellow 1" was Dillon's last reflection before he fell fast asleep in the large white bed allotted him.

div.head: lIISTORIC DIXIRS LAND
div.p: THE lIISTORIC DIXIRS LAND

After the inevitable Customs examination, we pro- ceeded on our journey to St. Catherine's and Hamilton. The vegetation in Canada was a trifle more advanced than the portion of the U.S.,we had traversed, and the farms seemed in better trim, the fields better cultivated, and altogether showed a degree of finish that was totally lacking in the great Republic's northern states. The scenery, too, was brighter and more picturesque, and to me this run across Ontario was tile pleasantest part of the trip. We journeyed by the woods where the famous Benwell tragedy was enacted, and pulled up in Woodstock where Birchall paid the penalty for his mis- deeds. At London, a considerable Canadian city, I made enquiries for Mr. Wm. Littler, formerly of Runcorn,but learned he had left the city. At Sarnia the train was run bodily on to a boat, and ferried across a swiftly , flowing river that connects Lakes Huron and Erie to Port I Huron in the United States. Here we turned in for the night and were very nearly asphyxiated by what a local journal truly described as "the death-dealing rail- road car stove." About 9 p.m. the conductor came along, closed every ventilator' in the car, and then poked the smouldering contents of the car stove. This performance he repeated about every hour, until the car was filled with vile fumes , and vitiated air. The result was that next day I felt more dead than alive. I seemed unable to raise my head, or to totter along ; my appetite was quite s.Y.one,and I cannot say when I felt more miserable than I did for two full days after that night's experience with the abominable stove. Next morning at seven o'clock a coloured gentleman came through the cars distributing handbills, informing the passengers that "breakfast is now ready in the dining car attached to this train. A full first-class meal only 75 cents. Try it. Remember,4 this train does not stop for meals."

_ . .. . Dining Car. _ Hour after hour we steamed through the FLAT AGRICULTURAL TERRITORY

of Michigan, Indiana and Illinois, the monotony of the journey being broker:by stoppages at cities on our route. Vast farmsteads dotted the landscape,but very little stock was to be seen on the farms. As we neared ow destina- tion we were interested in seeing cities-yet-to-be, staked out in the prairie, all the houseless and tenantless streets and avenues being lined with trees and sidewalks laid out all through the embryo cities. Here and there small manufacturing cities were being " boomed," and next to the manufactory, the most prominent building was that of the daily newspaper office. At length the smoke of the

div.head: QUEEN CITY OF THE WEST
div.p: QUEEN CITY OF THE WEST
drew in sight, and in another hour we were safely de- posited in the streets of a remarkable city, " the city of destiny," respecting which I may say a few words in a subsequent letter.
INCIDENTS OF THE JOURNEY.

A striking feature in American travel is the number of young children who travel long distances with their parents. In many cases the mothers alone accompany the families, and they seem to think lightly of a night journey. But it is when night comes that the presence of the children is so very evident. During the day the juveniles are interested in looking through the window or playing on the cars, but when evening shades appear and their little eyes get heavy, then the elder travellers have to suffer. Those who can't afford to pay Bs. for a night's rest rough it in the day car, but their efforts, to sleep are frustrated by the children. They cry for mamma, then for papa, and finally they cry in chorus, and they manage to make things lively all the night through. Next morning the poor things are fretful and some of them decidedly cross, and the adult occupants of the train are heartily glad when the little disturbers leave the car.
THE ENGINES AND CARS.

About every eight hours on the journey, the train changes engines and then rushes on to the next stage, where another change is effected. During the day dining cars arc attached to fast trains that do not stop for luncheon, but the prices are very stiff, and not many passengers. avail themselves of the privilege. Most of the passengers provision themselves beforehand,or jump out hurriedly when the train stops, and raid the re- freshment room of the depot. As evening comes on sleep- ing cars are also taken on, but here too the price, Bs., is rather too high, and many respectable persons prefer to save their dollars and rough it. At least one sleeping car runs through the whole journey, and thus saves those who can afford to pay the necessity of changing cars. It is very pleasant to sitin the roomy comfortable cars, and gaze out at the surrounding 'scenery, but the very frequent unnecessary opening of the doors by the newsboy and others admits clouds of dust and passengers gers get very dirty by the time a long journey is con- cluded.

div.head: CHAPTER 111.
div.p: CHAPTER 111.

The next morning was magnificently frosty and sunshiny. The sleet of last night had hardened in.o crisp white ice, and the roads were perilously slippery, and the fields glistening with a thousand diamonds. There wis not a cloud visible in the sky, and the air was as still and clear as in sum- mertime. Dillon found Ltetitia in the breakfast- room when he came down, with a charming colour in her pale cheeks. "I hope you are fend of skating," she said, "thee is a capital sheet of ice down in the village, and it bears well ; I have just been down to see." " I like it immensely," he answered, "but it is so long since I had the chance of any that you will find me very clumsy. I'm afraid, and despise me." "I am sure you need not be afraid of me," said Izetitia, demurely, "and you will get into it directly, I have no doubt." Miss Priscilla now entered with every soft grey curl in its place, and her serene air unaltered by the cold. She was a little lady who despised the contemporary world for the rate at which it was travelling, and had a savour of the good old school, in her quiet dignity, though she had been born well on in the present century. The young ladies, the young gentlemen, the shopkeepers, and the clergy of modern growth all came under the ban of her mild displeasure. "You are all in such a bustle, my dear," she would say sometimes to a scion of the new school. Jessie Grayson, her own clergyman's sister, for instance. "You are all in such a bustle that no- body has time for anything, and yet, I cannot see what it all comes to."

"We are' getting very clever, for one thing, Miss Prisailla," Jessie would answer, and "we are being wranglers. and lawn tennis champions and all sorts of things that you never thought of." "But you can none of you curtsey properly, or write a good letter, and as to conversation you can none of you talk fit to be heard. The clergy too! Wily look at your brother—a very good young man I admit, and a great favourite of mine, but where is his clerical dignity? I see him lying about in all weathers, and I wonder he does not realize that these constant col ections in the churches are destructive of all real devotion. In my young days the vicar was a personage to be looked up to, and not a play-fellow of the choir boys.' Jessie would laughingly continue her defence of the party of pro. gress, but Miss Priscilla was not to be convinced, and hal a fixed idea teat; the whole civilised world was rapidly deteriorating. Lxtitia had caught so much of her cousin's spirit as to make her more reflective and less brusque than the girl of the period ususlly is, or rather her cousin's influence had developed her natural tendencies. Her solitary life had also nourished a dreamy enthusiasm in her, which tinctured her views of life and made her shrink from the commonplace world and its rough ways, and dwell to a large extent in a secret world of her own, ruled by lofty thoughts and peopled with heroes. She and Dillon set off in good time for the pond, and thoroughly enjoyed the skating. There were several of her friends there, and Dillon made his way with them at once, and after the first few minutes was quite at home on his skates, and was busy helping everybody. "Where did you find such a jolly cousin, LlBtitia ?" asked Jessie Grayson; "Isis moustache alone has taken me captive, and what lovely eyes! I tell you what, now, I have only just thought of it, but he is exactly my idea of a Crusader! How should like to see him in a long white garment with a red cross on his breast 1 Can't we get up some charades?" "I am afraid there is not time, for be only stays till to-morrow," said Lretitia. latighing. Jessie was a pretty and energetic little body, and irre- pressible when she had once taken an idea into her head, so she went on—" Then why not to-night? Lei us think it out this morning and act it this
evening." "Nonsense, Jessie, it is impossible. Besides I do not think he would care for it, even if there WAS time."

"Is• he serious, then?" asked Jessie, looking rather disconsolate, for she was used to carry her ulans, and did not like to be refused, "has he got erotenets tie looks just the sort of young man te waut to set the world to rights." Do you think so," said Lmtitia, looking at her with a new ideerest. "I wonder if he does." That was just the kind of hero to suit Ltetitia.'s imagination, but in the short time of her acquaint- ance with Dillon, he• had struck her as merely. pleasant,and intelligent, and she had not suspected him of any more depth of character. than Mr. Delatield, who floated moit respectably with the stream, or Tom Jenkinson, who had aspired to her hand, and whose whole being was centred in getting "a position." These latter, and more of her in- timates, she had soundeA with a quiet contempt, and was growing somewhat cynical with regard to the male character, and slew to accept outward attractions. She wanted no lover, she thought, hut an heroic friend she did want, being fatherless and brotherless, and having a great store of latent faith and love and devotion.

" What does your cousin do?" asked Jessie when they had watched Dillon for a moment in silence as he swept round the opposite end of the pon.l with Jessie's youngest sister under his win..." "He is special correspondent to the Chronicle." "How charming," cried Jessie; "I never saw .n.e in my life befere !. and was it really he that

I wrote those dreadful stories last spring about their I burning the villages and cutting up the babies! To think of his skating here just like other people, and just see how he is making Effie laugh!" Dillon came up to them and deposited Effie under her sister's care. " What time is it, Robert ?" asked Ltitia, " I left my watch at home." "J ist one." "Then we ought to go in to lunch, for Cousin Priscy is as punctual as clockwork." "J ust take two turns with me before we leave," said he, and Letitia hesitated and then yielded. As they flew round the wide pond, over the glassy black ice, with her Little clinging hands in his, Dillon was seized with a keen regret as he thought how much he had lost in not having known Letitia earlier; how natural she was; how fresh and well-bred! What a sweet cousiuship theirs might have been! But now, as circumstances had willed it, they were almost strangers, and to- morrow he must turn out again into the wide world and lose sight of her, and she would no doubt become Mrs. Delaiield. "How have you got on ?" asked Miss Priscilla, when they appeared, glowing with exercise, at the luncheon table. "I have had one of the pleasantest mornings I ever had in my life, and I am afraid my appetite will astonish you," answered Dillon. "And cousin Robert skates splendidly," said Letitia, "a great deal better than I can or ever shall."

"What a pretty village yours is," said Dillon. "And haven't we got some pretty girls ?" said Lmtitia, who happened to be at that moment thinking what a charming picture Jessie Grayson and her sister and Carry Jenkinson had made, gliding round the pond hand in hand with their bright dresses and bonny faces. "Indeed you have," answered Dillon with a mischievous look into her eyes, "but I found that out last night." ',Letitia laughed gaily, but she was wondering all the while whether Jessie was right about him, and whether he was anything more than " l'homme moyen sensuel ;" she has as yet seen nothing in him to betoken it; except perhaps a certain sad- ness that crept over his features in repose. But ten she had seen Tom Jenkinson look much the same, and had discovered through his sister Carry, a young lady by no means reticent on family matters, that the grief oppressing his soul was a heavy tailor's bill, or a stroke of bad luck at billiards. There is a modern picture which represents the god Pan, bending over a rough stone toward Psyche, who pale and forlorn, is looking up at him with a strange yearning in her face; has she lost some treasure, or has she the intuition of some ineffable good as yet unfound? The last, I think; and it was such a look that Letitia from time to time that day fixed upon Dillon. Once or twice he saw it, and it puzzled him sorely. (To be continued.)
LANCASHIRE AND TriE GENERAL ELECTION.

The position of Lancashire in anticipation of the general election is peculiarly interesting. It con- tains fifty-four constituencies returning fifty-eight members, and four boroughs having two members each. At present it is represented, as to the boroughs, by eight Liberals, twenty-six Conserva- tives, and one Dissentient Liberal; as to the county divisions by seven Liberals, fifteen Conservaties, and one Dissentient Liberal. Eleven of the boroughs and nine county divisions now held by Ministerial- ists, will certainly be fought at the general election, candidates being already in the field. Candidates are still wanted for sixteen borough seats and seven county seats. Since the general election two seats have been won in Lancashire from the Ministerial- ists—Eccles from the Conservatives, and Barrow from the Dissentient Liberals. A careful estimate of the probable chances promises twelve more seats to be won at the general election.

div.head: ROYAL ROMANCE OF ROUMANIA.
div.p: THE ROYAL ROMANCE OF ROUMANIA.

A Bucharest telegram contradicts the report of the projected betrothal of Prince Ferdinand, heir to the Roumanian Throne,and Mademoiselle Vacarescu, one of the Queen's Maids of Honour. The story of the loves of Prince Ferdinand and rslctlle. Vacarecu, which has just been cruelly nipped in the bud, is the topic of the day in the fashionable circles of Paris, where the young lady was well-known. In this prosaic age it is so rare to come across anything like a real romance, that one feels sorry (writes a Paris correspondent) that the young couple were not allowed to bring their adventure to the traditional happy termination, instead of being separated, and living for ever after- wards in sorrow and despair But Royalty is no respecter of romance, and, in spite of what the poet says, love does not always rule the Court. It is true Mdlle. Vacarescue is not of Royal blood, but she is of good family, and possesses charms both intellectual and personal. She has also attracted the favourable attention of Queen Victoria, as well as of the Queen of her own country. Politics, however, stepped in and pro- nounced the projected nuptials impossible. King Charles, it appears, was not altogether opposed to it, and, like the Queen, felt for the lovers; in fact, he apologetically remarked that the Prince had evi- dently set his mind on the match; but his advisers said," Well, sire, lie can marry as he wishes; but if he does, he will never reign, and the marriage will be fatal to your dynasty." This settled the matter eo far as the King and his Ministers were concerned and although the people objected that the union of the heir-presumptive with a born Roumanian would be popular, it was there and then vetoed. The Prince, on learning this decision, threatened t,o throw up his succession to the throne in order to marry hi 3 lady-love, and a strict watch was kept over the couple lest they should elope ; but his Highness, on reoovering from his disappointment. thought better of it,and promised to obey his uncle. Prince Ferdinand was sent on a voyage, and Mdle. Vacarescu, according to the latest accounts, will withdraw to Russia on a handsome pension by way of consolation. Here the romance ends.

div.head: TERRIBLE WIFE MURDER.
div.p: TERRIBLE WIFE MURDER.

A DESPERATE STRUGGLE. A terrible murder was committed in Smith's-buildings, Bermondsey, on Saturday. Robert Bradshaw, aged 54, and his wife Emma, aged 51, have resided at number 24 in the buildings forsome time. The man, it is said, had more than once assaulted his wife, and a day or two ago she obtained a summons against him at Southwark Police Court. On Saturday the warrant officer called and left the summons. After his departure Bradshaw said to his wife, "Well, you won't be able to appear at the Court on Monday." Shortly afterwards he almost cut off his wife's head with a razor. He then left the house, and meeting Police Constable Wm. Archer said, "I was just going to the police station to give myself up, for I have murdered my old woman." He was conveyed to Grange- road Police Station. The police, on reaching the room, found Mrs. Bradshaw lying on her back dead, with a gash in her throat. Blood despattered the room in all directions, and the woman appeared to have had a strOggle with her murderer. When charged at the station he said, " Quite right. I have done it." It is said that deceased's married daughter called at the liuse shortly after the warrant officer left, and her father told her also that she would not be able to go to the court on Monday. Shortly afterwards she had to go home, and probably thus =aped a terrible fate.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY AFFAIR IN IRELAND.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY AFFAIR IN IRELAND.
A GHASTLY DISCOVERY.

It has been ascertained that the body of Mr. Arthur Thompson, late petty sessions clerk of Derrylin, county Fermanagh, had been buried in his own garden for four months, and Mrs. Thompson, his daughter-in-law, who is in custody, is alleged to have adopted the most extraor- dinary measures to conceal the fact of his death, in order to secure his pension. On the medical men examining the remains they found that every bone:in the body had been broken. There was a fearful fracture on the skull. The arms, legs, feet, shoulders, and literal' every bone in the body were smashed apparently by a hatchet as regards the legs, but a saw seems to have been used on the hands and wrists. After all this process of mutilation had been gone through there were evident signs that—a most determined attempt had been made to burn the body, as the legs, arms, and head, and in fact the whole landy bore remarkable traces of burning. When the rector called to have the deceased's pension paper signed, Mrs. Thompson used to make a pretence of going 91)- stairs to the old gentleman, but last week the rector in- sisted on seeing him, and then she made her escape. vigorous search was commenced all over the deceaed house and farm, no drains or alley being left unnoticed, and, indeed, the flooring of one of the rooms was actually lifted. Late in the evening, when all hopes of retov ing the body had been given up, the head constable dis- covered it buried under a rose tree in about three feet deep of earth. The accused is well connected.

'the Paving and Sewerage Committee stated in their minutes that the owners of property adjoining Howley Brook, with the exception of two, have agreed to con- street a new street according to plans prepared by the Borough Surveyor; and they resolved therefore, that a sewer be constructed down the cetre of such new street, and that so much of Howley Brook as is co-extensive with such street be filled up, and, further, that the Corpora- tion contribute so much of the cost, according to the award of Mr. William Owen, of laying out the new street co-extensive with the land of the owners who have re- fused to make such street, and that a fence be erected on the boundary of the property belonging to such owners. The Committee also recommended as follows :—That the tender of Mr. Wm. Williams for constructing new pipe sewer in Howley, according to plans and specification, at £55975. 11d., be accepted; t at Horsemarket-st. from Market-gate to Lyme-st. be re-laid with dressed Newry setts; that the tender of the Wigan Coal and Iron Co., Limited, for the supply of slack during the next three months, at ss. per ton, be accepted; that the .tender of the Municipal Appliances Co., to supply a 75-gallon pitch boiler. at £22, be accepted; that the tender of Mr. F.J. Dell, for the painting 'of Storekeeper's house at Howley, at £l3 10s., be accepted. Alderman WRIGHT moved the adoption of the minutes and, in answer to Councillor Pierpoint, he .said they should certainly not proceed with regard to the new street unless the whole of the agreements referred to with the owners of land were signed. The minutes were then adopted.

div.head: SCISOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE
div.p: SCISOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE

This Committee's minutes contained the following : The report of the Inspector was read from which it ap- peared that 21 cases had been inquired iuto by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 23 cases for 53 children. That 47 cases had been taken before the magistrates, and fines inflicted in 37 cases, 2 bows sent to the" Clio," 1 girl to St. Elizabeth R.C. School, Liver- 'pool, and seven cases adjourned. The average attend- ance at the Public Elementary Schools, during the month of May was 7,655; corresponding period last year, 7,762. Decrease 97.
Councillor FLEMING moved the adoption. Councillor SHAW GRENN seconded.
- Councillor CANNELL asked if the fact that the whole of the Committee or a portion of it that were going away were going at their own expenses or that of the Corporation.

Councillor FLEMING declined to answer this question, as the matter was not on the minutes. Councillor 6ANNELL said he asked because on one oc- casion they were told by the Town Clerk that they could not question such an account after it was passed. The CHAIRMAN said the practice of the Council when- ever a deputation from a Coinmitte was appointed to go to some other town for inspection purpose, these ex- penses were invariably paid by the Council. (Cries of "hear, hear.") ' The minutes were adopted.
MUSEUM, LIBRARY, ARTS AND TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION
COMMITTEE . -TECHNICA L . EDUCATION . '.-COUNCILLOR H.
ROBEETS AND THE TEACHING OF BREWING.

Return for the month of May: Visitors to the Museum 2,395, decrease 11 per cent.; books issued in reading- roam 922, slight increase; books issued in lending department 2,374, increase 14 per cent. compared with May, 1890. The following gifts were contributed for which the thanks of till? Committee were ordered to be sent to the donors :—Fragment of horn of red deer, and fragments of Roman pottery, found at Thelwall, from Mr. Percy Davies; tokens of H. Atherton, of Ormskirk, 1671; and Robert Markland, of Wigan, 1655, from Mr. Nathan Heywood ; nests of sandpiper and corncrake and four eggs, frem Mr. J. A. Jackson; "The Microcosm" and other books (3 vols.), from Mr. R. Pierpoint ; "Wire, its Manufactures and Uses," by Smith, from the Author; Year Books of Scientific Societies, 1891, from the Literary and Philosophical Society. A letter from the National Gallery was read, stating that the Director agreed to the request of the Committee that the Turner drawings should remain here for a second year from September next. The remainder of the minutes dealing with the subject of technical education have already appeared in our columns. Mr. C. H. ROBERTS moved the adoption of the minutes. They contained, he maid, some important matters refer- ring, more particularly to the question of technical edu- cation, the carrying out of which would, of necessity, in- volve a considerable outlay. He gave the Council the assurance of the Committee that it was not their inten- tion to involve themselves in the expenditure contem- plated until they were assured on reliable bases that they would have from the County Council such a grant as would, with the assistance of the fe?.s and Govern- ment grant, enable them to carry out the work. The reason they were getting their programme ready, was that the time was limited, and they wished to get their operations complete for the winter which will shortly be upon us. In regard to the subjects included in the pro- gramme the Committee would be glad to give considera- tion to any suggestions that might be made. Councillor PIERPOINT seconded the motion for adop- tion.

Alderman GREENALL asked whether there had been before the Committee the subject of the advisability of opening the Museum and Library on Sundays. Councillor BOLTON said he was surprised at the incon- sistency of Countillor H. Roberts in consenting to brew- ing being one of the subjects proposed to be taught. Alderman HARRISON said he was glad to hear Mr. Councillor H. Roberts say that the Committee had no intention of committing the Council to expenditure until a final answer had been received from the County Council, that the grant expected would be given. At the same time he could not help thinking that there was a source of danger in passing the resolution that the People's 'College be engaged for evening classes for next session on the terms offered by the Committee of the school before the result of the application to the County Council was known. He understood in the first instance that matters were entirely dependent upon the Council getting £7OO. But supposing that they only got £5OO or £4OO the Council would have to make it up if they committed themselves to this expenditure. Alderman SUTTON said the £25 a year for the People's College was only required for the schools for evening classes. The question of establishing day schools was deferred until the amount of grant from the County Council was known. Alderman HARRISON: But you cannot dispute the fact that you are going to increase considerably the amount of expenditure without first being assured that you will get the amount from the Council. The CHAIRMAI4 as one of the managers of the People's College assured the Corporation that no payment would be expected from them unless they got the grant from the County Council. Alderman HARRISON said he was much obliged for that assurance, but moved that the question of establishing a day school be deferred until the amount of the grant was known. He should like to apply that to the expen- diture of every other sum of money in connection with the Technical Instruction Act.

Councillor F. A. ROBERTS: Including that of sending a deputation of tivelve men to the continent to know how to expend the money. Councillor H. ROBERTS assured the Corporation that it was not the intention ot the Committee to commit them to any serious expense, which would not be justified by a definite assurance from the County Council. Unless the Corporation put themselves in a position by preparing for their classes to justify the County Council in making the grant, they would have no right to expect the grant. He was quite pleased, really delighted, to find that Aid. Greenall was marching along with the times go rapidly as to be able to announce publicly for the first time in that hall that he was prepared to support those of them who had been advocating for ycars the Sunday opening of the Museum and Library ; and they should not forget that announcement when the subject came up for con- sideration. He had been charged with a little inconsis- tency, and the charge coming from those it came from, was somewhat amusing. Whenever Councillors Bolton or Jenkins, or both of them, might catch him in incon- sistency upon the question they referred to, they should have all the capital they could possibly make out of it. He knew it was impossible for some gentlemen to think of brewing except with regard lo the brewing of the most despicable thing on earth. (Ironical laughter.) He was speaking his own opinion. (Renewed laughter and cries of "hear, hear.") Whether it suited the opinions of other members of the Council or not. He was not there that /light to ask the Coporation to sanction the teaching of the brewing of beer. Be had opposed in Committee in the strongest way he possibly could the introduction of this question within the programme so strongly that he threatened to resign his position upon the Committee if this were persisted in. (Hear, hear.) If ever there was a serious attempt to carry out the inclusion of that subject, he would never be a party to it. It would be grossly inconsistent on his part if he
