were, and he was not going to allow himself to be held up as buing a sham. The minutes were adopted. CEMETERY COMMITTEE. The minutes of this Committee contained the following: —Report of the vgistrar. from which it appeared that the interments for the past four weeks were :—Adults, 67 ; minor, 60; stillborn and premature, 12; correspond- ing period last year, adults, 41; minors. 42; stillborn and premature, 9." The receipt for the past four weeks were £97 18s. 6d.; corresponding period last year, £5B 3s. Bd. .. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Alderman HARRISON seconded by 47,ounctllor HUTCHINSON.
WATER COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the above Committee, the Mayor was appointed Chairman and Alderman Platt, deputy-Chair- man of the Committee'. The Chairman, deputy-Chair- man, Councillors Green, Hepherd, and H. Roberts were appointed a Managing Sub-Committee. Councillor SHAW GREEN moved, and Councillor HEPHERD seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor DIXON asked whether the services of Mr. John poss would be retained. Councillor HEPHERD : It is in the Bill. The minutes were confirmed. THE PROPOSED STIPENDIARY MAGISTRATE.

At the General Purposes Committee the Town Clerk was instructed to obtain information from towns similar to Warrington as to the appointment, emoluments, and duties of stipendiary magistrates. It was resolved that Councillors R. T. Fairclough and Heaton be appointed members of the Open-Spaces Sub-Committee. The minutes were confirmed, on the motion of Alder- man SurroN, seconded by Councillor HIITCHINSON.
THE CORPORATION AND ITS CONTRACTS. A LIVELY DISCUSSION ON "SWEATING."

Councillor FLOOD mved.—" That in the opinion of this Council it is the duty of the Corporation in all Cor- poration contracts to make provisions against the evils recently disclosed before the Sweating Committee of the House of Lords, to insert such conditions as may prevent the abuse arising from sub-letting, and to 'make every effort to secure the payment of such wares and the ob- servance of the working hours as are generally accepted as-current in each trade for competent workmen." He said that more consideration had been given to that ques- tion during the past twelve months than to any other question which affected the interests of the public. He had a vivid recollection that when he introduced it at a previous meeting of the Town Council, there was quite a flutter among some of the members, but since that tune, he was pleased to say, they had had time for calm reflection and now viewed the matter from a practical standpoint. The resolution he now submitted had been accepted in most of our leading towns, and had also almost word for word been accepted in principle by the present Government in lieu of a re- solution submitted by an hon. member of the House, Mr. S. Buxton. How was it that labour was able to command such a small return? It arose from the fact that their municipal bodies were more to blame

than anybody else: having fallen into the very dis- reputable habit of allowing themselves to be sur- rounded by a class of men largely known in trade as "bummers." It was a straiwe expression, but it was well-known hi certain organizations of working-men. It referred to men who were not legitimate tradesmen, or men of reputation, but who were prepared to button-hole him or any other member of the Council and ask them to,support them in obtain- ing certain contracts. His experience in that Council alone convinced him that the custom prevailed in War- rington. It was not long since a tender was submitted to ,a Committee of which he was a member. From Min immemorial it had been the custom of that Committee to accept a certain tender, subject to sample. He would not state the price at which the article was Supplied, but upon a certain occasio,n an article was submitted at just one-half the cost. The offer was jumped at by-the Com- mittee. Some members rather questioned the reality of the thing, and the matter was referred to an expert out- side the Committee to decide which was the better. article. The expert decided that the cheaper article, which was exactly one half the original cost, was the better of the two, and there were only two conclusions to he drawn, either that the Committee had for a num- ber of years mismanaged their business in accepting a certain tender, or that they were not competent jades and had paid double prices, or were prepared to accept something not according to sample. Then there was the ' question of the contract for police clothing. It was a fact that certain firms made police clothing a specialty: they worked itup to such a system,that they brought about this result they had no hesitation in charging £2 for the p )lice officer's tunic, and they had less hesitation in askin, . for it to be made for is. 9td. If they asked a practical man what was the value of the cloth they were told it was not much more than 12s. or 135., and if the tunic was made for 2s. in round figures, they might value the article at 14s. And yet from £2 to two guineas was charged. 'lf these articles were made by a legitimate firm, they would nay their employes wages which would not enable them to realize such enormous profits. (Hear, hear.) Another question had come before his notice. They had in the town some of the most practical engineers and mechanics who hould be found in any part of Lancashire, indeed in any part of the kingdom. On a certain occasion an engine was wanted by a Committee. A number of ten- ders were submitted, and what was the result ? One firm Outside the town—something over a hundred miles away—got the contract in face of the bona fide tender of men who were prepared to supply the article according to sample—in the face of local tradesmen whose reputa- tion as mechanics and engineers they could not question. Having mentioned that they had a member of that Council who prided himself on having laid more sewers and drains than any other man in Warrington, Councillor Flood added that owing to fatal cases of fever in the locality in which he lived drains were opened and five out of eight were found to run the wrong way. It was said they should buy in the cheapest market, but he did not consider that was always right. It was quite possible they might get a cheap article equal to the sample, in the first instance; but it required constant supervision and close inspection to keep the contractor up to the strict letter of the law. The Surveyor had had to come before the Committee to object to a certain tender, and it was necessary to put their foot down and to say that no tender should be entertained by the Council except it was of a bona „fide character, and one which would bear the strictest investigation. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Councillor H. RoßEars said he had much pleasure in seconding the motion, but entirely upon different grounds to those which had been advocated by Council- lor Flood. He (Councillor Roberts) wag' not a trades unionist. It had not been his good fortune to have had experience in that direction, but looking upon that Cor- poration as the dispenser of public moneys he had no hesitation in saying that they had no right to apply those moneys in the acceptance of contracts which mhzlit to their knowledge be the means of unscrupulous men sweating their employes. (Hear, hear.) He strong- ly believed in the Scripture which said" That the labour- er was worthy of his hire," and when they had scores of cases adduced before the recent Royal Commission which were a scandal and a dispace to a country like theirs, they ought to be exceedingly careful that they did not in the slightest possible degree lend themselves as a public body to the merest possibility of such a condition of things entering into a single contract with which they had to do. He was strongly fortified in his desire to support the resolution by Vie fact that the highest deliberative assembly in the world—of which they as Englishmen were justly proud,namely, the House of Commons—had seen fit to accept a similar resolution with regard to all its public contracts. The London Comity Council, some of the principal corporations and school boards, and other, local bodies had unhesitatingly followed in the wake of the House of Commons : indeed, the matter was almost beyond discussion. All they had

to do as Englishmen and as men was to take care that no man supplied them with material, or did work for them, who attempted to make his profits unfairly and to the prejudice of the people he employed. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BOLTON said he was an advocate for working- men being paid good wages, having reasonable hours of work, and also being well educated. A certain gentle- man had made a remark upon a public platform, to the effect that when a particular resolution was brought be- fore the Council, the members retired— Councillor PIERPOINT : SO you did. Councillor BOLTON, continuing, said that when one did not like a subject the best pourse to adopt was to leave it alone—(hear, hear\ —and let someone else push it through. The motion on the previous occasion went so far that it amounted to the ridiculous. It asked them to do something they would not do in their own private affairs. It asked that they should require a written con- tract for everything they spent. He should like to ask Councillor Flood if, every time he purchased a suit of clothes, he had a written contract from the tailor that he did not encourage sweating, or unreasonable hours,or whether when he gave his wages on a Saturday night to his wife or his housekeeper he had a written state- ment from her of every penny she spent. So far as the present motion stood, he had no objection to, it. What he objected to was the Town Council being made a judge of what a man's wages should be, and what number of hours he should work. The law of supply and demand should be sufficient to make a contractor find his own skilled labour without compelling,the Corporation to ask details when' entering into a contract. They had the money of the ratepayers to spend, and they ought to spend it as well as they could in their favour. Alderman SirrroN said he could not agree that the Council Chamber was the right place to decide questions arising between employer and employed. He opposed the resolution which had been submitted by Councillor Flood, not because he had sympathy with those who were called sweaters, because he was as much opposed to the sweating system as Councillor Flood, Councillor Henry, Roberts, or any other member of the Council. He ob- jected to the Council being formed, as it were, into a board of arbitration, to settle matters between em- ployers and employed, as to the rate of wages they ought to receive, and the hours they ought to work. He believed that every man should have fair play. It would be perfectly impracticable for them to carry out the resolution which han just been proposed by Coun- cillor Flood. In many cases, when they had accepted contracts, if they had asked the contractor what he paid his men, or how many hours they were employed, in nine cases out of ten they would have received the ans- wer,
"Mind your own bizsiness, and if you are not satis-
fled with the -tender, leave it alone." tie was of opinion that the resolution was a ridiculous one for anybody to propose.... _ . .

Councillor FLOOD: I wish you were coming out on the Ist November, and ynu would see whether it is ridi- culous or not. (Laughter.) Alderman Surrorr : I should make the same remarks, and believe that I was talking to men of common sense, who would perfectly understand what I meant. I will support working-men as much as anyone, and I will do everything I can for them, but, at the same time, I don't think we ought to have these matters introduced into our public affair. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PrimPoixf thought the arguments against the motion were amusing. Councillor Bolton had stig- matized the previous resolution as ridiculous, and gave that as his reason for running away from its considera- tion. If Councillor Bolton and his fellow Councillors who held the same opinion were satisfied that the motion was a'ridiculous one, it was their duty to remain to say so. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Councillor BovroN : I rise to a point of order. I did not say that it was a ridiculous motion.

Councillor. PIERPOINT : If you withdraw I will do so, but you certainly did stigmatise the previous" motion as a ridiculous one. He (Councillor Pierpoint) said,he was strongly of opinion that the motion was a fit and proper one to be placed on the paper. (Hear, hear.) On the 13th February, 1891, a similar motion to the present, ex- cept that the word " Government " was inserted in- stead of the word "Council." was introduced into the House of Commons, and carried. He did not see one single reason why they should hesitate to adopt that re- solution. (Applause.) Councillor ,Issitrss said that no man who had the good of the working-classes truly at heart could hesitate to support the motion. This was not a question of politics. it was a question of trying to do good, which was a far higher law than any question of politics. The House of Commons, he pointed out, did not adopt the motion which had been submitted by Councillor Fiord in its en- tirety ; they excluded the words "and the observance of the working hours." He liked a reasonable amount of ease, and he did not know why working-men should not possess the same benefit. If the House of Commons and other bedies had adopted a similar resolution, it was the duty of that Council to do so. He had, therefore, no he- sitation in supporting the motion. Councillor PLUMPTON said there had been a system of buying in the cheapest market the cheapest goods, but sometimes they had been found in the end to be the dearest. Before the passing of the Merchandise Marks Act, German cheap cutlery was sent to this country and disposed of as Sheffield make. That was to the injury of the working classes in Sheffield and other towns where , cutlery was manufactured. It caused the English manu- facturers to make a cheap 'article to compete with the Germans. Consequently, a lot of cheap rubbish came into our market. Now, however, there was a change, and people were not so anxious as they formerly were to buy cheap stuff. The resolution submitted that evening by Councillor Flood had a tendency in the right direction, and it was with very great pleasure that he supported it. Alderman CHANDLEY said he was not afraid to say dis- tinctly that he hoped the motion would be opposed by every member of the Council. He considered that the motion in itself was absolutely unnecessary. The reso- lution was also impolitic. To fence round the discretion of any body of men on the lines laid down in that resolu- tion should be discountenanced. It was nothing more or less than the last plank from the Trades Union platform, and altogether it was a most suicidal policy, and taught the Corporation they must buy in the dearekt market. Mr. Flood, in his allusion to the contractors, had made some very dangerous remarks with regard to police clothing. Councillor FLOOD: I didn't allude to this borough. Alderman CHANDLEY : It was generally understood by this Council that you alluded to this borough. Councillor FLOOD: I did not. Alderman Surrox : We understood so.

Alderman CHANDLEY said he would ... accept Councillor Flood's denial. He had a very high personal esteem for Councillor Flood, but at the same time he could not espouse his utterances in the way of trades unionism in the manner he expounded them. He disliked sweating as much as anyone. In his own business he could not, he thought, be accused of it, and indeed was the victim of jr. The Warrington Slate Company, which Councillor Roberts represented, furnished the Corpora- tion with-
Councillor HENRY ROBERTS: Are we going to have a discussion of a personal character to-night ?

Alderman CHANDLEY : No. Councillor HENRY ROBERTS: If we are, I am prepared to defend my position as a member of the Slate Com- pany. Alderman CHANDLEY : I am afraid your conscience smite you. I am not in the habit of indulging in personal argument. Councillor HENRY ROBERTS: Then why quote my company at all? I contend that it is a most improper thing to refer to either individuals or parties. I appeal to you, Mr. Chairman, and shall take your ruling. Is it proper to the discussion of questions of this character that firms with which members of this Corporation are connected should be mentioned? The CHAIRMAN: I must admit that I did not hear what Alderman Chandlev said. Alderman CHANDLEY : I cast no aspersion upon your firm. Councillor HENRY RouErers : It is not a question of aspersion. I object to my firm being mentioned. Alderman Surrox : That shows at once that it is a question which should not be discussed at all. Councillor HENRY ROBERTS: It is a matter of exceed- ingly bad taste, and I am surprised that Alderman Chandley cannot see it. Alderman CHANDLEY : If you will sit down you will find that I intvad no reflection on your firm. Alderman HARRISON: Alderman Chandley was simply illustrating his remarks. Councillor HENRY ROBERTS: I decline to have my firm used as an illustration. Alderman CHANDLEY : You may forget yourself. I will not forget myself. Councillor HENRY ROBERTS: You have forgotten your- self by mentioning my firm. It is a piece of exceed- ingly bad taste. The CHAIRMAN said Aldernian Chanelley would go on with his speech. Alderman CHANDLEY, continuing, said that firms delivered goods to -the Corporation—the Warrington Slate Company, Messrs. Clare and Ridgway, and other firms delivered goods to the Corporation—and orders were given them because faith was placed in them, and it was believed that they would supply goods of the best quality and so much as could be given for the money ; but the Corporation could not follow those contractors so far as to go into details respecting the manufacturers of the goods supplied. Take, for instance, the Gas Works. How were the Gas Committee to know whether the people supplying pipes paid proper wages to their workmen? Councillor FLoon : You ought to know. Alderman CHANDLEY : Or that the men had worked the proper number of hours? flow were Messrs. Clare and Ridgway, or the Slate Company, to know whether or not the pipes were made by women who were poorly paid? Surely they could not go so far as to inquire into the manufacture in all its ramifications. Let it be suffi- cient for the Corporation to buy in the best market the best material produced at the lowest price; but if any instance of sweating came to their knowledge, there was not, he felt sure, a member of any Committee who would countenance it. (Hear' hear.) Councillor FLoon : Affirm that by my resolution

- - That is all I want you to do. Alderman CII.INDLEY said he objected to the motion because it was unnecessa,ry. In the contracts given out for police clothing every care was used. The Committee advertised for tenders, and each tender was considered on its own merits, and the firm which could produce the best goods, to the satisfaction of her Majesty's Inspector, for the lowest price received the contract. The Commit- tee had gone so far as to entreat some of the tradesmen in the town to tender in order that they might have the satisfaction of giving the work to be be done in the town, instead of allowing it to be taken out; but in very many cases the local tradesmen had declined. Consequently, the orders were given to to large firms who had the ad- vantage of appliances for making police clothes. Councillor PisaeorxT : And sweating. Alderman CRANDLEY said he did not know that, but it was certainly the fact that large firms were able to do the work better and cheaper than anyone else. Were the Council to say that they would give 25 per cent. moie to local men? If they did that, they would be simply sweating the ratepayers. Councillor HENRY ROBERTS said he had been challenged to show how it would be possible to carry out that reso- lution. If the Council accepted the resolution and made inquiries of the contractors, the latter would, as a matter of course make similar inquiries of the firm, with whom they dealt. It was•as simple as possible, and anybody but an obfuscated Conservative would see it in an instant (" Oh, oh," and laughter.) Councillor VOISEY said the sentiment underlying the motion was undoubtedly good and, so far as it sought the advancement and good and profit of the working-men he was entirely in favour of it; but he was of opinion that the motion was totally inapplicable to municipal corporations. Take the case of a Committee with half a dozen contracts in front of them. How were they going to determine all those questions? Individuals might work them out, but as a Corporation they could never give the Motion the effect which, its promoters were seek- ing, and, therefore he should oppose it. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Dr. CANNELL said Couwillor Henry Roberts had made a remark ab.ait Conservatism, and as that was to be a Radical vote he should vote against the motion. (Laughter.) . _

CoUncillOr R. T. FAIEtCLOUGH would not like to be compelled by anyone to work a certain number of hours and he did not think he ought to compel other men to work a certain number of hours. Councillor B ROWNE pointed out that the Aldermen who had not to face their constituents were about to vote against the motion, and it was very amusing, while those members of the Conservative party who were corn- ing ont on the Ist November supported it. (Laughter.) This was a question which had nothing to do with politics. Councillor CANNELL Mr. Roberts says it has. Councillor BOLTON: We are obfuscated Conservatives. (Laughter.) Councillor BROWNE said 29 Corporations had already passed a similar resolution. Ccuncillor SHAW-GREEN thought there was not a man round the table who was not opposed to the sweating system, and he considered the Council ought to set the best example it could. Councillor DIXON supported the motion, and referred to instances in which firms who paid trade union wages were prevented from getting contracts by others who did not pay those wages.
Councillor F. A. ROBERTS also briefly supported the resolution.

Alderman HARRISON said he should vote against the motion, and was surprised to hear that some members of the Council were disposed to upset all the writings and opinions of such men as Stuart Mill. Alderman BunnEss made a few remarks, in a vein of broad—in fact very broad—humour with regard to the " sweating " that went on at Longford depot, after which
Councillor BEAMAN said he would support the resolu- ion on higher groundsthan any which had had y.et be9n
adduced
He Would do sO- be- he should not like the

moral influence of the Council to go in the direction of that detestable and despicable class termed "sweaters." The arguments against the resolution had wanted force and point and power. Alderman Sutton had termed it an" unfortunate" motion. Very probably he was right from his standpoint. It was unfortunate to some in that Chamber, but it showed in which direction their sympathies went, whether in favour of what Councillor Flood termed the " bummers " or in the direction of the
amelioration of the condi' (near, hear.) Councillor FLOOD hayiN
- ,ton of honest working-men.
briefly replied, the Council

... - divided, with the following result For the motion-- Against the motion— Alderman Burgess Alderman Sutton Councillor F. A. Roberts „ Harrison ~ Green . Wright Fleming ~ Chandley Flood Councillor Dr. Canoell tt ~ H. Roberts „ R. P. Fairclough ~ Brown „ Voisey ~Hepherd 19 Beaman Jenkins „ J. Fairclough f 1 Ashton ~Walker It Hutchinson ~ Hill ~ Dixon ~ Garner Pierpoint Plumpton ft —l5 —ll The CHAIRMAN : There are 15 in favour of the resolution and 11 against it. I, therefore declare the resolution carried. (Applause.) Owing to the lateness of the evening—about half-past nine—the resolutions which stood in the names of Coun- cillor Hill and Councillor Dixon were deferred till next meeting of the Council.
THE LEEDS MURDER.

Walter Lewis Turner was charged on remand at Leeds on Monday, with the murder of the child Barbara Waterhouse, his mother being charged with being an accessory after the fact. The court was crowded. The accused were remanded.

Walter Lewis Turner was on Wednesday committed for trial by the Leeds magistrates on a charge of murder- ing a child named Barbara VVaterhouse under circum- stances of shocking barbarity. Turner's mother was committed for trial on a charge of being an accessory after the fact.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT..
HOUSE OF LORDS.—Mow'my. The EARL of Morley, in the absence of the Lorl Chan- cellor took his s2at on the woolsack at a querter past four.

ITHE VOLUNTEER REVIEW.—In reply to Lords DORCHES- TER and WEmyss, Earl EROWNLOW state I that while it would destroy the whole value of tin oc.asion to give to , the members of the citizen army anything in the shape of " pay " in connection with the forthcoming volunteer review before the Emperor, the Secretary for War re- cognised that the men might suffer hardship in reference to travelling and food expenses, and propled to allow each man two shillings in respect of those items. BILLS ADVANCED. —Various bills, including the Fairs and Markets (Weighing of Cattle Bill), were advanced a sthge, and the House adjourned at 4.45. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The speaker took the chair at three o'clock. 1 VOLUNTEERS IN THE CIVIL SERVICES.—Mr. W. H. SMITH stated, in answer toa question by Colonel Howard Vincent, th.at a circular would be addressed to the heads of all departments of the Civil Service asking them to give the utmost possible facilities to clerks who are volunteers to attend the review at IVimbledon on Satur- day next. . A WIGAN CONVICTION.—Mr. CHAFLIN, in reply to Mr. Barclay, referring to a recent conviction at Wigan for concealment of an outbreak or pleure-pneumonia and the imposition of a penalty of only 20s. and costs, said that the Department would, if magistrate; failed to deal vigorously with such casPs, have to exercize its rlzht of withholding compensation for animals that might have to be slaughtered in a particular area. , THE ABDUCTION OF AN ENGLISII GIRL. Sir JAMES FERGUSSON said he was hopedul that tit,. eariy release would be secured of the English girl recently captured by Kurds. BILLS ADVANCED. —The Redemption or Rent (Ireland) Bill,was read a second time, and the County Council (Elections) Bill passed through Committee, and was re- ported to the House. The Stamp Dutivi; Bill was read a third time, as also the Stamp Dories Management Bill. The Western Highlands and Islands (Public •Works) Bill passed through Committee, and . The House adjourned at 12.10. HOUSE OF I.OIMS.—TUESDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the -woolsack at half-past five o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—A bill presented hy the Lord Chan- cellor, to amend the Lunacy Act of 1390, was read a first time.—Lord Dp Rlitismy moved- the second reading of the Penal Servitude Bill, and stated that its most imp)rtant part was the first clans, which was virtually a proposal to reduce sentences of five yoars' peal( servitude to three. The Bill was read a second thn.). BILLS ADVANCED.—TIIO Public Health(London)Bl was read a second time. The Municipal Registrati).! !)üblin and Belfast Bill passnd through Committee. The House ruse at twenty minutes past six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at th•ree-o:do-Jc:• QuEsTros.---Sir J. FEROIISSON informed M. Woodall that British consuls were (1.-.!barred by the i:i14:•;» In laws from performing marriages within the limits of the German Empire. Sir J. ,Fprgnscon also inforol.,rl Mr. Woodall that the commercial treaty betweeu Great Britain and China would remain in forc;-? for another ten years. Replying to Mr. Hanbury and Mr. Summer, Sir W. 11 ART-DTICE said that sub-election 3of the.El-ment- ary Education Bill placed no diffiroilr.v whatever in the way of provision of free vhool plsce.s by the managers of voluptary Schools. Mr. W. TI. SMITH in formed Mr. Caldst•ell that any financial difficulty caused in Scotland by the amendment of the educa- tion code, signified by a Treasury minute on the 11th of June, would be larlely, if not entirely. met. Mr. STANHOPE, answering Mr. Labouchere denied the accuracy of some recent statements made by Lord R. Churchill in the "Daily Graphic" as to the obsolete character of the defences at Cane Town, Table Bay, and ' Simon Bay. Lord George Hamilton informed Mr. Gourley and Admiral Field that an exlia,,stive inquiry would be ordered int ) the fatal gun explosion on her Majesty's ship Cordeli i. Mr. W. H. &will!, replying to Mr.. Elliott Lees, undertook to consult the trustees of the National Gallery as to the possibility of arranging for an interchange of pictures with provincial art galleries. Sir W. Hart-Dyke was questioned by Mr. T. Ellis as to the necessity for evening schools in Wales. and stated that there was nothing to prevent School I3oards from establishing such schools.

Tips EDUCATION BILL.—The Elementary E.lucation Bill as amended in Committee was considered. Mr. LLOYD GROROR moved a new clause providing that where the fee grant should exceed in any school the ag- gregate amount of fees for the year 1891, the surplus should be applied to such educational purpost.s as might be approved by the Education Department. Sir WM. HART DYER opposed the clause, reza.rding it as a direct challenge to the Education Department as to whether it would or would not do its duty and secure the efficiency of schools. The new clause was rejected, by 143 to 93. An amendment that except in sch Pois under a Scho)l Board no fee grant should be paid to any school of which at least 'one-sixth of the total' expenditute wa.s Tot met by voluntary contributions was defeated by 159 to 90. The report stage being concluded, the third reading of the bill was set down for next day. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. _
The Speaker took the chair at half-past twelve,. and five minutes later a house was made. _ TFIE EDUCATION BILL. .

On the motion for the iliird-Wa-dirTg:-.;iihe Elementary. Education Bill, Mr. Roar congratulated the Govern- ment on the straightfcrwardness of Sir William Hart- Dyke in the conduct of the measure.—Mr. BAartryspoke disparagingly of the measure, and Mr. JESSE CoLLINGS and Colonel Corrosi-JonnEr.t, congratulated the Govern- ment.—Mr. BRUNNER felt that the bill would do a great deal of good, but thought credit for it was as much due to the Liberal party as to the Government.—Mr. S/NCLAIR warmly approved of the measure, but joined in the ex- pression of regret that the Government had not seen its way to give some assistance_ to continuation schools..— -- _
Mr: JA:S6IS LOWTHER spoke disparagingly of the measure, and Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT, in declaring that it con- . .
tamed great good, and also- some evils which miv,ht be - remedied in future, ascribed its introduction to the desire

of the Tories to avoid destruction at the veneral election. The bill was road a third time amidst cheers. - COINAGE BILL.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHRCILIER moved the second reading of the Coinage Bill, under which £400,000 would beappropriated to the replacement of light gold —Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT was speaking in criticism of Mr. Goschen's policy, when the debate stood adjourned in accordance with the standing order, Mr. Goschen expressing great disappointment. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter-past four.—The Elementary Education, the Consular Salaries and Fees, the County Councils (Elections), and the Craters' Commons Grazing (Scotland) Bills were read a first time.—The report of amendments to this bill was received and agreed to.

The House adjourned at 4 30. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIITMSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. Quitmorts.—Mr. MArraEws, in replying to a ques- tion by Mr. W. Maclaren, said he was not disposed to interfere with the lawful exercise by a scientific man of operations on animals which were directly for the bene- fit of the human race. In answer to Mr. B. Robertson, Mr. E. Stanhope said he proposed to make a commence- ment this year with his scheme for the relief of destitute survivors of the war in the Crimea and th Indian Mutiny.

CIVI-L SERVICE ESTIMATES, &c.—The House went into Committee of Supply and resumed the consideration of Civil Service Estimates. On the vote for the offices of the House of Commons Mr. MORTON moved to re luce it by £l,OOO as a protest against the sal,. of spirituous liquors at the bar of the inner lobby. This amendment was rejected by 127 to 55, and the vote was agreed to. On a vote for the Home Office a discussion took place on the desirability of appointing Welsh speaking inspectors of mines in Wales. Mr. BROADHURST asked for an in- crease in the number of inspectors of factories and work- shops. Mr. ADDISON supported the appeal, remarking that it was of little use passing Ads for the more efficient control of factories unless there was an adequate staff to carry them out. Mr. Ma rramvs said that until he saw in what shape the Factory Bill left Parliament he could not give any pledges on the subject of additional inspectors. On a vote for the Foreign Office, Mr. LABOUCHERE again brought for- ward the subject of the" understanding" between her Majesty's Government and Italy„. Sir JAMES ItEttoussox said we had entered into no agreement or under- standing against any Power. Our sympathies and influence would be to keep peace, and lie denied that the British Government had any animus against France. Mr. LABOUCHERE said the statements of Bir James Fer-
gusson were entirely unsatisfactory. He rejoiced- t-11;,t Lord Salisbury could not pledge Parliament_ in iti3 at-

report progress. The motion was agreed to. MISCELLANEOI7S.—On the motion of Sir M. HICKS- BEACH, the Fisheries Bill was read a second time.—The Public Health (Scotland) Act Amendment Bill was read a third time.

The minutes contained the following :—Report of the bathkeeper. from which it appeared that that the in- come from the baths for the past six weeks was £35 14s. 10d. . and for the corresponding period last year £5O Bs. 4d. Resolutions : That the tender of Mr. P. Caldwell for the supply of 100 lineal yards of iron rail.
ings at ss. 4d. per iira be accepted. That the tender of Mr. John Chorley to Supply a 22in. lawn mower at £sl6s. be accepted. _ _
On the m`otion of Alderman CHANDLEY, seconded Councillor Bolton, the minutes were approved:

MARKETS COMMITTEE.—WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT. At a meeting of the Markets Committee, held on the 22.1 d June, it was reported that the total income from all sources was £303 4s. 10d. ; corresponding period last year, £270 Ds. 10d. ; increase £32 13s.—At a meeting held on the Bth June, the Town Clerk reported that the regulations adopted by the Corporation under the Weights and Measures Act. 1889, had received the approval of the Board of Trade. It was resolved that the Town Clerk give public notice thereof.—At a meeting held on the 22nd June, it was resolved that the Paving and Sewerage Committee be requested to take up and re- move the slippery setts in that portion of Cheshyres-lane under the new market shed,. and to relay with Newry setts, and that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to have the under side of the roof of the Market Hall washed and cleaned, and the skylights in the new shed white- washed or painted. Alderman GREENALL moved, and Councillor ASHTON seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor BROWNE asked for an explanation why Frederick Simpson, a stallholder in the market had re- ceived a month's notice to quit after he had been there 15 or 16 years. Alderman GREENALL said the matter was not on the minutes. Alderman BunoEss : It is one of the suppressed min- utes. (Laughter.) Alderman GREENALL: I think I am not bound to answer the question. Alderman SurroN asked the Committee to give in- structions to stall-holders not to allow hampers to over- hang the footpath in Market-st. Councillor HUTCHINSON promised that the Market In- spector should have his attention drawn to the obstruc- tion. Councillor BROWNII moved that the mimite relating to Mr. Frederick Simpson, the stall-holder of whose case he had spoken, be referred back to the Committee. He ex- plained that Mr. Simpson had received notice without any cause being assigned, though he had been about 23 years in the market shed as an inspector, and during the last 15 orl6 years a tenant of the Markets Committee. On the motion of Councillor HEPHERD, seconded by Councillor FLOOD, it was resolved that the Council con- sider the matter in Committea, Councillor Dixon at this exclaiming: Is the businness of the Council to be do ne In secret. The matter was then discussed 'at length in Committee in the presence of the reporters, and ultim- ately the minutes were passed with the exception of that in question, which was withdrawn
OAS COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the above Committee, it was reported that the average illuminating power of the gas for the past four weeks was equal to 1915 candles at both works. At another meeting Councillor James Fairclough was appointed a member of the Committee, and it was re- solved that the sum of 30 guineas be voted to the borough auditor for auditing the accounts of the depart- ment for the past year. It was resolved that the order given to Messrs. Firmstone Bros., for pipes be counter- manded, and that the order be (riven as fellows :—Stan- ton Ironworks Company, 4in. ;'Cochrane and Company, 9in.
The CHAIRMAN moved the confirmation. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH seconded. Councillor BEAMAN asked why the order for pipes had been transferred.

The CIIAIRMAN explained that it was because the pipes had been found defective. Councillor Dixox asked why that had not been stated in the minutes. There seemed, he remarked, to be such a tendency to secrecy first in one committee and then in another. The Council ought not to be treated like children.

Councillor PIERPOINT prOPOSed that the name of Coun- cillor Plumpton be substituted for that of Councillor J. Fairclough for election on the Committee as if he were net he would be on no committee during the time for which he was elected.

The TOWN CLERK said a member of the Council could only be put on a committee on the recommendation of the Committee or in pursuance of a notice. Councillor SHAw GREEN remarked that there was a vacancy on the Museum Committee. Councillor PIERPOINT said there were already 23 mem- bers on that Committee, and they did not want another. He moved that the resolution of the pth May be referred back tp the Committee. Councillor DIXON seconded. Alderman SUTTON: It seems to me that Councilllor Pierpoint takes a real pleasure in creating a difficulty. Councillor PIERPOINT : I am like this poor unfortu- nate man Simpson, evidently. You had better give me notice. (Laughter.) Councillor Flurcanisorr suggested that Councillor Pier- point retire from one of the Committees of which he was a member to make room for Councillor Plumpton. (Laughter.) Councillor PIEHPOINT : If he will name any Commit- tee from which he wishes me to retire, I will retire immediately. Councillor JENKINS : Seeing that the Sanitary Com- mittee are likely to resign on Councillor Dixon's motion, there will, in remodelling that Committee,be ample room for Councillor Plumpton. (Laughter.) After some discussion Councillor Plumpton expressed his readiness to withdraw his claims, upon which Coun- cillor Pierpoint withdrew his amendment. The minutes were then confirmed.

Corporations THE members of the Town Coun- " Sweaaatding." cil of Warrington found them." salves in a novel position, on Tues- day, in having before them a motion bearing on the ' "sweating " system in relation to Corporation Con- tracts; and to some of the members the situation was evidently more novel ,than agreeable. Last year when notice was given of a motion upon the subject, a number of the Tories prevented discu§- sion by walking out of the Council Chamber.. This, as we urged at the time, was a cowardly way of shirking an important issue; and it not unnaturally excited b. feeling of indignation amongst the working-class electors. This year the matter has not only come to a discussion, but a vote, and—what is more—the motion has been carried by 15 to 11. It is true only two Tories voted for it, Councillor JENKINS and Councillor HUTCHINSON ; and if, as has been suggested, both these gentlemen are having an eye tet the fact that their term of office expires in November, it is at least indicative of what they believe to be the general feeling of their constituents on the subject. We are glad to observe that not a single Liberal was to be found voting against the motion; and we would put it to the working-men who are agitating this citiestion whether the division is not one which reveals who are their supporters and who are their oppo" nents. It reveals another thing, too, and that iS that if they will act unitedly, and ask for what if 4 reasonable, they will be likely to succeed alwaYS in getting what they want. The main thing of course is that they should be fairin their demands ; but when did it happen that the masses, after due deliberation, made a demand which was not fair? With regard to the " sweating " system, there can be no two opinions that it deprives the labourer of a portion of the hire which is due te ' him, and grinds the faces of the poor in the most abominable manner. The difficulty, we grant, ie to determine how it shalr be Suppressed; and, further, we are prepared to admit that cases can be conceived in which a Corporation nould wasW time in inquiry, and in the end do more harni than good. But the evil is in existence, and lt needs to be grappled with. If, as we believe, there is not much " sweating " in connection with the carrying out of contracts in such small towns ae Warrington, that is no reason why the Corporation should not show on which side it takes its stand io the matter. In the course of the discussion/ Alderman HARRISON said it was their duty ..na their privilege to buy in the cheapest market and sell in the dearest. That is the rule of trade, It' may be granted, but, like other rules, it has lte exceptions; and this is recognised when the Corporation insert a clause on a notice for tender saying they do not bind themselves to accept the lowest tender. This implies that it is not alwal a duty to buy in the cheapest market; and • e exception may be taken to a merchant with thb lowest tender because there is a reasonable dolih: as to his doing the work satisfactorily, why not r a step further and set his tender aside when he is known to be a "sweater ?" Alderalan CHANDLEY, although lie opposed the motio.2l: accepted its principle when lie said "if any ill stance of sweating came to their knowledge, there was not, he was sure, a member of the Comicnite°_ who would countenance it." This led Counc!llor, FLOOD to exclaim—" Affirm that by resolutioo ' that is all I want you to do." And this is all that is affirmed by the resolution which was adOteci.... It will be seen from the terms of it that it is notrisau much a mandate as an expression of opinion; ad, if this had been sufficiently borne in mind we _ri.. not see why the Council should not have been .u_io aniinous in its approval. This much is quite eery' mean that; if the resolution is to be interpreted as ing that no contract is to be accented until :rid inquiry has been instituted as to the "wage hours "of the contracting firm, it will cause inype sant friction, dangerous delay, and waste of ntte:l, on the part of Committees. Ruskin in the Political economy of "Unto this last" exposes the fallacy of Ricardo's statement that "the inatural rate of wages is that which will maintain the labourer," by saying—" Maintain him! Yes, but how ?" We are endeavouring to furnish an answer to Ruskin's soul-searching question when we take measures to deal with "the sweater." Shall we so "maintain" the tailor of the East- as to live less like a human being than like a rat in a hole; or the shirtmaker in such a way that she must eke out her maintenance by pro- stitution; or starve, or steal? Human nature revolts at such a proposal; yet that is wkat it comes to so long as "the sweater" is allowed to Pursue his course unchecked. The conscience of the nation is being stirred on this question; the check must be applied; and one way of helping to apply it is to pass such resolutions throughout the country as that which was adopted by the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday last.

INVENTORS are not a numerous Our Patent Laws. class; they do not count at an elec- tion as many other classes do; and that is one reason why their grievances do not obtain the attention which they ought to receive. But they are a most important body nevertheless; and if the nation sufficiently considered its inter- eats, apart from allaying growing discontent, there Would soon be no room fur unfavourably compar- ing our patent laws with those of other countries. It is true a great change was effected when Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, in 18S3, was the means of reduc- ing the initial fee for a patent from £25 for three years to £4 for four years. The result has been very satisfactory ; it has enabled poor men to get into the patent market; but having got there they find there are other tolls to pay in the shape of ruinous renewal fees; and after taking the first step the way is in a measure blocked to them. There must of course be fees of some kind to cover the expenses of the Patent Offict ; but will anybody say that the Patent Office is entitled to make a large profit out of in- ventors? We should think not; and yet that is exactly how the matter stands. The annual cost is between £58,000 and £60,000 per year; and this is fully covered by the initial fees. But the renewal fees amount to over £90,000 per year; *Aid inventors complain, and rightly complain, that they are being plundered by this unnecessary tax upon their skill and industry. More than this, it was disclosed so far back as 1883, that the accumulated funds derived from patents amounted to £2,000,000. This large sum, at three per cent. interest, would realise £60,000; that is to say, it is quite sufficient in itself to cover the Patent Office expenses. Questioned at the beginning of the Session as to the surplus funds, Mr. GOSCHEN sug- gested that the present scale "operated rather to the advantage of manufacturers, causing insignifi- cant patents to fall out." But if patents fall out because of renewal of fees, and are yet worthy of being used by manufacturers, it is obvious surely that the poor inventor is the victim of the rich manufacturer. Further, how can a patent be said to be insignificant which is at the same time to "the advantage of manufacturers?" We were on the right track in reducing the ini- tial fee ; but we need to go further and American- Ise our Patent Laws by abolishing renewal fees. In the United States, a valid title to a patent is given for 17 years upon payment in fees of RI. In England the title is for 14 years —three years less—and, instead of £7, the sum exacted in fees is £154. The difference is glaring; and having regard, to the fact that such a sum is not required at the Patent Office, it must be admitted that it is as iniquitous as it is glaring. Another thing; when a patent is granted in America, it is issued as a valid one; that is to say it holds good against all corners. In this country it is quite otherwise. The Patent Office takes the money, but that is not to say that a patent is thereby rendered valid. That is a point which is left for settlement among patentees them- selves. Indeed, the Patent Office has been known to grant patents for the same invention several times over; and when a discovery of this kind is made there is no such thing as returning fees. It may seem a small matter to mention that the time f.lhould be extended to 17 years as in America; but it happens that English patents running in the United States lose the benefit of the longer time when they lapse in this country. It comes to this that England ought to be in a position to give her inventors as much encouragement as is given in other countries ; and there is no reason, so far as We can see, why this should not be done. Brother JONATHAN may be ahead in labour saving appli- ances, but who can say how much of this is due to the help which he has had from fostering patent laws? We have seen a great impetus given to in- vention in this country by reducing the initial fee, and we shall witness a still greater as soon as we are wise enough to abolish renewal fees. The Patent Office is worked at present as if it was in- tended to repress inventors ; it should be worked 80 as to encourage them. We cannot afford to deal unjustly with our pioneers of progress.

Brunner, M.P., <opened on Tuesday bazaar in the Town Hall, Sand- bach, for the purpose of clearing off a debt on the Sandbach Liberal Club, and establishing a library. Mrs. Brunner explained that Mr. Brunner would have been present, but, as they kne*, in North- wich and the salt districts the land subsidences Were causing the houses to crack and tumble about their heads, and Mr. Brunner had stayed in London to watch the last stage of his Bill, which would bring compensation to their neighbours, who were heavy sufferers. (near, )ear.) She expressed sym- pathy with the object of the bazaar. It was quite light that there should be social centres for Liberals in every town. She was not a politician herself but Mr. Brunner quite made up for that. 'She generally trusted him in his politics, for he was anxiousto do right, to help the poor, and to keep ritaincin the front rank of nations. div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Croft has been keeping up an old custom by holding a Strawberry Fair. Strawberry fare is good—especially crushed with sugar, and with a liberal sprinkling of cream. The man who " always comes home to tea," ought to have it every time whilst the season lasts.

A "Ratepayer" suggests that the horses which cost the Warrington Corporation £7O or I:80 should be ticketed. Otherwise, ho says, nobody will be able to distinguish them from other horses in the street. Ratepayers ought to have an op- portunity of admiring these high-priced animals.

We seem to be getting the better of the in- fluenza fiend; there is an improvement in the mortality returns issued by the Registrar-General. La3t week the lowest return amongst 28 large towns was 13 per 1,000 at Nottingham. The highest was only 24, and that was at Wolverhamp- ton.

The Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants held a meeting, on Monday, to discuss amongst other things a general federation of trades. It i was pointed out that t might result in cAiers being induced not to work on Good Friday; and that would mean, in some parts of the country, a release to railway SPTVarlt, That would make a real Good Friday.

Female candidates for the civil service continue to be successful. As many as 78 have recently been added to the staff, no small number of them going to the Savings Bank department. There was a time when there would have been an outcry against these appointments; but that day has gone by. It is recognised that "our girls" as well as "our boys must have a chance in life.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, Thomas Bate, described as a herb collector, was committed to take his trial at the next Quarter Sessions for obtaining sixpence by means of a trick. He had, it is alleged, taken some herbs to a house, representing that they had been ordered, and obtained the money. He has not ceased to study herbs, but the herb which at present receives most of his attention is "rue."

The touch of nature which makes the whole world kin has been seen in the universal expression of sympathy with Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone on the loss of their eldest son. Mr. Gladstone appears to be bearing up bravely; but" sorrow ends not when it seemeth done ;" and there is reason to fear that the shock and strain may be too much for "The old man eloquent." That he may live to complete his work by giving freedom to Ireland is the prayer of many an earnest heart.

When it comes to an election contest, Mr. Par- nell is like the man who fell out of the balloon— he isn't in it. It was thought his nominee had something like a chance at Carlow; but what is the result :—Hammond, (Nationalist), 8,755; Kettle, (Parnellite) 1,539. This is not merely knocking the bottom out of the Parnellite " kettle "as suggested—it is knocking it all to pieces. Well done, Carlow! "Old Ireland shall blossom again."

Liverpudlians have shown a disposition to magnify any mishaps that have occurred in connec- tion with the Ship Canal ; but they have something else now to occupy their attention. It Las been d•scovered that the leakage in the temporary pipe across the Mersey is no trifle, as at first suggested. It is stated that out of six million gallons of water per day discharged from the Vrynwy Lake about four millions finds its way into the river. This is bad for Liverpool, but good for the Mersey; it will help to purify it.

Councillor Dixon is like the farmer who tried champagne—he doesn't get "no forrader." This anent his proposals to discharge the Sanitary Committee of the Warrington Corporation "in con- sequence of the mismanagement of Longford and the Intercepting Depots." The Committee are ahead of him in the discharging business; they have discharged two managers in as many months, and yet they are not happy. Those who ought to know say that the condition of things at Longford is a case of" chaos come again."

The giant Electricity is being got more and more under control. In the form of lightning, many people are killed by it every year, and there is not much likelihood of checking its destruction in that direction. But electricity is now being applied in the execution of criminals. Four condemned men were put out of existence by this method in New York on Tuesday. Popular feeling is as yet against the process; but when it is established beyond doubt that death is sudden and painless there will be a change of opinion on the subject.

Lord Randolph Churchill has been showing up the neglect of the Government in the defence of Capetown. He does not spare Lord Salisbury, who, he says, falsely accused him of being desirous, when Chancellor of the Exchequer in 1866, of leaving ur coaling stations in a de- fenceless condition. It appears that the garrison at Capetown is as ridiculously weak in men as it ridiculously strong in officers. But what is the use of having officers, if they are not to draw their pay, and, in some corner of the world or other, help each other to do nothing?

The sceptic, (he 'was understood to hail from Liverpool), who said the Ship Canal would "never be made" would do well to pay a visit to the Eastham section, on Monday, to witness the open- ing of that end of the Canal for traffic. According to present arrangements, about four o'clock the vessels for Ellesmere Port will enter the big locks at Eastham Ferry, and the Canal then being open, the present entrance at Ellesmere Port will be closed and immediately filled up. The sceptic need not think that he will be alone. There will be plenty of people present to "give three cheers and one cheer more" for the success of the undertak- ing.

The School Board of Runcorn, on Tuesday even- ing, had under consideration the effect which the , Education Bill would be likely to have upon the Board Schools. From calculations which had been made, it was found that the Government scheme would leave them in such a position that they would have to levy a Halfpenny Fee in each school under the Board, or take what would be equivalent to this fee from the rates. It was thought that the latter course would be by far the best, and the Chairman intimated his intention of moving a resolution to that effect at a future meeting.

Runcorn happily finds an easy way out of the difficulty; and the same course will probably be taken in othcr towns. But what of such places as Warrington' and St. Helens where there is no School Board F They will be under the necessity of levying ridiculously small fees, or trying to make up the difference by increasing their volun- tary subscript;ons. They will thereby struggle against fate, and that fate is the establishment of a School Board soon or late. Better soon than late, thns equalising the burden,andtaking advantage of the extensive powers conferred on School Boards. Warrington and St. Helens are standing in their ownlight, but as yet they are not able to perceive that they are doing so.

We are on the eve of another revolution, and yet how little most people realize it! It is not an outcome of the labour movement, or the social question, or the efforts of the Salvation Army. It is—whisper it softly—because, according to "The Royalist,' " Jacobitism is spreading fast in the country." So fast indeed is it spreading that we are told " the whole business looks ominous for the destinies of the usurpini House of Hanover." Thus it happens that we are all panting for the restoration, of "the Stuart dynasty"; but were not aware of it until the fact was pointed out by the editor of" The Royalist." That editor mast tell us some More—before his retirement to Rainhill.

Mr. W. IL Walker and Mr. George Woods were the Warrington witnesses who gave evidence on Monday, before the Lords Committee, in support of the proposed new railway from the East Coast to Warrington. The Mayor arid Borough Sur-

veyor were in attendance, but were not called upon to give evidence. On Wednesday, Mr. Mar- shall Stevens, General Manager of the Ship Canal, stated that it was the intention of the Ship Canal Company to construct a line of railway, as they have power to do, from Warrington to Manchester —along the canal. The idea is to reduce ter- minal charges, and save time when required. This line would be worked of course in connection with the East Coast Railway; and it is therefore evi- dent that the whole project is one of great moment to WaErington. The Bill will pass this session, for the preamble has been proved to the satisfac- tion of both Houses of Parliament.
MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday, at St. Paul's Chapel, a marriage was solemnised between Mr. Wm. Coventry. son of Mr. Samuel Coventry• tailor, Church-st.,and Miss Kirkham, daughter of Mr. Wm. Kirkhain,plumber, Lowlands-road. The wedding party and guests were conveyed to chapel in three carriages drawn by pairs of grey horses supplied by Messrs. Yarwood Bros. The invited guests were so numerous that Bethesda Lecture Hall was engaged for the luncheon. Probate of the will, dated sth March. 1874, with codicils made the 21st December, 1881, and 14th August,lBB4,of the late Mr. Edward Abbott Wright, J.P., of Castle Park, Frodsham, Cheshire, who died on the 24th April last, aged 83 years, leaving per- sonal estate of the value of £674,821 12s. 4d., has been granted 'o the executors, his brother by half- blood, Mr. James Collinge, of Kinnerton Lodge, Flint; Mr. John Knowles, of Westwood. Pendle- bury ; and Mr. Lees Knowles, M.P., of 45, Upper Grosvenor-st., Bryanston-square, and of Westwood. To each of his executors the testator bequeaths , I £100; to his housekeeper, head gardener, and a farm servant, £l9 19s. each ; to an old servant, a life annuity of £25; to his daughter Mary Berry, £14,500; to his daughter Harriet Elizabeth,.Clo,ooo ; and to his daughter Emily Priscilla, £5,500. The testator's unmarried daughters are to have the use and enjoyment of Castle Park and its furniture,and he devises all his real estate upon trusts for his three daughters above-named, and his daughter Julia Lees, or, on failure of the trust's for his daugh- ters, then upon trusts for this said half-brother, Mr. Coinage, and his sister, Mrs. Barlow.
VIOLENT ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN LANDLORD.

At Runzorn Police Court, on Monday, Frederick Williams was charged with drunkenness and refus- ing to quit the Stanley Arms, Rnncorn, and with as- saulting the landlord, Mr. Harrison. On Saturday evening, about seven o'clock, the prisoner entered the house and asked to be served with beer. He was refused, and then declared that he would go ovet the c minter and take it himself. Mr. Harrison went to the door to look for a policeman, as he could not geZ, rid ot him any other way. While at the door he got a "rattle on the side of the head," which knocked him down. As he lay On the ground he received two kicks. He got up, but had scarcely reached the perpendicular when he received a blow on the jaw. Down he went again. Some young fellows came up and rescued him. The prisoner with much difficulty was forced outside the door,but he soon rushed in at another door. Some men in the vaults threw him out into the street again, and he again tried to re-enter. He then went to the cocoa shop near, and created a dis- turbance there also, but after a time he was put out. He then made direct once more for the Stanley Arms. He entered, and seized the landlord, and dragged him across his own tap-room floor. When the police were seen corning up the street he bolted for his lodgings in Brook-st. He was shortly after arrested. Mr. Harrison did not know prisoner, and the only cause of the vio- lence was the refusal to serve him with drink.—The magistrates fined him 10s. and cgsts for being drunk on licensed premises, and £1 and costs for the assault, in default 28 days in prison.

div.head: HOME IHON TRADE.
div.p: THE HOME IHON TRADE.

The English iron market continues very quiet; but prices are still steadily maintained. The Glas- gow warrant market remains in a lifeless condition and Scotch makers' iron is inactive, with the majority of brands showing a reduction of 6d. per ton on the week. Bessemer pig is fairly steady, but Cleveland pig is somewhat lower, with only a poor demand. Manufactnred iron shows little im - pro vement, and nearly all descriptions of steel are quiet. Tinplates are dull and prices have a declin- ing tendency, *tuplAulderl and engineers are fair- ly employea.—/ros.

div.head: HIRE SYSTEM.
div.p: THE HIRE SYSTEM.

At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Judge Shand, Robert Pownall, jeweller, brought an action for the recovery of a silver lever watch, valued at .£3, from George Cammack, pawn- broker. Church-at. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. H. L. Riley for the defendant. The watch had been sold by PoWnall on the hire system to a man named Roberts. and it was after- wards found pledged at defendant's shop. The defence was that the watch was obtained in the ordinary way of business, and that there were tech- nical objections to the validity of the hire agree- ment. His Honour intimated that he would reserve his decision. 1. W. Darrow's SIMMER SALE now on.—Advt. • MACHINERY FATUITY AT Sr. HELENS.

Henry Webster, 18 years of age, of 69, Traverse- at., Parr, died at the Providence Hospital, on Tues- day night from injuries received during the after- noon at the brick works of Messrs. Kurtz and Co., Langtreerst., where he had been employed as a booking clerk. The unfortunate young man entered what is known as the "elevator room," and by some means his clothing got entangled with a strap round the revolving shaft near the ceiling. He was drawn to the top, and on the machinery being stopped he was found to have received shocking , injuries. His left leg had caught the skylight in roof, and his foot was completely torn away, while his right arm and side were lacerated. Dr. Reid was summoned,and the injured youth was removed to the hospital. His leg and arm were subsequently amputated, but he gradually sank, and expired at ten o'clock the same night. _

John Gibbon, a Ship Canal labourer, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court, charged with wilfully damaging a sweetmeat machine belonging to the Variety Automatic Simply Store, Limited, and also with assaulting P.C. Worth. On Saturday evening the priioner placed !I penny in the slot of a ma- chine on Runcorn Railway -Station, and drew forth a packet of sweets in return. He then placed in another penny. but not working the machine pro- perly, be failed to obtain a second packet, where- upon he broke off the knob, smashed the glass front, and finally threw the machine over bodily, seriously damaging it. P.C. Worth was called in, and the prisoner attacked him violently, kicking him and striking him with his fists.--The prisoner was ordered to pay .E 2 damage and costa us. 4d., and 10s. and costa for the assault.
