div.head: BATCH OF WIFE DESERTERS AT
div.p: BATCH OF WIFE DESERTERS AT
RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Benjamin Taylor, a flat man,- was summoned by his wife Eliza, for deserting her. Mr. Lake appeared for the plain- tiff and Mr. Knowles of Widnes defended. It was alleged that on several occasions the defendant had thrown his wife out of doors, and the nolice had also been called in to protect her from his violence. On the 18th June he assaulted her and smashed most of the furniture with an axe. The furniture had been removed from the house and she was now. homeless. Complainant said she would live with the defendant if he would take the pledge as he was actually mad when in drink.--Mr. Knowles said breaking up the furniture did not amount to deser- tion although it was reckless drunken conduct. There was no doubt the wire had struck her hus- band with the poker several times. He was willing to take her back, and become teetotal and he did not know why she should not avail herself of the 'offer unless her affeccion for another man was greater than that of husband.--The defendant said they could live comfort- ably if his wife's .son-in-law would keep away. He charged his own son by his first marriage with impro- priety with the plaintiff. He 'was going to get com- mand of a flat, and she could live comfortably in it if she plmsed.—The plaintiff denied the charges of impropriety, and said she only wanted to be kept as a wife should be. —The Bench considered the desertion proved and made an order for the payment of ss. per week together with costs.—George Evan Jones, was summoned by his wife Mary Ann, for deserting her. Mr. Lake prosecuted and Mr. Humphreys defended. It appeared the parties had been married three years anti fiad one child and it was said the defendant's mother.and sister were the cause of the disagreement. A few weeks .ago they entered and after some talk about the defendant being lazy, the , sister attazked complainant, and the defendant encou- raged her to thrash her. He had sold all the furniture, and was now living with his mother at Weston. He had offered to nay her fare home to Birmingham, and to pay her ss. a week, but she had refused it.—ln answer to Mr. Hinnplireys, complainant said she had run into debt, but it was for necessaries.—The defendant re- peated the offers he had made to-her. He had remon- strated with her for keeping bad company, but she had merely sworn at him and defied him. She had laid com- plaints against him at the Ship Canal works, with the re- sult that he was dismissed. He had still £l2 of her debts to pay. When his sister thrashed her he saw "fair play," and she got no more than she deserved .He did say "Give it to her,Nance,"when they were fighting. —The magistrates held that ,there had b'een desertion, ordered the defendant to pay 10s. a.week to his wife, and the costs 23s.—Annie Bowden summoned her hus- band, Thomas Bowden, ' for neglecting to support her. The defendant admitted having left his wife, but said it was through her drunken habits. They had been mar- ried 11 years and had been.separated five times.—The complainant said her husband got drunk and abused her. He earned from £1 to £2 a week, but he never gave her £2.—The defendant said he was willing tO contribute towards her support in the Workhouse, but not other- wise. On one occasion she was brought home drunk by a number .of navvies, and on another occasion she was locked up in a house with a man.—ln answer to the

div.head: SEQUEL TO A GAME OF DOMINOES AT HALTON. EXTR &ORDIN A EtY CONDUCT.
div.p: SEQUEL TO A GAME OF DOMINOES AT HALTON. EXTR &ORDIN A EtY CONDUCT.

On Monday afternoon, Mr. H. Churton held an inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of William Stringfellow, aged 23 years, labourer at the Soap and Chemical Works, Weston Point, near Runcorn, at the Victoria Infirmary, Northwich. Robert Stringfellow, of Winnington Park, said the de- ceased was his son. Witness first saw his son after the accident, a fortnight last Sunday, when he was brought to his house in a trap from Halton. He was attended immediately by Dr. Hassell, of Northwich, who found his left leg broken below the knee. The limb had been set by Dr. Carruthers, of Halton. The fracture was a compound one. His son was removed to the Infirmary the same day, in accordance with the recommendation of the d )ctor, who continued to attend him. He seemed to be progressing satisfactorily until the Ist inst., when he began to suffer from lockjaw. lie was conscious and remained so until his death on Saturday. Witness never. asked under what circumstances the accident happened, nor did his son volunteer a statement, either to him or ' anyone else to his knowledge. Deceased was a strong heslthy young man, and quite steady when at home,but could not speak as to his conduct when away. Frederick Booth, of Rock Savage, near, Weston, , labourer, said he was acquainted with the deceased. He was at Halton Castle about eight o'clock on the night of the 20th ult., and saw Stringfellow and another person playing a game at dominoes. The men were not sober. After playing about a quarter of an hour Sringfellow ran out of the house, followed by the other man. He crossed the bowling green, and jumped from a wall, a depth of about,a dozen feet. Witnes3 went out and saw deceased lying on the road below with his leg broken. He did not know the reason of Stringfellow's running away, further than that Win. Snape, with whom he was play- ing, wished to create a disturbance, and deceased did not want to quarrel. Tire injured 'man was carried to the residence of his grandmother, where he remained un- til the following inorning.—ln answer to questions from jurors, witness said the deceased was neither drunk nor sober ; he had had a glass or two of beer. No word passed between the parties before Stringfellow ran out of the room. Deceased won the game, which was for 25., and he having picked up the money Snape made an effort to take it from him. Snap, pulled off his jacket, and there upon Stringfellow ran away, with Snape after him. He did not hear any threats used ; but Snap° assumed a threatening attitude by taking off his jacket. He appar- entiv meant bother.

William Snape. ot Halton,: said he had known the deceased some few months. He was a teiend of his. There was a good many people on the bowfin. green. He and Stringfellow were a little elated, witness having gin as his beverage. They commenced to play( a game at dominoes, and witness was the loser. Thinking there had been some cheating, and that the game was not a fair one, witness expressed dissatisfaction, whereupon deceased pushed him end then let the house. Witness remained for a minute to finish his drink, and then crossed the green asking " Where is Will ?" Snape fell over the wall, injuring his face 'slightly, as well as spraining his arm. He did not push the deceased in any way, nor did they come to blows. He was not chasing Stringfellow- in hot pursuit, for deceased had jumped over the wall a couple of minutes before witness fell over.

John Barrow, of Halton deposed that on the evening in question he was on the lower road, and saw the deceased put his hands on the bowling green wall and jump over. He chopped with one leg under him, and it was subsequently found that the limo was fractured. He was not thrown over, there being no one there at the time.—lly a juror: Snape came over the wall two or three minutes later, and he was going to hit Stringfellow, but witness drew attention to the fact that his kg was broken. The people on the bowling green also came and shouted, So that Snape never touched him. The. Coroner said he felt satisfied with the evidence, and he thought the only verdict the jury could return was "Died from tetanus, or lockjaw, caused by an acci- dental fall."

The jury agreed, and that verdict was recorded. Mr. Williams, a juror, asked if the police would take cognizance of the fact that the two men were playing a game for money in a public-house,and would they bring the matter before the notice of the magistrates?

The Coroner said that the Court had nothing to do with the subject further than inquire into the cause of the death of Stringfellow. With regard to gaming, it was for those residing in the locality to take action, and it was for the police and magistrates of the district of Halton to wnsider whether it was right and proper for people to assemble in a half drunken state, in a licensed house, and to be allowed to gable.
P.S. Hunt intimated that the matter would be fully re- ported to the Chief Constable.
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. Present Messrs. J. Pritchard (chairman), J. llowitt, A.Salkeld, and S. Taylor, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, and Mr. G. Moss (clerk.)

STAFF APPOINTMENTS. The Clerk read the minntes of a special meeting which was held on June 30, when Frederick William Upton was appointed a pupil teacher at Greenway-road boys' school Harriet B. Smith, a pupil teacher whose apprenticeship had expired, was appointed assistant mistress at Mill Brow infant school. A special meeting was also held on July 4th, when the selected candidates for the post of head teacher at Mill Brow school were in attennance. Miss M. D. Robb, of Fairford, Gloucestershire, was ap- pointed at a salary of £75 per annUm.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. The attendanca officers reported that during June the percentage of attendances was 84, which, although one less than last year, was considered highly satisfactory in face of the baa attendance caused by sickness.

TEACHING SEWING. The Clerk presented the requisition for sewing material for the coming year. amounting to £915. 3d. Last year the amount was £8 lls, and there were articles sold amounting to £5 es. id. In answer to some observations by Dr. Gastaldi, the clerk said in teaching the children to sew, there was considerable waste of material. It was the best spent money of the Board. __ FREE EDUCATION FOR RUNCORN.

The Elementary Education Bill now nefore Parliament provides for a grant of 103. a year for each child of the number ot children in average attendance at school in lieu of fees. Where this fee -grant involves a loss to a school as compared with the amount of fees received in the last school year ended before January Ist, 1891, a fee may be charged to cover the loss. Applying these provisions to the Gre.enway-road Schools for the year

ended June 30th, 1890, the amount of fees received was £263 17s. 6d. the average rate per child being us. BA-ci. on an average attendance of 451. The tee grant of 10s. per child would be £225 10s., shew- ing a loss of £3B 7s. 6d. or is. 80. per scholar per annum. The Board will be at liberty either to continue charging the present fees or to accept the grant. —ln the latter case a fee of id. per week might be ; charged, so as to cover the loss, but the power to levy this small fee would be subject to the provision of a sufficient amount of free accommodation in the district. At the Mill Brow Infant school the average rate of fees received for each scholar per annum is Bs. 9d. so that here the fee grant would be a gain of is. 3d. per child amounting to about £7 on the school. In this case it will be compulsory to accept the grant and to abolish fees.—The Chairman said he had been anxious to know what the result of free education would be in regard to their schocls.—Mr. Howitt : I beg your pardon ! It is not free education, unfortunately.—The Chairman: Pretty near so I think. At the same time it would be very much more satisfactory if the Government had made their proposals so that free education could have been obtained without any loss to the ratepayers. From the statement of the the clerk it appeared that 1 there would be a small loss of about £3O. The Board would have power to impose fee to cover that amount, but considering that the fee involved was only one halfpenny a week; he thought the ratepayers at large would prefer to bear this small burden and have their schools free. (Hear, hear.) The imposition of a small fee of a half- penny would be quite as troublesome and would involve as much loss of time to the teachers as an ordinary fee— (hear,hear)—and if a small fee of this kind was abolished it would be a gain in an educational pointof view, as the teachers would be prepared to give their whole time to instructicn. He gave notice that at theanext meeting he , would move that7thegrant of 10s. per scho'iir be accepted and that fees be abolished. If the Bill noa‘nefore Parlia- ' ment should pass the two Houses in the form it was at present, and his motion was passed, free education would come into operation so far as the Runcorn Board Schools were concerned on the Ist September next. —Mr. Howitt said he was exceedingly pleased that the Government, particularly this Government, had seen their way to give us the semblance of free educa- tion. He would rather they had given free education pure , and simple, but of course from the party in power we , could not expect much more than we had got. It was a bill that did not please anybody, but at the same time it was the thin end of the wedge and was a step towards , what they advanced people had been arguing for many Years past. The members would remember that at the - first meeting of the Board he gave notice of the motion to petition Parliament for free education; he did not expect that the present Government would ever do such a thing; but he was happy to say they were growing wiser day by day, and in a short time we should get Free Education.
THE EVENING CLAMS.

The Chairman said the evening classes were so success- ful last winter, and were shown to be so absolutely neces- sary, that it was the duty of the Board to make every effort to establish the classes early in September. There were about 150 students receivieg instruction in the ele- mentary subjects,and the Board would feel it incumbent upon them to continue that instruction. There were also classes for chemistry,other sciences,and modern lan- guages, which the Board were not then in a position to take up, but which the necessities of the district de- manded to be taught. There was now a fund in the hands of the Commissioners which would reach nearly £4OO, and would be available in aid of science and technical instruction, and in his opinion the Board ought to ask the Commissioners to make a moderate grant out of this fund towards any deficiency that might arise in working these classes. (Hear, hear.) Therefore he proposed " that science and art classes be held during the forthcoming winter months Pin connection with the evening school at Greenway-road and that Runcorn Improvement Commissisners be re- quested to make a grant to cover any defiliency that might arise out of the fund at their disposal for purposes of technical education." (Hear, hear.)—Canon Wood seconded the motion.—Mr. Howitt supported the motion. Nothing pleased him more than to see the success of these classes after the trouble and, anxiety they had in getting them formed. Several incidents occurred which were worthy of the notice of the members and of every educationalist in the country. He attended several of the meetings and saw young men learning the first rudi- ments of figures working hard to try and retrieve the steps they had lost by the negleqof their parents or their own want of determination when young. and some of them came through the examination marvellously well. One incident of this kind VMS sufficient far them as a School Board to go on more determinedly in the future to make the night classes a success.—The motion was carried unanimously.

At Widnes Police Court on Tuesday, a ma.rried woman named Crank, of Sankey-st., was charged with obtaining by false pretences a suit of clothes value 253. from J. Williamson, clothier, Victoria-road. div.head: RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE.
div.p: RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE.

At the fortnightly meeting of the above Order, on Saturday, an essay was read by Mr. James Johnson, on "Gambling." The various forms of gambling were de- scribed in a very lucid manner, and also the enormous evils resulting from the practice of the vice. The evil was not confined to one class of Society ; rich and poor, men and women, and even the young, indulged in the baneful hit. Homes were shattered, undeserved shame was brought on innocent children. Gambling withered and hardened the better feelings of our nature. A very interesting discussion followed, in which Messrs. Edw. Key,S. H. Temperley,Thomas Heesom, Daniel Bisbrown, T. Cook, James Bisbrown, and W. Cooke took part. Mr. Wesley Cook occupied the chair.

METHODIST FREE CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The anniversary of this school was celebrated on Sun- day, when to Rev. J. Billington, of Redruth, preached morning and evening in Ellesmere-sc. Chapel. Some years ago Mr. Billington was pastor of the chapel, and his visit was regarded with great pleasure and satisfac- tion the chapel being filled with a large congregation at each service. In the afternoon the choir and elder scholars rendered the cantata "Under the Palms" in capital style, under the leadership of Mr. John Holford, G.T.S.C. The collections in aid of the school fund realised £26 7s. On Monday evening Mr. Billington delivered a popular lecture in the Widnes U.M.F.C. Schoolroom, the chair being taken by Mr. A. G. Hale, of lloylake. The lecture was well attended, many of the old friends of the lecturer gathering together upon the occasion.
AUTToN's SUMMER -SALE now on.—Advt. ALLEGED BLACKMAIL AT DITTON.

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Timothy Con- roy, of Halebank, was charged with having obtained from Mrs. Taylor, landlady of the Clapgate Hotel, Hale- bank, the sum of £5 by means of menaces and -threats. On Tuesday Mrs. Taylor received a servant on prisoner's recommendation ;Ind next morning the girl told her she was going to leave as two men had behaved improperly towards her. Shortly afterwards the prisoner came and alleged that she kept a bad house, at the same time de- manding compensation. He threatened that unless she would give him £5 he would report the matter to Sergt. Nobblett and have her license taken from her. Mrs. Taylor became frightened and handed him over the money.—The prisoner admitted having received the money but alleged that he had obtained it as compensa- tion for the girl whom he had recommended. The pri- soner was remanded for a week, but was liberated on bail himself in £2O and two Sureties of £lO each.

BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL, RiniCons. The anniversary of this school was celebrated on Sun- day last, and was invested with more than usual interest, because it was the occasion of a visit from the Rev. W. H. Mann, of Natal, South Africa. On completing his theological training at the Lancashire Independent College in 1855, Mr. Mann became pastor of Bethesda Chapel and for four years held the appointment after- wards ministering at Mill Elill,Blackburn. At this time he was chosen by the Colonial Missionary Society to organise and superintend the mission churches of the Colony of Natal, whilst also having the pastoral oversight of the church of Dunbar. For 27 years he has been engaged Ln this work and with extremely succeesful results; and the esteem in which he is held is shown by the facts that he visits England to attend the International Council in London as the unanimously selected representative of the Churches of Natal and Cape Colony. That his old parishioners should flock to hear him ic therefore no matter for surprise, and crowded congregations filled Bethesda Chap9l on Sunday, and were gratified by listeaing to two eloquent discourses. In the afternoon the annual flower service Was helcl,and the sacred edifice beautifully decorated for the occasi^n. The IleY. John Simpson delivered an address on "flowers."

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday. Mr. T. S. Timmins presided, and there were present Rev. Father Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, Major Wareing, , Messrs. R. H. Davies, H. W. Deacon, B. Brown, and G. 11. Danby (clerk). On the recommendation of the General Purposes Committee the salary of Caretaker Noone, West Bank School, was increased from .E 1 is. 6d. to .4.:1 104. The District Education Committee reported that 187 applications had been made I for free schooling, and the fees were recommended to be Ipaid in 166 eases. Forty-one parents had been prose- cured and 40 convicted for not sending their children , regularly to school. Accounts amounting to £650 were pased for payment on the recommendation of the Finance Committee.—The Chairman referring to the Free Educa- tion Bill said said as it would CORM into operation on September Ist, it was time the Board considered their position in this matter. He thought they ought not to do anything without consulting the managers of the denominational schools in the town, and he proposed that a special meeting he held when the Bill had been passed and printed. He also suggested that the Clerk should supply each member with a copy and prepare a report showing how it would affect their schools if adopted.—The Chairman's suggestions were accepted.

div.head: PEN KETH.
div.p: PEN KETH.
TRIP TO BLACKPOOL.

The annual trip of th(-3--em—p-10-iis-Of the Penketh Tanning Co., Limited, took place on Saturday, to Blackpool. The trippers, numbering about 150, left the Ferry at 5.15 a.m., and Blackpool was reached shortly after nine o'clock. During the day, the Palace Gardens. the Winter Palace, the Aquarium, . and other places of interest were visited, whilst numbers amused themselves with bathing, sailing, and seeing the various attractions on the sands. After spending a pleasant day, the return journey was commenced at 6.45, and Warrington reached at 8.45. Great credit is due to the London and North-Western Railway Company for the admirable manner in which they carried out the arrange- ments.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

SUNDAYSCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.—Sermons were preached in the United Methodist Free Church, Frodsham, on Sunday, by the Rev. P. B. Newall, .of St. Helens, the subjects of his discourses lving—in the morning, "Jesus, the Master ;" afternoon, "A Model Home;" and evening, "A Perfect Man." The choir assisted by several friends, rendered effectively appropriate anniversary hymns and anthems. Tho collections realized £l4 16s.

div.head: CHURCH BAZAAR AT FRODSHAM.
div.p: CHURCH BAZAAR AT FRODSHAM.

In Frodshara Girls' School, on Wednesday after- noon a three days' bazaar was opened by Lady Brooke, of Norton Priory. The object of the bazaar was to raise funds for enlarging and recon- structing the boys' school, which is incapable of "providing sufficient accommodation for the demand made upon it. There was a large and fashionable company present, and included besides the stall holders Mr. C. Reynolds, J.P., Mrs. Reynolds, Miss IVright, Mr. 11. Reynold, .LP., Dr. Steele, J.F., Mr. John Simpson, Mr. J. W. Lightburn, Mr. U. Linaker, Mr. R. G. Linaker, Dr. Robinson, Miss Talbot, Miss Mathiesen, Miss Steele, Mrs. Nickson, Miss Cooke, Mrs. Jones, Mrs. G. Whitlow, Rey. Ca,non Wood, Rev. S. C. Barmby, Mr. Dunsford, sec., &c. In opening the pro- ceedings the Vicar (the Rev. H. B. Illogg) explained the object of the bazaar, stating that far some time her Majesty's Inspector had reported unfavourably of the boys' school and they had found it incumbent on them to improve, to restore, and to a very large extent recon- struct the school. Describing the bazaar, the Vicar pointed out that they were not having raffles. In his opinion they were a species of gambling and were illegal and immoral.—Lady Brooke after a few brief observations declared the bazaar open and then tne Vicar on behalf of the Committee presented her With a floral basket.—The ladies then commenced the sale of their wares, which were arranged on a series of most artistically draped stalls. The following were stallholders Miss Chap- man assisted by Mrs. Carpenter ; (2), Miss SimosOn as- sisted by Mrs. H. Reynolds, Mrs. Dunsford, and the Misses Simpson ; (3),Mrs• H. Talbot,Mrs. Heron,Miss Blaine,and Miss Reynolds; (4), Mrs. C. Linaker, Miss Linaker, Miss Davies, and Miss Chrimes ; (5), Mrs. C. Bevnolds.assisted by Miss Sarah .Crosfiel(l, and Mrs. Blame; (6), Mrs. Thomas assisted by Miss Jane Crosfietd, and Miss M. Crosfield (7), Miss Chapman assisted by Miss Pride and Miss Woodall. Dairy stall, Mrs. Edwards and Miss Clarke, assisted by Miss Aston and Mrs. Ben Rigby; tobacco 81.311' Mrs. W. Wigg : Refreshment stall, The Misses Ash- ley. Various entertainments were provided for the amusement of vi-itors. The childreri rendered a cantata entitled ‘• Cinderella " written by the Bev. J. Barmby, rural dean of Durham, and brother to the curate of Frodsham. The proceMs of the first day amounted to £219 138. sd. The bazaar on Thursday was opened be Mr. 11. Tollernache, M.P., who expressed the hope that they would now, after the passing..of the Free Edu- cation rally round thcir denominational schools

more eagerly than ever. It had been acknowledged by Mr. Gladstone that voluntary schools were of immense benefit to this country, and it wns well-known that they received and educated a considerably larger number of the youth of the population than Board scheols. The working-classes ought now to be able to accomplish more than ever for the support of such excellent and purely voluntary schools as those in the charge of the Vicar of Frodsham.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF A WOMAN.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF A WOMAN.

About one o'clock yesterday aft,Tnoon, Mrs. An Southern, agen 76 years, a widow residing with , her son, a French polisher, at 4 Grove-road, Latch- ford, was found dead at hisresidence. A neighbour named Mary Ellen Chorley found deceased leaning back in a chair in the kitchen, and on speaking to her could obtain no answer. She brought other neighbours in and it was ascertained to a cer- tainty that Mrs. Southern was dead. She had en- joyed good health, having merely occasionally complained of slight pains in the chest, which she attributed to rheumatism or indigestion, though about nine months since she was an out patient of the Infirmary for erysipelas in the face.

div.head: VOLUNTEER FUNERAL
div.p: A VOLUNTEER FUNERAL

On Sunday afternoon, the remains of Colour- Sergeant Bate of the Warrington Volunteer Corps, who died at Blackpool a few days after the encamp- ment there, were interred in the Cemetery at War- rington. At one o'clock, the funeral cortege started from the late residence of the deceased, at 64, Tur- ner-street. First in order of procession come the Volunteer Band, and a firing party, composed of 19 men and one sergeant, On the coffin, which was composed of oak with brass mountings, were the helmet, ',word and belt of the deceased, and about 20 beautiful wreaths from Colonel Greenall, Lieut.- Colonel Bolton, Captains Ridgway and Gooch, the sergeants' mess, Mr. and Mrs. Anderton, and others. The carriers were four sergeants belonging to de- ceased's company. Folio wing the hearse came a mounting coach containing the widow and five children and two other coaches with relatives and friends. After this followed the members of the battalion, numbering about 200, commanded by Captain Ridgway. When about 300 yards from the , Cemetery the band struck up the Dead March in "Saul." The burial service was read in the chapel by the Rev. Ef. V. Pigot, vicar of St. Paid's, and the Rector of Warrington (the Rev. P. W. Willis) offi- ciated at the graveside. After the battalion had returned to the Drill Hall, the men were addaessed by Captain Ridgway, who remarked that the de- ceased had neen upwards of 31 years in the carpel. He was always noted for attention to duty, and it had been a painful thing to him (Captain li,idgway) to follow his old comrade to the graveside.

div.head: SUICIDE IN A WARRINGTON SCHOOL.
div.p: SUICIDE IN A WARRINGTON SCHOOL.

On Tuesday morning an inquest was held by Mr. Coroner Brighouse in the Parade Room of the Police btation,touching the death of Alfred Earl, labourer, aged 49 years, of No. 9, Stevenson-st., which oc- curred under the circumstances hereafter detailed. Jane Earl, his wife, deposed that her husband got up on Sunday morning about 7.30, and left the house, leaving her in bed, and telling her he was going to the Hamilton-st. Schools. This had been his habit for the last five years. Recleaned the schools, ancl he went to get them ready. She expected him back at 8.30 to breakfast, but lie did not come back, so she went to the schools in search of him. She found th 3 cellar door wide open, and found the deceased hanging by a rope to the cellar grid. She touched him and he was cold. She went and told Mrs. Ellen Chadwick. The deceased had taken a clothes line from behind the closet door. Mrs. Chadwick told the police, who came and cut the deceased down. Witness and Mrs. Chad- wick thought he ought not to be cut down until the police came. He had been drinking for the last fortnight, and been overworked, and he had eaten nothing. He never threatened to take his life, and she never thought he would do so. He could not sleep at night, and that was the reason he had been taking too much drink. He had no trouble at all, and worked well.—Mrs. Chadwick said she was called to the school by Mrs. Earl, and found the deceased hang- ing up.—P.C. Wheatley said about 11. o'clock on Sunday morning he received information of the suicide of the deceased. Ho went to the school and in the coal cellar found the deceased hanging there quite cold and stiff; and at once cut him down. The women had been under the mistaken impression that they hathno right to cut him down. The place where he hung was very low, so that his feet were out and his knees only about four inches from the floor. He had hung himself to a chain, that came from the cellar grid. A verdict of suicide during temporary insanity was immediately returned.

div.head: DARESBII RY HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBII RY HIGHWAY BOARD.

fThe ordinary meeting of this Board was held on Thursday afternoon. Mr. J. C. Parr presided, and there were also present Messrs. W. Long, T. Darlington, J. Lee, J. L. Jones, P. Tickle, W. Bee- wick, T. S. Burgess, H. G. Linaker (clerk), and J. Swinton (surveyor).
LICRNCES TO WAYWARDENS.
Th.lClerk read a letter from the Local Government Board acknowledging receipt of the resolution of tha. Board inquiring if something could be done to reduce: the cost of these licenses.
TIER COUNTY COUNCIL AND MAIN ROADS.

A letter was read from the County Council stating that the Roads Committee for the Council assented to the request of the Board to take over as main roads the portions of the Northwich and Runcorn roads indi- cated by the Board, but that the Board would have tQ pay for such repairs as the county surveyor considered necessary. The Surveyor, in answer to Mr. Long, said the roads mentioned were in good repair. In reply to the Chairman, the Clerk said it was optional on the Board's part whether they confirmed the agreement or not.
TEE NEW 120A.D LT BOB'S BRIDGE.

A letter was read from Mr. Evans,agent to Sir Richar4 Brook, with reference to the construction of a new road in place of the ferry at Bob's Bridge, Moore, from which it appeared that there was no inclination to do anything in the matter.—The Chairman: If he doe 9 not move in the matter, I suppose we need not do so.-- Mr. Jones considered the Board could move in the mat- ter, and adopt the road in lieu of the ferry.—The Clerk said if the Board did so the Canal Company would tell them to mind their own business.—The Clerk was directed to ask Mr. Evans for a reply as to what was proposed to be done.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE

The minutes of this Committee were read. These showed that Mr. T. S. Burgess had been appointed Clerk, recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £665 Us. id., and mentioned that the balance in the Surveyor's hands was £72 us. 2d.--The minutes were adopted.
DEATH OF A WAYWARDES. The death of Mr. Joseph Clarke, waywarden for Cog.. shall, was reported.
THE SHIP CANAL CO.

The Surveyor reported that the new road over the rail- way bridge in Lapwing-lane, Moore, had been opened by the Ship Canal Co. and the traffic forced over before the road was completed, or certified by him.—The Chair- man: That is not as it should be.—The Surveyor said he had written to the Company, but had no reply, though there had hardly been time for that.—The Chair- man suggested that the Surveyor should write to Mr. Leader Williams stating that the Board had had o7.casion- to complain several times, and hoping that there woulci not be another cause of complaint, and pointing out to him that no road could be taken over until the Surveyor had çertified that it was fit for traffic.—This suggesttoti was accepted by the Board.—The Surveyor reportedthat a temporary crossing had been placed across the public road near the temporary bridge at Walton Inferior, and wa,s being used by the Canal Company before it, had been made safe, and to his satisfaction. He had complained to Mr. Walker on the subject, and had had. a reply.—The Clerk read this reply, which promised that the crossing should be made as stipulated in the agree- ment.—Mr. Beswick stated that the road had been opened since Whitsuntide, and was dangerous and much complained about. Somebody," he feared, would be killed on it some day.—The Board resolved to enforce the agreement as to this road. NEXT MEETING.-It was decided to hold the next meeting on October 15th.

BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A • CUNNING HERBALIST.

At the Magistrates' Court, on. Monday. Thomas Bate, labourer, was charged with stealing by means of a ttlick, the sum of 6d., William Woodland, and Annie, his wife, who reside at 42,Eustace-st:The case was proved by Mr. and Mrs. Woodland,. and Detectivc,Sergeant Monaghan. On Saturday afternoon the prisoner called at prosecutor's house with an armful of herbs, or plants, The plant he called "the main of the vale," and he told the defend- ant's wife that her husband had requested him to bring them, and they .would be fid. The prisoner asked if he as in, but he being asleep she told him so, and gave him sixpence. Subsequently it proved that the man was a perfect stranger ti) " her husband, who had never re- quested him to bring the herbs. The prisoner had tried the same trick somewhere else: The prisoner was com- mitted for trial to the Sessions. SAVAGE ASSAULT ON A FATHER. At the Warrington Police-Court on Monday morning, Francis Wade, a sailor, who has recently returned from China, was charged with assaulting his father, Patrick Wade, his uncle, Larry Wade, and his aunt, Margaret Dolan, in Gee-st. on. Saturday night.—P.C. Cooper 20 said he was on ditty in Winwick-road that night and heard a disturbance going on in Gee-st. He went there and found the prisoner and several other men in the street. The prisoner was threatening his father who was in the entratice'of the house. He said" If you come outside you cat. I will finish you, you cat." The father cattle to the door, when the prisoner knocked him down, cutting his head so severely that he had to be taken to the Infirmary. When his uncle and aunt remonstrated with him he knocked both of them down.—Evidence wasl given which was very conflicting, and the quarrel, had, it'appeared, originated through the loss of the key of the clock, awl it was stated that Patrick Wade came, out with a poker but some witnesses said he did not. Others said that he did. A female witness who testified to this caused much amusement by her production of the poker, and flourishing it about in illustration of the manner in which he made use of it. It was stated that the prisoner was under the influence of drink at the time. The pri- soner said all the complainants were drunk, but denied that he was, and stated that he simply shoved them and they fell down. Ile also 'stated that he was provoked by an insulting reference .to his past service in the navy. The prisoner was sentenced to a month's impri- sonment with hard labour, the Chairman telling him that he did not reflect much honour upon tier Majesty's avy.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATUDDAY.-13efore, Alderman Burgess (chairman), and Councillor Voisey. DRUNK AND DISOUDERLY.—Martin Towey was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., the pre- vious day. T.C. Clough said the defendant and three men and two women were under the.influence of drink, and were very noisy, and taking up all the footpath and passers by had to get off the footpath into the road. Towey was fined ss. in default 7 days. Alderman Bur- gess told him the iootpath was made for respectable people and not for such drunken fellows as he, and if he wire brought up again under such circumstances he would be severely dealt with. . WIFE ASSAM:V.—John Cobb, 63, Wellington-st. was charged with assaulting his wife,Annie Cobb, on the 2nd July. The complainantsaid they had been married 21 years, and during all that time he had been in the habit of assaulting her. He only gave her 10s. a week to keep him, and her two children and herself. She had had to go to the Infirmary through his violence. On the day In question he knocked her down and kicked her twice: The defendant was fined 205., in default a month's im- prisonment ; and the Bench granted her a separation order, the defendant to allow her 10s. a week. Daum( AND DISORDERLY.—SamueI Beesley, drunk and disorderly in Marsh-st., the previous afternoon, ss. John Dooney, in Bridge-st., on the same date, ss. MONDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (chairman), and

Alderman Harrison. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—AIfred Marsh, drunk and disorderly, in Bridge-st., on Saturday night, 55., and costs.—John Hughes, in Wilderspool-road, on Saturday night, ss.—Alfred Mannion, in Bridge-st., on Saturday night, ss.—Annie Wade, in St. James's-st. on Sunday- night, ss. and costs.—Rosanna Finley, in Bultermarket- st., on Sunday night, 55., or seven days.—Frank Broad- bent, drunk and disorderly in Napier-st., on the 29th ult., ss.—Elizabeth Riley, Winwick-st., 27th ult., 55.- 3ohn Vickers, Smith-st., 28th ult., ss. FIGHTING.—.Tohn Galvin, apprehended under a war- rant, for fighting in Bridge-st., on the 20th, was bound over in the sum of £3O to keep the peace for six months and ordered to pay 16s. and costs.—John McMountref, and Matthias Woods, in Winwick-st., on the 27th, bound over and to pay costs. • DRUNK. IN CHARGE OF A HORSE.—Archibald Mannion, drunk in charge of a horse and cart, in Horsemarket-st., on the 27th ult., 10s. and costs. A DISORDERLY GANG.—William Mulligan, Patrick Casey, William Griffiths, and Martin McGuire were charged with being disorderly in Tanner's-lane, on the 29th ult. P.C. 15 deposed that fighting was going on amongst the defendants, and that Griffiths was bleeding from the head. They carried on the disturbance for more than three hours. It was stated that the row had commenced two days before, and was renewed on the 29th. Mulligan and Casey were bound over to keep the peace, and the other defendants were sent to jail for a month each. FIGHTING WOMEN.—Sarah Riley, Mary Jane Dagnall, and Annie Denby were charged with fighting in Buckley- street, on the 20th of June. P. C. Wade said the three women were all on the ground, and it was very difficult to separate them. They were bound over to keep the

peace. INDECENT CONDUCT.—Catherine McGuire, for using indecent language in Tanner's-lane, on the 28th of June, was fined ss. PITCH AND Toss.—James Costello, Walter Miller, Jas. Higgins, Thomas Daily, James Dailey, William lAwless, Patrick Coulter and John Appleton, boys, for playing at pitch and toss in lower Ship Yard, on Sunday last. All of them pleaded guilty except Thos. Dalley and Coulter, who were fined 2s. 6d. each, in default a day's imprison- ment, the others being discharged. FURIOUS DRlVlNG.—Williatn Thompson was charged with furiously driving a brake and three horses in Horse- market-st. to the danger of passengers, on the 27th of June. He pleaded not guilty. P.C. 33 and a witness named John Hudson proved the case, and the former said the defendant was driving round the corner at the rate of eight miles an hour, and Hudson said eight to eight and a half miles an hour. The constable after- wards in reply to the defendant, said the defendant was really going at the rate of twelve miles an hour, but he had given him the benefit of four miles an hour.—The defendant maintained that the rate was only five miles an hour, and said ordinarily his rate was seven miles an hour. The Constable: These strange drivers generally put a bit fly driving on just to show off.—The defendant was fined 20s. and costs, £1 17s. 6d. in all. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Patrick Kelly, drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st. on Monday night, was fined ss. TUESDAT.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (chairman), and Mr. E. M. Crosfield. _ -
LODGING-FIOUSE orman,Sanitary In- spector, prosecuted Ellen,Kimbling, lodging-housekeeper, 17, Dial-st.,,who was charged with allowing a Married

couple to sleep in her house in the .same room with a girl over ten years of age. It was proved that a married couple had been sleeping in one bed in the room, and a woman, her daughter aged eleven, and an infant in the other bed. The defendant was fined 20s and costs, and informed that if tie like occurred again she would be deprived of her Leense.—Maria Price. single woman, a fustian cutter, was charged with allowing two male lodgers to sleep, on the 2nd of July, in the same bedroom as that in which she herself and her two sisters slept. The defendant said the lodgers had gone, and she was fined 2s. 6d., including costs. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. Fairclough. - - - - - - -
DRUNIC.—Wan. Henry Conway, drunk in Winwick-rd., the previous night, was fined is. THURSDAY—Before Major Pickmere (chairman) and
Alderinan Sutton.

ANOTHER DISORDERLY CHARACTER IN THE MAREET.— Edward Crosby, labourer, 17, Dial-st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Mill-st. the previous after- noon, also with as4aulting John Hill the same afternoon. —P.C. Hardy deposed to seeing the defendant drunk and go up to the complainant and telling him with an oath that he had been looking for him, to assault him. But for his being locked up for this offence he wculd have been reported for being disorderly in the market.—John Hill confirmed this evidence, and said the prisoner had insulted his wife in the market.—Mrs. Hill said the pri- soner came out with very foul expressions to her, and she took her clog off to strike him. Then she brought her husband to him, and the prisoner said he would do the same to him.—The defendant said a farmer gave him is. to load potatoes and George Higham came to him and got the loan of is. from him, promising to return it when the parties were ready for loading. Afterwards Higham' who was employed by the complainant, came and said he and his mate would load the potatoes, and he would not give the defendant the shilling back. Then Mrs. Hill came and struck him with her clog. He was bound over to keel) the peace. DESERTION FROM THE ARMY.—William Hancock, was charged with being a deserter from Her Majesty's Royal Welsh Fusiliers,and was sent to Stra.ngeways jail to await an escOrt. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White (chairman), Alderman
Harrispn, and Dr. 6ornall,

DRUNK IN CHA.RGE 'OF' A HORSE AND CART.—Thomas Sumner, greengrocer, of Asliton-in-Makerfield was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and spring cart in Buttermarket-st., at 9.55 the previous night. Police-Sergeant Clieny and P.C. Evans. proved the case. They said he was drunk and having an•alter- cation with a woman of disreputable character, the horse and cart standing still. As he was unfit to ,take the horse and cart to Ashton-in-Maknileld, where he was going, they took him to the police station. He was very rough and used 'very bad language all the way there.— The prisoner said he had only had three small ports dur- ing the day, and was not drunk. He quarrelled with the woman because she grabbed at some money he had in his hand, and the police locked him up instead of her. —ln reply to Alderman Harrison, the defendant said the police were telling an untruth, and they did this regti- larly.—Alderman Harrison said this statement disentitled4 the prisoner to credit. It only showed how reckless he. was.—He was fined ss. and costs. A FIGHT BETWEEN TWO IRISHMEN.—Peter Ford, an Irishman, of 7, Back Stamford-st., employed at Dallata Forge, was charged with assaulting and beating Michael Logan, another Irishman, of 36, Stamford-st., employed at Bewsey Forge, and Michael Lpgan was charged with assaulting Margaret Ford, Peter Fora's wife— Mr. A. Browne appeared for Logan, and Mr, P. Davies for Ford.—Logan said he gave evidenee against' the defen- dant that day week, in that Court. On the morning of that day witness heard the defendant and his biother passing his door, and heard the former say it would not be many.days before he (witness) would be in his coffin. About half-pt at three Ford came up to him as he was sitting on his doorstep, with his coat off, and playing with his little daughter. Ford said Whistle up, Mike," twice' but witness made no reply. He did not know what he meant, as he was not whistling. Ford called him an Irishman (strengdiening this expression with an oath), for swearing against him in Court; and said he would have his revenge. He struck witness three times, then he struck him back. Then his brother came and knocked him down and kicked him; and three women came and loosed him from him and dragged him into his house, and washed his face. His shirt was. all torn off his back. On Sunday morning, at four o'clock, Ford was hanging about witness's house, and passed the door several times after that..—Mary Logan, the complainant's wife said she saw her husband 'on the " floor " and the defendant and his brother " agate "of him. He did not kick Mrs. Ford, who was there.—Mary Ellen Jolley said she saw Logan take his coat off, to fight after he had been challenged. There was no advant- age taken by the defendant. It was a fair stand up fight. When.the defendant was' getting the worse of it his brother helped him. He was on the floor and Logan on the top of him.—Several other witnesses gave evidence' including Dr. C. McDonnell, assistant to Dr. Adams' who deposed to Mrs. Ford having been bruised on the , thigh, as by a kick or fail.—John Massey and Margaret Rowlinson swore to Logan kicking Mrs. Ford. She her- self deposed that the wound refei red to had been caused by Logan's kicks.—Both the defendants were bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for, six months. Camwry TO HonsEs.—Wm. Barton, 65, Leigh-st., Golborne. was charged by Inspector Dowty, of the R.S.P.C.A., with cruelly abusing and torturing a horse, on the Ist. inst., by woaing it while in an unfit state.— Mr. Browne appeared for the defence.—The Inspector said the animal was attached to a spring cart, and had an old wound on the saddle and twelve large weals on its body, five of them bleeding. The defendant was fined 20s. and costs.—Peter Ellis was charged by Inspector Dowty with ill-using a horse by i i korking it nan unfit state in St. James's-st., Latchford, on the 4th inst.—Mr. Dowty said the horse was suffering from contraction of the tendons, and one leg was swollen and inflamed. The defendant was fined 10s., including costs.

div.p: WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.

TUESDAY.—Before Major Pickmere. ALLEGED ASSAULT ON THE POLICE.—I-GeOrge Patrick, a builder's labourer, was charged with being drunk and assaulting thepolice. P.S Devlin,Sankey Bridges,stated that the prisoner was drunk and interfering with pedes- trians the previous night in Liverpool-road. On seeing witness, he ran at him, caught him by the throat, and threw him to the around. With assistance, the officer handeuffed the prisoner, and conveyed him to the lock- up. div.head: SHOiIKING ACCIDENT AT A ROTHERHAM COLLIERY. FOUR MEN KILLED.
div.p: SHOiIKING ACCIDENT AT A ROTHERHAM COLLIERY. FOUR MEN KILLED.

A fearful accident happened at a new colliery which is in course of course of construction at Rotherham, be- longing to Messrs. John Brown and Co., late on Tues- day night. Two shafts are being sunk, and the opera- tions are conducted by means of eight hours shifts. When work bad been proceeding about half-an-hour the whole of the men were precipitated to the bottom of the shaft a distance of 20 yards. They were working on an ordin- ary two half-moon scaffolding or platform, which fitted the shaft, and which was suspended by four chains, when a beam, about six inches square, to which* was attached one of the chains, suddenly broke in two, the result being that the platform tipped on one side, throw- ing the men to the bottom. Four men were killed in- stantly, and the other four sustained serious injuries.

Lee at 47 gave a hard chance to Nicholls, whilst two rims later Fullalove appar- ently made too sure of a lofty catch. Voisey meanwhile was hitting in VI directions, and Whitelegge relieving Fullalove got Voisey caught in his, third over, the retir- ing batsman having made 25, and helped to raise the total from 80 to 120. Clark, Poarnore, Captain Adam, and Reynolds gave little trouble, but on Dun joining Lee the former hit out brilliantly, but after 15 runs had been added for the last wicket Lee attempted to pull one and got his leg in front. His score of 77 was a fine perfor- mance, and despite the chances he gave at 47 and 49, was well worthy of the applause which greeted him at the close. MR T. HEALY'S LIBEL ACTION.

The hearing of the libel action brought by Mr. T. M. Healy, M.P., against the "Freeman's Journal" com- menced on Tuesday before Lord Justice Barry and a county special jury. The damages are laid at £5,000. The court was crowded with Roman Catholic priests, including Dr. O'Donnell, Roman Catholic Bishop of Raphoe, and Father M'Fadden, P. P. Gweedore, who with others are to be examined as witnesses. A con- siderable time was occupied in swearing the jury.—Mr. Wright, Q.C., for the plaintiff, occupied four hours in his opening statement. The gist of the alleged libel was that plaintiff betrayed his clients (charged with the murder of District-Inspector Martin at Gweedorb) for ' gold, inducing them to plead guilty Of a crime which they never committed :and for his own ends.—The case was concluded on Wednesday. The jury found that certain of the publications were libellous, but could not agree as to damages, and were discharged without a verdict.

div.head: PROPOSED LOCAL RAILWAY.
div.p: PROPOSED LOCAL RAILWAY.
MONDAY.

Lord Bating's Select oo—m—m-it-tee of the House of Lords sat on Monday for the purpose of further considering the provisions of the Lancashire,Derby- shire, and East Coast Railway Bill, which seeks powers for the const.ruction of a line from Sutton- on-Sea through Derbyshire to Warrington. Mr. E. Ross Bryant stated that he was an export merchant; of Newcastle-on-Tyne. He exported coal to the extent of 120,000 tons a year. He knew practically that the Derbyshire coal was the most suitable for the Spanish market, and also for the Italian. The reason was that it stood the climate better than any other except, perhaps, the South Wales coal. lie was of opinion, thereiore that a largetrade must spring up in Derbyshire coal for those markets, and he had no doubt also that a large export trade would be opened up by the line in iron ware.from Sheffield and the general manu- factures from Staffordshire.

Mr. Stephen. Oats, shipbroker and marine surveyor, stated that his firm was the oldest firm of shipbrokers in Grimsby, and he was formerly Lloyd's agent there. At Sutton Harbour the disadvantage of having to navi- gate the Humber would be obviated. The Humber was not available at all periods of the tide for approach to the docks: He understood., on the other hand, that vessels would be able to enter Sutton Harbour at low water. It would be quite possible for the Sutton Dock not to be a paying thing in.itself but still to be a valuable adjunct to a railway.. Another important factor was that dredg- ing which was necessary at Grims,by would not be required at Sutton. Mr. W. HI Mills, of the firm of Coke, Mills' and Coke, mining enelieers„ stated that they were also mineral agents to the Duke of Rutland, Earl Cowper, Earl Mex- -IPorough, Lord Hothfield, and Sir Harry Verney. Some of these properties would be traversed by the proposed railway. His firm had been asked by the lessees on the various properties to 'support this Bill because of the necessity for a. further outlet for minerals both to east and west. This new railway would bring the steam, coal, and limestone districts into direct communication with the ironstone works near Lincoln. They were in- formed by theiriessees that this would be a most valu- able line -for them.—Cross-examined by Mr. Richards: In 1888 and 1889. he gave evidence in favour of the Annesley line, and stated, that the extension would give direct access from the coalfields .rOund Chesterfield to both Grimsby and null. That was a purpose which would .not be served by the proposed railway. The con- nection with the Manchester Ship Canal at Warrington would be of advantage to the Derbyshire'Coal. Mr. Arthur Henry Stokes, examined by Mr. Pember, stated that,he was an, inspector of mines in charge of, the Midland district. As an official, he attended under what was ,equivalent in their lordships' ;House to a Speaker's order. He was intitnitely acquainted with the whole of thecoalfields in Derbyshire and Nottingham. lie had over and over again inspected the underground workings ; in fact, he thought he had inspected every mine in his district. HO would draw a line from Work- sop to Nottingham asthe boundary of the existing work- ings of the coalfield. No, coal was worked to the east of that line. He thought there -was' every indication that the coal measures extended to the eastern boundary of Nottingham as far as the Trent, which meant that there was an enormous quantity of, excellent steam coal un- developed. He calculated that there were 500 square miles of untouched coalfields in Notts. This railway would command perhaps 120 square miles of that.

. . Mr. Emerson Bainbridge, examined by Mr. Pope,Q.C., stated that he was proprietor of the Nunnery Collieries, Sheffield, arid was also connected with the Bolsover Col- liery Company. He had just leased about 7,000 acres from the Duke of Portland. He knew of no area simi- lar to that affected for coal production by this line that could be compared with what the new railway would serve. Out of the 1.74 millions of tons of coal produced annually in Nottinghamshire and Perbyshire, only about half a million went over the sea, whereas in other coal- fields he believed as much as one-third was sent. He estimated that two millions of tons of coal might be shipped from the district if such access as that proposed were provided. Mr. Thoiiias Ward, of Saltburn, stated that he was'a director of the Salt Union. They used 2,000 tons of coal per day at the present time. They would use more from the Nottingham and Derbyshire coal fields but for the rates, as the coal had to be sent by very circuitous routes. They would be able to send away salt by the new line and bring back coal: _ _

Mr. W. El. Walker, a member of the firm of brewers at Warrington and Liverpool, said their principal breweries were at Warrington. their turnout was bet- ween 8;009 and 9,000 barrels weekly. They got their malt principally from the Lincolnshire district where barley was grown. They consumed about 70,000 quarters a year. They would be very glad to see a direct railway frOrn Warringtbn to this portion of. Lincolnshire. It would be of great service to them, not so much on ac- count of any possible reduction in rates, but through a shortening of the time of transit. Malt suffered in quality through being carried a long distance. Mr. Richards : Are you going to support thisscheme financially ? I have not given that point any consideration.—Mr. George Wood, manaLfing director of the Longford Wire,lron and Steel Company, Warrington, gave evidence in support of the Bill. Other Lancashire evidence followed to show
that manufacturers would either take their coal over the line or send their manufactures over it.
TUESDAY.

Dr. Hewitt, of Northwich, said he was managing director of the firm of Messrs. Brunner and Co., the largest alkali manufacturers in England. They. con— sumed very large quantities of steam coal—some hun- dreds of thousands of tons in a year. A considerable proportion of this supply came from thd Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire coalfields. The quality of this coal was very good for steam-raising purposes. They also used large quantities of limestone, which they obtained from the Buxton district. , If this line were constructed they would be able to send their trucks from their sidings to the coal and limestone districts .—Cross-examined by Mr. Richards: At present the Midland brought their coal in one load from the Derbyshire and Nottingham coalfields. They brought the coal to Knutsford, and continued the journey over the Cheshire Lines. The Midland Company were joint owners of the Cheshire Lines. The new line would have no interest in those lines on running powers, but if the Cheshire Lines were offered traffic at Knutsford he knew they would not refuse it. The advantage which his firm would gain would be that they would have to pay less mileage. They also preferred to have two strings to their bows. Mr. It. E. Cooper, engineer for the line, was examined by Mr. Pembroke gtephens in detail regarding the var- ious portions of the line. He said no engineering diffi- culties whatever were experienced before Macclesfield was reached. From Macclesfield to Chesterfield through Buxton, Chatsworth, Sze., some obstacles were encoun- tered, but they could all easily be surmounted. In Monsall Dale it wcruld be necessary to construct a via- duct 272 feet high, but the work in comparisiim with the Forth Bridge sank into insignificance. The Irapital of the company was £5,0001000, with £1,688,000 borrow- ing powers. The estimated cost of the line was £4,227,422. To that had to be added £200,000 the cost of the Newark and 011erton Railway, which they had to take over; £lOO,OOO which they had to subscribe to Sutton Docks; and Z 15,000 for additional land at Sutton, bringing up the total to £4,542,522, or something over four and ahalf millions, leaving a margin for un- foreseen works and for additional accommodation,wh en the time might arise, of £457,478. The present was an exceedingly good time to undertake a work like this lbecause the works.of the Manchester Ship Canal were I rapidly drawing to an end. This would release some- thing like 12,000 men, who would be on the spot and ready to proceed with the work. The committee adjourned. WEDNESDAY.—WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.

On Wednesday Sir Benjamin Baker, CE., expressed his approval of the way the line had been designed and laid out, and Mr. John Wilson, engineer-in-chief to the Great Eastern Railway, gave it as his opinion that the line was as well laid out as could be. Mr. Marshall Stevens, general manager of the Man- chester Ship Canal. who was examined by Mr. Pembroke Stephens, informed their lordships as to the way in which the railway would be connected with the Ship Canal Docks at Warrington. The railway would come alongside the docks at the higher level, so that coal could be tipped by gravitation. There were 183 acres of land available for coal sidings, but there was only one level of water between Warrington and the sea. In his opinion the distance of the Derbyshire coal would not act prohi- bitively, as he found that the coal at present shipped from Grimsby had to travel 50 to 60 miles by rail, and the Derbyshire coal was within 60 miles from Warring- ton. There would also be a large traffic for the rail- way in the limestone at Brunner, Mond's works.— Cross-examined by Mr. Worsley Taylor (for the M., S, and L. Company) :) He agreed with the promoters that the principal traffic to Warrington in respect of quantity would be coal. He could not give an estimate as to the probable proportion of coal for export and for bunkerpurposes. They intended coal to come from the Wrexham district to Warrington, which was about half the distance which coal from the Don- caster field would have to travel. The same applied to the North Staffordshire coalfield. The Ship Canal would probably save the Staveley Company £5,000 a year by enabling them toship from Warrington instead of Liver- pool.—The Chairman: The ManchasterShip Casa/ Com- pany are no parties as promotera to the Bill? No, my, lord.—The Chairman: But you are friendly to it? Yes. —Re-examined As it was now worth the while of the Ship Canal Company to pay a higher price to get coal of the description they required, it would probably be equally worth the while of the steamers which would be on the canal to do the same. Mr. W. Birt, general manager of the Great Eastern Company, stated that his company used no less that 400,000 tons of coal a year for their own purposes. At present they were the only great metropolitan company that had not a direct access to a coalfield. Theproposed line would give them that access. This concluded the case for the Bill. Counsel on behalf of Mr. Leslie and the Monehester, Sheffield, and I,l4colnshire Cexopany then aadrened the
Committee, . and finally the. Cbrumittee deliberated in private, and subsequently announced that the Committee had agreed to the preamble, and the Bill was proved.
THE LADY CRICKETERS AT W ARRINGTON.

On Wednesday afternoon, the lady cricketers, most of whom hail from the metropolis, made their appearance on the Warrington cricket ground, Play commenced about ten minutes past two in fine but windy weather,- the blustering breeze proving exceptionally unfavourable to the fair cricketers on account of the difficulties they experi- enced in running against it in feminine costume. The lady cricketers number 22, one of whom was in Manchester.and as there was thus an odd number on the ground, only 20 could play; and a match accordingly todk place with ten on each side. The team was composed of nearly all the same Mies who played at Warrington last year; and a decided im- provement was observable in their playing; their scientific style of batting and their graceful an& easy deportment demonstrating clearly that, as Herbert Spencer says, field sports, in the case of females no more prevent them from being ladies than the same in the case of males hinders them- from being gentlemen. The club was divided into two tens known as the reds, and the blues, each team wearing sasheh of their distinctive colours. The umpires were Mr. A. Clark for the reds and Mr. Fred Lee the Yorkshire professional, for the blues, the place of Mr. Lee being taken during.the latter part of the game by Mr. Adamson, secretary to the Warrington Cricket. Club. Mr. Matthews, an old Surrey professional, was the manager in chief, he having taken that position in the place of Mr. Michel, the founder of the ladies' cricket club, and Mr. E. C. Perris -was the business manager. Miss Parsons of the blues distinguished herself by three -beau- tiful catches she made in the first innings of the reds. Miss Ella Heather of the blues who had made TOO runs, without being out, at Bury, the previous day,- and Miss Lizzie, Sanders, of the same team, who made 110 'runs at Chiswick Park this year, were presumably formidable opponents for the reds to contend with, but both these ladies had to succumb to the splendid bOwling of Miss Violet Westbrook,Miss Heather only getting ISr runs. the second best individual score for her team. while Miss Sanders had to retire with the low figure of 3 appended to her name. Miss Westbrook' whose reputation as a batswoman also stands high,she having scored 10@runs at Burnley last year, did better for the reds than her rival bowling celebrities of the blues for she made tho highest score in the former's first innings, and the highest hut one in their second. Great admiration was ,expressed both by tongue and hand for the beautiful bat- ting and alert fielding, and the generally excellent style of the female cricketers. The play was stopped at a quarter to four by rain, and there was an unceremonious stampede by the fair cricketers for' shelter. The rain, however, ceased in a short time, and play was resumed. It continued, with uninterrupted fine weather, until 20' minutes to B,the blues being then in for the second time, svith 11 runs and no wickets down. There were some hundreds of spectators, and what was remarkable these included surprisingly few ladies. The following were the scores :

div.head: RAILWAY COLLISION AT SALFORD.
div.p: RAILWAY COLLISION AT SALFORD.

A PASSENGER KILLED AND SEVERAL INJURED. An alarming accident, unfortunately attended with i fatal results, occurred on Monday afternoon, on the Lan- I cashire and Yorkshire Railway, to the twelve o7ClOck noon express from Fleetwood to Manchester, whimis run dur- ing the summer excursion‘season in connection with the Isle of Man steamer which leaves Douglas about half-past eight o'clock in the morning. On the arrival of the steamer on Monday the passengers for Manchester and district took their seats in the train, which was in waiting, and all went well with them untanear Oldfield- road, where the trainis usually turned matto a loop line for the purpose of enabling tickets to be collected at the Salford Station. Thepointsman turned the train on to this loop line as usual, under the impression that the line was clear. This was, not so, however, and the express came into violent collision with some. empty carriages. that were standing on this particular- line of rails. The result, as may beimagined, was disastrons. The engine. dashed into the standing carriages, and-the compartments immediatdly behind it were telescoped. In one of these sat Mr. Richard flinchcliffe, of Prospect House, Crag Valley, Mytbolmroyd, who was killed almost instan- taneously. Some others were very badly injured, and many more escaped with a severe shaking. Some damage was done to thepermanent way, but the traffic was not interfered with to any great extent. The injured persons are Herbert Hinchcliffe,broken beg; his wife, shock and contused leg ;Mr. and Mrs. Langden, Manchester ; Mrs. Smith, Didsbury ; Herbert Obenalt, Swinton;: Mr. and Mrs. A. G. Longshaw, Manchester; John Cooper, Manchester; and Joseph Nieklin, Droit- wich, all slight injuries.

div.head: TUE POINTSMAN BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: TUE POINTSMAN BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

Before the Salford Stipendiary Magistrate,on Tuesday, Charles James Ulover, pointsman at Salford (Lancashire and Yorkshire) station, was charged with causing the death of Richard Hinchcliffe, Mytholmroyd, Hebden- bridge, Yorkshire. The prisoner was remanded until Thursday. The inquest on the body of Mr. Hinchcliffe, resulted on Wednesday in a verdict of "Death by misadven- ture."

Charles James Glover, the Salford pointsman arrested for the alleged negligence in connection with the recent railway disaster, was on Thursday discharged, the police offering Q. evidence in view ot the verdict el the oroner's jury,

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
TRAFFIC ARRANGEMENTS.

The construction of the Manchester Ship canal is now so far advanced that it is intended to open the first sec- tion—from Eastham to Ellesmere Port—for traffic on Monday next. Since the admittance ot water into the completed portion,. work at the mouth of the canal at Eastham has been pushed forward with all speed, the efforts of the engineers being specially directed to the re- moval of a portion of the damoutside the lock gate,which had been left intact until the banks or the canal,after the ' gradual admission of water frem Mesmer° Flirt, had proved themselves free from any flaw of a serious nature. The solidity of the bank having been ascertained,the next step was-to cut a channel through the dam which would admit shipping from the river to the middle lock, the lock which will be utilised until the whele scheme is com- pleted. The cutting of this channel has now been ac- compiished, and the cempleted section now lies ready for traffic, which, as already indicated, will commence on Monday. The vessels using the first section of the canal will consist mostly of barges, and the traffic secured will be what may be termed a,purely canal traffic. The com- pletion of the second section to the River Weaver will enable' •the canal interest to offer facilitiee,tbr the salt tra- ffic, and it is expected that this section willebe finished in a few weeks. ALL ALONG- THE WATERWAY.

I have no intention of once more describing, the condi- tion of all the sections. The great fact that now,. as al- ways since the work began, impresses itself: upon the sightseer, is the marvellous synchronism, if I may use the word, with which the ‘operations are carried on. One set of looks isalways as far advanced as another: as a few girders or a half-rnile of spoil banks ate- added to one -railway deviation, so every other of theso gigantic erections seems to have progressed in exactly the same ratio. Secondly, the nearness of the whole vast enterprise to its completion is evidenced by the deserted appearance of at /east three-fourths of the cuttiogs. The -swarming clouds of spadesmen, blasters, rock-hewers; steam,navvy drivers, concrete mixers, and practitioners of half a hun- dred other crafts have vanished. Wherever there iswork yet to be done they cluster more thickly than ever,. but of the great army of twenty thousand men and boys, at • least half have done what there was for them-to do and . have found employment elsewhere. For miles of the track the task of bank-pitching is the Only welkin hand: Whereever the still-aces are soft the plantine-of interlaced willows and osiers is going forward • and balready over hundreds of yards of the slopes the 'bright new-sprung greenery from the plants that have struck in their roots . and tendrils makes the scenic vistas gay. The foul old river, now well under control, either winds - its, devious course along its ancient channel or is allowed to &iw in The completed sections where this seems advisable.. This is the case at the Barton section, for instance, where, after being diverted from the old bed so as tonllow of the • masonry being put up in connection with the great swing aqueduct of the Bridgewater Canal, it flows in full mea- sure down to the site of Stickings Island, only being inter- rupted for the completion of the Barton locks and sluices. Several correspondents have written to ask the old ques- tion as to the best place to see good work upon the Ship Canal at a minimum of trouble. I can only repeat my advice that they should

GO ,TO LATCHFORD STATION take the track up stream, see the superb lochs, the im- mense railway works, and the stupendous rock-hewn cutting ;then push on to Thelwall Station, only a mile or so away and thence take the train home again. There is grand work to be seen at Irlam, hut it is heavy travel- ling from the station and dangerous withal; on account of the number of locomotives constantly on the move. The Barton -Aqueduct is well worth a visit, but it is a long tranip,down the cutting to the locks, and the sight-seer must perforce return over his own track. The Weaver stuices are accessible from Runcorn, and will 'way an inspection, as being the finest structure of their kind in the world. Finally' the Eastham section, as a sample of what the Canal will be throughout its whole length when full of water, provides a delightful day's-outing 'ilia Liver- pool and the ferryboat, may be seen without the toilsome travelling that other parts of the works demand. RUNCORN, .SIZ.

From the point where the Vyrnwy water is siphoned under to the mouth of the river Weaver, the labour of making the canal is so stupenduous as to seem almost beyond human compass. The outer, bank, of solid con- crete, moulded between piles, is being built in the bed of the Mersey,. leaving an immense lake of mud at low tide enclosed between Runcorn town and the line of oper- ations. Thewall passes beneath Runcorn Bridge, is in- terrupted again by the opening of the Bridgewater docks, and beyond these tt) Weston Point is still m the embryonic stage. As a feat of engineering the work yet to be done is gigantic, monumental. The railway connection,.however, between the great Weaver sluices and the sections above and below them, is now com- plete, and there is no longer occasion to cross the Weaver mouth ha a boat as heretofore. From here to Ellesmere Port there is a nine miles stretch of completed canal. Across, and beneath this cutting now flows the river Gowy at a depth of 16ft. under the bet, of the Ship Canal—" siphoned under" through two pipes of 12ft. diameter each. This had to be done, like the building of the Weaver sluices, to satisfy the exacting conserva- tors of the Mersey, who insisted that the tributary streams- should still discharge themselves at their old mouths, instead of being impounded. From Inca to Ellesmere Port, barring a few finishing touches, the canal is made, and now has some six feet of water in it. The banks are immensely high-70 feet in some places— and the whole cutting by ince, 300 feet wide, presents a handsome spectacle, but is almost inaccessible to the ordinary traveller. Inca railway station is more than a mile away, over sodden fields ; at least, our Party found them, so, for one of the finest thunder showers of the present monsoon season was on hand as a finish to our day's experiences. Ellesmere Port, however, can be reached by train and the work there is highly interest- ing. In about a fortnigut the passage through the bank tothe Mersey will be closed, and the canal to Eastharn will be open for traffic. • THIL WEAVER st.htors, Ten in number, and each thirty feet wide, now present a, coup d'eil of unrivalled splendour, visible from every part of the country for miles around. Through them the water will enter at high tide from the Mersey, while at all other times any surplus from the Weaver above the :28 feet required in the canal will find an exit. The old Egyptians put some big stonework together at Thebes and Luxor, but nothing to equal this structure has yet. been brought into existence by the genius of man. American opinion,, as expressed by my fellow travellers, is highly sanguine as to the future of the Ship Canal. If it be true that onlookers see most of the game, share- holders should take much comfort from this statement. The gentlemen. I refer to are large exporters of produce to England, devoid of prejudice., and thoroughly conver- sant with the details of American trade with Manchester. Their views of the new waterway are hopeful almost to enthusiasm. Already they areorganising their arrange- ments to take full advantage of the coming: facilities of traffic, and their opinion, briefly stated, is that while the Ship Canal may give fits to Liverpool, it mustinevit- ably make Manchester one of the greatest, wealthiest, and most flourishing ports lathe world. One thing only they cannot understand, and that is why the plutocracy of Lancashire allowed the working-class population to do so much, towards financing this vast and beneficial, public undertaking. And that has been a puzsle to not a few Englishmen also.

A YOUTH KILLED. On Ttesday morning,George Avery,aged 17, a points- man on. the Ship Canal. at Partington, was run over and killed by some waggons. Deceased was on the wrong:side of the points when the accident happened. FATALITY NEAR EASTFIAMi;

During Wednesday the length between, Eastnam and, Ellesmere Port was the•scene of an exciting and tragic occurrence. Betweentwo and three o'cicelnn the after- noon a party of engineers and assistar.t engineers en- gaged on the canal steamed from Eastham to Ellesmere, Port in a dredger of about 1,000 tons burden, called the, Manchester. The object in proceeding to Elles- mere Port was to, leave the dredger there, for the purpose of removing the embankment which has to be taken away before the canal can be opened on Monday. It appears that three youths and a man, who worked on the canal, attached their punt to a. small steamer, the Fanny, in order that they might thus be towed down the canal. When. about a mile ancLa half from Easthana the occupants of the punt weighed it down at a particu- lar point, the boat was swamped; and all wereprecipi- tatted into the water. The boat belonging to the steamer was cut loose, and every endeavour was macleto rescue the unfortunate men. One swam unaided to the bank, ' and two of the others were finally rescued' but the fourth, a youth, sank before he could be reached, and was drowned. A diver was sent for from Ellesmere Port, and tlaofficials on the Fanny also assisted in the search for the body.
