DEATH OF MR. W. H. GLAD-

Mr. W. H. Gladstone, eldest son of the Right Hon: W. E. Gladstone, died on Saturday morning, from the effects of an operation, at the house of hislather-in-law, Lord Blantyre, in Berkeley-square, London. Mr. W. H. Gladstone had for some time been in a delicate state of health, and his long and severe illness at Hawarden will be fresh in the recollection of our readers. He happily succeeded in partially regaining his health, and was able not long since, in the absence of his father, to address a Party of visitors to Hawarden Castle. He had recently been suffering from tumour on the brain, and as an Operation was deemed advisable he removed to the Lon- don residence of his father-in-law, Lord Blantyre, for the Purpose of undergoing it. The operation was successfully Performed on Thursday, and it was hoped that he would recover and regain his former health, but unhappily the Patient took a sudden turn for the worse, and, rapidly sinking, died on Saturday. When his condition became critical, his father, Mr. W. E. Gladstone, who has been staying at Cotton, near Lowestoft, the residence of Mr. J. J. Colman, M.P., was telegraphed for, and left by the first train for London. Mr. Gladstone was looking bet- ter for his short stay in Corton, but was naturally ter- ribly anxious about his son,whose death occurred before he could reach London. Mr. Henry Gladstone, Mr. Her- bert Gladstone, Miss Gladstone, and Lord Blautyre's family were present at the time of his death. Mrs.Glad- atone, who was also present when her son died, arrived in London from Lowestoft on Thursday morning. At Hawaraen, where the news caused a painful sensa- tion, it was common knowledge that Mr. Gladstone had never recovered from his late severe illness, which un- fortunately took the form of partial paralysis. He was then attended by Dr. Dobie, of Chester, and for weeks lay in a most critical state. On his canveleszence Dr. Dobie recommended that in his exercises he should be accompanied by someone, for fear of a recurrence of the attack. Mr. Wm. Henry Gladstone was born June 3rd. 1840, the son of the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstcne, M.P., by his Wife Catherine, eldest daughter of the late Sir Stephen Richard Glynne, Bth Bart. He was educated at Eton and Christ Church. graduating. B.A. 1862, M.A. 1865. He took a first class in classics m moderations when he was twenty. and a second class in classics two years later. In 1875 he married the Hon. Gertrude Stuart, youngest danghter of the twelfth Baron Bl•mtyre. He was formerly a lieutenant in the Flintshire Rifle Volun- teers. He was first elected to Parliament in July, 1865, for the city of Chester, as a Liberal. He sat for Chester till November 1868, when he was elected for Whitby, which borough he represented till March. 1880. In 1880 lie stood for East Worcestershire, when he was elected in conjunction with Mr. G. W. Hastings,theirConservative Opponents being Sir Richard Temple and Mr. Henry Allsopp. This was the last occasion on which Mr. W. H. Gladstone was a candidate for Parliamentary honours, as in 1885 he retired from active participation in poli- tics, and settled down to the life of a country gentleman at Hawarden, which estate was handed over to him under a family arrangement, wkich left his illustrious father The more free to prosecute his great political career. From November 1869, to February, 1874, he was a junior Lord of the Treasury. Very general Sympathy is felt for the aged ex-Premier, who now, at his advanced age, at a time when he himself is in feeble health, is thus suddenly deprived of the comfort and support of his eldest son's companionship. On inquiry at Park-lane on Sunday evening a press representative was informed that Mr. Gladstone con- tinued in fair health, and bore up well under his sad !lereavement. The right hon. gentleman attended church ill the morning, and in the afternoon went for a drive. Her majesty and the Prince and Princess of Wales have Written letters of condolence. Mr. Gladstone's world-renowned woodcutting has been Chiefly undir the son's direction, and in all home affairs, as contrasted with political, the interchange of ideas between the two has been invariably close and cordial. indeed, the three houses of the Gladstones at Hawarden may be said to have formed but one home, and it is on that account that the great statesman's nearest friends feel anxious as to the effect this blow may have on him. There has been no other death within his family circle since the loss of a little girl, some forty years ago. Doubtless since the son's paralytic seizure two years ago a fatal termination to his shattered heath has been re- garded as only too probable should the attack recur, but When a, man in his 82nd year is himself only recovering from an exhausting complaint, a shock of this kind may well cause grave anxiety. Mrs. Gladstone has been much distressed by reports Which have been published concerning the illness of her son' which were to the effects that life was no pleasure to him. Although he had not been well for two years, he had been all the time in the enjoyment of life, and there was always a hope of his complete recovery. As he was not making any progress, however, and was re- maining in the same state since be was taken ill, he decided to have an examination made of his head. On the morning he entered the room where the examination was to be made in cheerful spirits, and was hopeful as to the result. He was placed under chloroform, but upon an opening being made in the head it was found to be dangerous to attempt to removethe tumour, which was an accidental, and not a constitutional one. All idea of all operation therefor.) had to be abandoned. .The !Jeceased never rallied to consciousness and died, his heart being tco weak to stand the effects of the chloro- form.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

Mr. Gladstone's eldest son was buried, on Wednesday •afternoon,in the churchyard at Hwarden. "The Squire of Hawarden," as Mr. William Henry Gladstone was commonly styled, was popular in this northern corner of Wales, and many friends were present at the obse- quies. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone arrived at the Castle on Tuesday night. The right hon. gentleman looked far from well when he stepped on the platform at Chester, and it was evident that his bereavement, following on an illness of which the effects are not yet past, has told considerably upon him. Not till the sad ceremonial was all but over did his great spirit at all break down. In the last moments, when the tears were forced, a thousand eyes were dimmed with his. The day was • Opened at nine o'clock by tha celebration of Holy Coin- Mullion. The villagers and tenantry on the Hawarden estate assembled at the parish church at this hour; the Members of the family and visitors at the Castle met at the Orphanage of Mrs. Gladstone, within the Castle •grounds. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone were accompanied by Mrs. W. H. Gladstone (the widow), Lady Baird, her 'sister, the Rev. Stephen Gladstone, •Mr. Herbert Glad- stone, M.P. Mr. Henry Gladstone, the Rev. Harry and Mrs. Drew. Wickham, Miss Helen Gladstone, Sir John Gladstone, Bart., of Fasque, Lord Cobham, Mr. 3John Gladstone, of Bowdon Park, Chippenham, Glouces- tershire ; Mr. Arthur Gladstone, Liverpool; Mr. Arnold morley, M.P. • Lady Frederick Cavendish, and the Rev. E. C. Talbot, Vicarof Leeds (late Warden of Keble Col- - hundred Oxford). Betwen ten o'clock and noon the five • tenants on the estate, with representatives of 'Public bodies, assembled in front of the handsome new 'entrance to the Castle, built by members of the family 111 celebration of Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone's golden wed- ding. The weather, which had heen gloomy and in- clined to rain,brightened very much as noon approached. 'Very soon after the procession was properly marshalled c lose by the courtyard of the castle. The coffin, under its burden of wreaths, was placed on a wheeled bier, of 'Which a score of stalwart tenants took charge. At the WYritzate a small crowd was in waiting, and all hats 'Were,raised as the procession moved on. A much larger -crowd was assembled in front of the Norman archway 'Which, is the noble park entrance from the village. Here also was the band of the Second Volunteer Battalion Welsh. Fusiliers, which, as the mourners approached, struck upthe mournful notes of the" Dead March" in 'Saul." Hardly had the music sounded when Mrs. 'Gladstone, and her daughters, passed through the gates. ati one hand she bore a wreathcf pink and whiteflowers. and all the other mourners except Mr. Gladstone himself 'were similarly laden. Only one lady,of the household Ives missing, and that was Mrs. Wm. Henry Gladstone. The widowed lady was already lin ,front of the altar at the church. Before the procession reached the main gate- way of the edifice, the clergy, headed by the Bishop of St. Asaph, and the Rev. Stephen Gladstone (who. had left the ranks) and the white-robed choristers of the church, and of the cathedral of Chester, .had entered the churchyard. When the strains of the " Dead March," played by the band, had ceased, the Rector of Haward- -en said the opening lines of the burial service. The choristers, chanting on the way, re-entered the church, and Dr. J. C. Bridge (organist of Chester Cathedral). Played the" D.ad March." When the edifice was filled the service was •opened by the singing of the hymna " When our heads are bowed with Woe." The Rev. S. Gladstone read the 39th Psalm and the Rev. E. C. Talbot the scripture lesion. The procession was reformed to a portion of the grave- Yard overlooking the green valley of the Dee, stretching ft to the Welsh bills. The coffin was placed near the 4)., Pen grave. The mourners gathered round it, and were ISt turn circled by the choristers and clergy, and then by a deep ring of sympathetic onlookers. The ladies sat down Mr. Gladstone stood, hymn paper in hand. The choir began the hymn "Through the night of doubt and fic)rrew, Onward goes the pilgrim band," in which, with ;mach effors, Mr. Gladstone joined. The body was lowered to its resting-place, and the last words of the service were said. Then, in sight of the people, Mr. Gladstone again knelt on the grass in silent prayer. All he members of the family took a farewell look at the "ffio. The widow, who was very deeply affected, was !,‘lPPorted by Mr. Henry Gladstone and her sister, Lady aird. The choir sang the hymn commencing " 0 .rength and Stay uphelding all creaticn "; and the last _elessing was said by the Bishop of St. AsaPh• When all 77se over Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone and the other mem- ers of the family left the churchyard, and by a private trance walked to the Castle. Wreaths were sent by n. Edward Cavendish; Misses Alice and Constance adstone' the Duke and Duchess of Leinster, the Duke letivcastle, Mrs. Colman,Sir P. and Lady Millbank •I'dord Rosebery, Lady Stepney, and many others.
kr. and Mrs. Gladstone, in a special communication, Xpressed their heartfelt thanks for the messages of ympathy they had received from all rrtors on tile '"gatilQtthat zon.

div.head: 25 MILES BICYCLE RACE.
div.p: A 25 MILES BICYCLE RACE.

On Saturday the annual 25 miles bicycle road race by members of the Warrington Wheeler's Club came off. The course was really understood to be about 261 miles, the race commencing at Grappenhall and ending at about 24 miles on the other side of Knuts- ford. The entries numbered 16, but only ten com- petitors took part. The machines included 2 pneu- matics, 7 cushions, and one solid frame. There were three prizes, which with those won at suc- ceeding races, will be distributed at a smoking concert. The competitors were as follows :-Ist N. Seddon (8 minutes' start), who rode a Burton diamond anti-vibrator, a borrowed machine, 2nd, F. J. Hughes, :(5 minutes' start), who had a Winallie spring frame machine. 3rd, James Keeran, limit man, (23 minutes' start), whe rode a cushion safety. 4th, Thomas Roe, (8 minutes' start), cushion safety. sth, James Maya% (3 minutes' start), pneumatic. The other competitors were Joseph Davies, W. Bamber, H. S. Hayes (scratch), S. Johnson and R. Chaloner, all of whom gave up before finishing thecourse. The timekeeper, starter, and judge was Mr. F. Massey, of the Roe Buck ' Hotel, and Mr. James Forster acted as timer. The best time (1 hour, 34i minutes), was made by Mr. Hughes, Mr. Seddon's time being 1 hour 364 minutes.

div.head: BANQUET TO LANCASHIRE
div.p: THE BANQUET TO LANCASHIRE
LIBERAL MEMBERS.
TOUCHING LETTER FROM MR. GLADSTONE.

On Wednesday evening Mr. W. Mather, M.P., as preside-at of the Lancashire Liberal Federation Councii, entertained the officers of that body,as well as the Liberal members and candidates for Lancashire constituencies, to dinner in the Devonshire Club. Mr. Mather presided, and amongst those who accepted invitations were Sir William Harcourt, Sir Henry Roscoe, Mr. Jacob Bright, Mr. C. S. Schwann, Mr. T. B. Potter, Mr. Caleb Wright, Mr. Isaac Hoyle, Mc. J. A. Duncan, Mr. T. P. O'Corinor, Mr. R. Neville, Mr. J. S. BalfoUr, Mr. H. J. Roby, and the following candidates :—Messrs. Armitage, Agnew, Hopwood, Hall, Leese, Kennedy, Huntington, Bentley, Munro, Chatham ,Barlow. Maden , Pollard ,Deacon, Woods, Holland and Snape ; also the officers of the Lancashire Liberal Federation Council—namely, Messrs. Midgley, Watts and Barlow ; and Mr. L. Harcourt, hon. secretary of the Home. Counties Liberal Union, and Mr. Arthur G. Symonds, secretary of the National Reform Union. The company numbered about fifty guests. Amongst the invited guests unable to attend were Sir Ughtred Kay-Shuttleworth, M.P.. Mr. Leake, M.P., Mr. William- son, M.P., and Messrs. Heller, Hibbert and Isherwood. When the dinner was first proposed, Mr. Gladstone ac- cepted an invitation, but was of course prevented by the death of his eldest son from attending, and sent a letter instead. The letter was as follows: - -

Dear Mr. Mather,—l cannot finally dismiss the idea to which I had chum, perhaps rather too closely, of enjoy- ing your kind hospitality without sending you my heartiest good veihes, by reason of the present sadness, for the occasion on which you are to meet your own and my friends. We, in our affliction, are deeply sensible of the mercies of God, who gave us for fifty years a most Precious son, and has now only hidden him for a very brief space from the sight of our eyes. It seems a violent transition from such thoughts to the arena of political contention: This transition may, I think be softened by the conviction we profoußdly hold, that in the first and greatest of our present con- troversies we are working for the honour, thewell-being, and the future peace of our present opponents no less than for our own,—l remain, dear Mr. Mather, very

faithfully yours, W. E. GLADSTONE. Park-lane, July 7, 1891. It was cordially agreed that Mr. Mather should, on behalf of the company present, send a telegram to Mr. Gladstone, expressing their sincere condolence on his recent bereavement.
Sir William Harcourt, owing to another engagement, could only be present during a portion olf the proceed- ings, and he delivered a brief speech. The occasion was not open to the Press.

div.head: HEYWOOD DIVISION.
div.p: THE HEYWOOD DIVISION.
MR. T. SNAPE'S ADDRESS.

On Saturday afternoon, at the Co-operative Hall, Bury, a largely-attended meeting of the members of the Liberal Council for the Fleywood Division of Lancashire was held for the purpose of receiving the report of the Executive Committee with respect to the selection of a candidate to contest the division in the Liberal interest at the next election. Mr. Hoyle, the present member, who has represented the division since its formation in 1885, intends to retire at the general election through ill-health.—Alderman Isherwood, J.P., C. Ald. (Hey- wood), who presided, briefly introduced Mr. Thomas Snape, of Liverpool and Widnes, as the gentleman whom the Executive had decided to recommend for adoption •as the Liberal candidate. Mr. Snape met with a most ' cordial reception. He avowed himself as a Radical of the Liberals, and said he believed that the progress of the country politically had been due to the Liberal party. (Applause.) He was in favour of Home Rule. for Ireland. The laws affecting Ireland were quite different from those affecting England, and there was a Crimes Act in force in the former country, which would, if applied to England, .cause a revolution': (Applause.) Another subject which was at present before the country was free education, and this he was decidedly in favour Of. The Bill at present before Parliament must be carefully watched to see that it. was not made an additional endowment to denominational schools. Disestablishment was also closely connected with free education. They had disestablished the Church of Ireland he Welsh and Scotch people had declared un- mistakably that the establishment must go—(bear, hear) —and after they had disestablished the Church in those countries it could not be very long before they would re- move it in England. (Applause.) Referring to the:land laws, Mr. Snape said it was one of the most important questions of the present time. The transfer of land wai most difficult, and there should be a registration of titles so that land could be transferred without the present enormous cost. He would support the taxation of ground rents, and he would also support the taxing of land, whether it was rented or not. If that was done, landowners would consider whether it paid them to keep those lands in their own possession in the' expectation that they would at some future time yield them a fortune. (Applause.) Turning to labour questions, he said he would try, if he were elected, to do that which would be to the interest of the great bulk of the people—the labouring classes. He was in favour of local option and Sunday closing.—ln answer to ques- tions, Mr. Snape said he was thoroughly in favour of ending or mending the House of Lords, and more in favour of ending it than of mending it. (Hear, hear.)— Mr. S. Knowles moved a resolution which, whilst regret- ting that Mr. Hoyle., had found it necessary to rotire from the representation of the division, stated that the meeting "having heard Mr. Snape's expression of his views, and being fully satiAel as to his qualifications, hereby cordially invites him to contest the division, and pledges itself to use its utmost endeavour to carry him at the poll by a triumphant majority."—Mr. John Buck- ley (Heywood) seconded this, -mid it was carried unani- mously.—Mr. Snape will commence his candidature on the 18th inst., when, along with Mr. Isaac Hoyle, he will address a meeting at Heywood.

div.p: 'ILLUSTRATED PAMPHLET FREE ON APPLICATION
NOTES ON GAMES AND AnitETICS.
CRICKET.

The position of the leading counties now stands as follows :—Surrey, 6 wins; Kent, 2 wins, and 2 draws; Sussex, 1 win, 1 loss, 2 draws ; Notts, 2 wins, 2 losses; Somerset, 1 loss, 1 draw; Middlesex, 3 wins, 4 losses, 1 draw; Lancashire, 1 win, 3 losses, 1 draw; Gloucester, 1 win, 3 losses, 1 draw; Yorkshire, 2 wins, 4 losses.

The play of Albert Ward, the Lancashire County Cricketer, has lately come in for some criticism, and, says the "Manchester Guardian," "In the match at Rossall it was gratifying to see that he had profited by the hints that had been given to him. He hit with great vigour, and followed up an excellent innings by a very fine innings against Warwickshire at Old Trafford. The bowling during the greater part of the innings at Old Trafford was very good, Shillton, Pallett, and Cresswell doing their very best, but Ward played them splendidly; one of his hits from the Stretford end went clean over the ladies' pavilion. There is nothing to prevent Ward, if he chooses, from becoming the English M'Donnell. He has all that famous Anglo-Australian's physical power; he has "the eye of an hawk ;" and he ought not to give him self away by pottering about the crease."

In the Warwickshire match there was some curiously bad fielding on the Lancashire side, but it was a merely temporary aberration, and will pass. The visitors could hardly have expected to win in any circumstances, but they certainly had all the worst of the luck as regarded the wicket. Distinctlytthe hero of the match, from the visitors' point of view, was Lilley their wicket keeper. He hit out splendidly, and although his "lives," like the virtues of the American backwoodsman, were " numerous to behold," he is entitled to the credit of having played a forcing game just when it was wanted, and in the most gallant manner.

Whiteside, the Lancashire wicket keeper, seemed more at home with Mold than with Watson's peculiar deliveries, and made one egregious mistake; but no disaster followed, and the spectators were lenient, in the belief that with practice Whiteside will develop into a very good wicket keeper. We ought not to omit to mention the two catches which Yates made at long-on. The second was most admirably judged, and reminded one by its clever- ness and neatness of the memorable catch by which Mr. Docker dismissed Giffen seven years ago on the same ground, in the famous match in which Mr. Hornby played the best innings of his life against Spofforth and Giffen and Palmer. The recollection of that match, to say nothing of the subsequent defeat of the M'Donnell team on the same ground, should charm away same of the depression that has come over Lancashire cricketers. As Mr. Gale says in an article published a few days ago, there will be some "coming back" of a few of the foremost horses when the Tattenham Corner of cricket, the return matches, comes off, and some in the rear rank will be seen in the front.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The Manhattan athletic team were on Saturday de- lighting a large gathering of Frenchmen in the Bois de Boulogne, and, as could only be expected in the absence of English Competitors they were successful all along the line. The youth oeFrance do not take' kindly to outdoor athletic exercises, which in England are so dearly prized, and although they are ready at all t:mes to give a hearty welcome to visiting teams, be they pro- fessional or amateur, they never offer any opposition worthy of the name. Luther Cary of course won the 100 metres race, his nearest opponent being 10 or 12 metres behind, and Dadtnun—who made a rather dis- appointing show in the half mile championship at Old Trafford a week ago—very easily secured the French equivalent—viz.. the 800 metres race. Remington took the 400 metres very easily,and Roddy to his intense satis- faction was successful in the 15,000 metres, defeating Beret, the French champion, with ease. Hallock won the high jump, being credited with a jump of eft., the correct measurement of which may be doubted. On July 15 the whole of the American team will take part in the evening sports of the Manchester Athletic Club. Cary and Remington have signified their intention of making every effort to lower the English records. We do not fear that the quarter-mile figures are in serious dan- ger, as, good runner though Remington undoubtedly is, we hardly think him equal to Tindall or Wood, whilst Myers, whose training is so evidently responsible for Remington's greatest attraction, viz., style, was a good many yards his superior in point of speed. With fine weather and good health,Cary is sure to do a very great performance both in the 100 and 200 yards,but it is in the latter distance that we anticipate his success as a record breaker ; as somehow we cannot reconcile his style with that of an athlete capable of beating evens. The Man- hattan athlete is a great runner whose speed is the result of an iron will and remarkable strength, but the freedom of limb which marks the natural action is wanting, and his mode of progression displays a lack of cultivation hardly creditable to his trainer ; yet withal, he is much faster than our best sprinter. House, and would on a fair course be capable of giving him three yards start.

div.head: BRADLAUGH HALL.
div.p: BRADLAUGH HALL.

The people of Northampton have resolved to perpetu- ate Mr. Bradlaugh's memory by erecting a statue and building a " Bradlaugh Hall.' It is estimated that £3,000 will be required, and a large part of it has been already subscribed.

div.head: BOLTON KICKING TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE BOLTON KICKING TRAGEDY.

Michael M‘Dermott, 22, was again before the Bolton Magistrates on Monday, for the murder of *Henry Clay- ton, 27, by kicking him in the public streets on Saturday, the 27th ult. PrisonPr has already been committed to the Assizes for tl ial . the capital charge on the Coroner's warrant. The fatal quarrel arose in a public-h ouse, the deceased being accused of being a " knobstick "or non- unionist workman. M‘Derrriott was finally committed for the murder.

A COMPLAINT FROM WINWICK-ST.; &C., &C. Sir,—l would like to ask whether we have a nuisance inspector in Warrington. Reason why. Somebody in Tanner's-lane have instituted a system of burning all their refuse, and as a result throwing a deluge of noxious smoke in all the surrounding neighbourhood. The business people of Winwick-st. are complaining of severe headaches and aching:eyes as a result. We have sent a petition to the Nuisance Inspector. We have also I sent complaints to the offenders bat they treat our com- plaints with coetempt. The inhabitants of Winwick-st. and neighbourhood desire the Sanitary Committee to take the matter in hand, if only for the health and coin- fort of the inhabitants. Hoping this letter will open the eyes of the Committee and cause some action to stop the nuisance,—l remain, yours, Sze.

div.head: WALKING DAY BANDS.
div.p: WALKING DAY BANDS.

Frodsham appears to be leading the way in dis- pensing with the aid of raffles. at'hazaars. A short time ttgo the Wesleyans of that place successfully endeavoured to "raise the wind" by a bazaar, and raffling was sternly and strictly prohibited. This week the church have held a bazaar with the object of raising funds to restore the boys' school and again has raffling been discarded. The Vicar (Rev. H. B. Blogg) described the practice as illegal and immoral. It was not always so, and one is glad to see that religious demonstrations are practising scmething of what they preach, in this matter of gambling.

Sir,—Referring to your correspondent "A Lover of 31111SiC" in your last Saturday's issue, I am at a loss to understand howthelforms his opinion. I should think that had he heard, or tried to hear, some of the other bands he would:have:found some who played far better 'music, than that played ;by the League of the Cross Band. "A Lover of music " evidently has some inter- est in the one band, and must have ignored the various other bands who played in the procession either through bigotry or shortsightedness, and in either case he must have a very poor idea of what good and sound music really is. Now, with respect to the eulogy which he passes upon the conductor, one would think that he was a Godfrey, Gladney, Owen, Swift, or some other great musician, whereas I find that he was playing on that day a second or third cornet either of which instruments is anything but suitable for the conductor to lead a band with. _ _

While the Commissioners are maturing their plans, the School Board are determined not to be idle. The unique success of their evening classes last winter, has caused them to determine not merely to continue them for the purpose of elemen- tary teaching, but also to establish classes for the teaching of science and art, I presume under South Kensington. This is one step towards technical education in the town, and the School Board will never have reason to regret the step they have taken.

Education is still the theme. The Widnes School Board have instructed the Clerk to prepare a report showing bow the Free Education Bill will affect their schools; and they will then proceed to con- sider their position. Mr. Moss, the clerk of the Run- corn Board,has,however,taken time by the forelock, and on Tuesday evening presented a report which showed that if the Board accepted the 10s. grant from Government and threw their schools open free there would be a loss of about £3oa year. The Board could, if they chose, charge a halfpenny fee but, as Mr. Pritchard remarked, the ratepayers will prefer to bear this burden and have their schools entirely free; and in virtue of that opinion Mr. Pritchard has given notice of his intention to move that fees be abolished at Runcorn Board Schools. Should the Board accept this proposition —and of this there can be no reasonable doubt, because the Bill makes it compulsory that a certain amount of free education must be provided—then we shall have free educa- tion in our midst on the first of September.

And now for the" men who have left." I think that "A Lover of music "knows little of what he writes and seems to care less, or he would not attempt to make strife between the members of the Leagueof the Cross, and the Catholic United Brass Bands, by his sarcastic remarks, especially had he known the reason why the men left the League Band. I hope" A Lover of music" will explain his letter snore fully to oblige, Yours truly. A LOVER OF FAIRPLAY. July 7th, 1891.

THE ITRYSWY WATER. SCHEME. _

• A remarkable statement was made on Tuesday at the meeting of the Liverpool Water Committee. It was explained that comparatively little if any water had reached the city from the Vyrnwy Lake, and that, although nearly six million gallons were being discharged into the pipes from the new re- servoir, less than two million gallons reached Pros- cot. A temporary pipe line has been laid on the bed of the Mersey. and it is believed that the chief leakage takes place there—that the greater part of the water supply is mingling with the river. ANOTHER STOPPAGE AT PRESCOT. There was another stoppage in the flow of water from Vyrnwy into the Prescot storage reservoir on Wednesday. The supply suddenly ceased about noon, and no water was obtainable until about half past six on Wednesday night, when the liquid again made its appearance. No reason for the stoppage could be given by the officials tit Prescot, but it was considered that it had been necessitated by the operations at the Mersey crossing. The reservoir Ntas a little more then half filled on Wednesday night,the quantity of Vyrnwy water in stock being estimated at about 25,000,000 gallons. On a visit being paid to the works at Fiddlers Ferry yesterday afternoon,oit was ascertained that tunnelling operations were proceeding as usual,and that during the day a diver had been engaged in an endeavour to stop or lessen the leakage from the temporary pipe. The divers complain of the diffi- culty of working in the water of the Mersey, which at this spot is not only dirty, but contains chemi- cal matter that is presumably turned in at Widnes.

div.head: NEW THEATRE FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: NEW THEATRE FOR WARRINGTON.

Sir,-1 have read with interest the letter addressed to you by " Thespian " in your paper of Saturday last, headed "A Theatre wanted in Warrington." Will you allow me to reply thereto, as I have been acting as soli- citor for Mrs. Sheridan, widow of the late Brinsley Sheridan?

Your correspondent is quite right in saying that there was a report circulated in Warrington about 12 months ago that we were having a place of entertainment worthy of being called a theatre. You will be well aware that I made an application for the renewal of the theatrical license on behalf of the late Mr. Brinsley Sheridan some 18 months ago, and I produced to the Bench some plans which had been drawn by the eminont theatrical architect Mr. iidfred Darbyshire, of Manchester, for the improve- ment of the theatre in Scotland-road, at a cost of from £4OO to £5OO. Everything was prepared for the carry- ing out of such plans, and the contract was actually let to a Salford builder, and the written contract was pre- I pared ready for signature, but " L'homme propose, and Dieu dispose," as poor Brinsley Sheridan died before the contract was signed. This completely upset matters, and Mrs. Sheridan did not feel herself in such a position as to be able to carry out the large undertaking that her late husband intended. Since that time negotiations have been going on between a number of theatrical proprie- tors and myself and Mrs. Sheridan, as to the sale of the theatre, but nothing has yet been done. I myself am quite of opinicn that what your corres- pondent suggests, viz., a good theatre carried out on the plans Mr. Darbyshire has prepared, would pay some enterprising manager for his trouble and the money he would have to lay out. If your correspondent will show his interest in the matter by corresponding with me, I have no doubt that if he is a gentlemen of influence we should be able to get it few townsmen together and form a company, and set in our midst a theatre which would not only be an orna- tnent to the town, but would be as a kind of memorial to the late Mr. Brinsley Sheridan whose hopes, Mr the last 18 years were for the completion of a good theatre for Warrington. Thanking you for allowing me so much space in your paper. I remain, Sir, yours &c.
„ Warrington, Bth July, 1891.
ARTHUR BROWNE.

Sir,—I noticed in your columns last week a letter signed by one " Thespian " inquiring how it was that Warrington was so ill-provided for; with regard to theatres. This is a matter that it is well known has interested many for years past, and is also a matter over which it is high time some steps were taken by the gen- tlemen who look after our interests in this respect. I would wish to endorse his remarks as to the success which would attend the establishment of a large sized house. I, for one, and I know of many others like me, would gladly take my family regularly to see the first-

div.head: HEALTH
div.p: HEALTH

class productions of the day. when Ido not counten- ance the wasting of a single penny over the weak repre- sentations of the drama which are only too often per- mitted to occupy our boards. It is to be hoped that,now the subject has been opened in your columns; it may be the means of bringing some pressure to bear on the gentlemen who cater for the public amusement of Warrington. —I am, sir, yours, WILSON FATTEN-ST.

Sir,—The very able letter which appeared in your is- sue of the 4th inst. on the above subject is most oppor- tune. I agree most heartily with your correspondent ' "Thespian." Until quite recently, I resided in Liver- pool, where you can have all the latest novelties in the way of dramatic and operatic productions for the same price that you have to pay here in Warrington for third or even no rate performances. It is certainly a very great sacrifice for anyone who is a lover of the classical in music or drama,and who is at the same time in the posi- tion of Dickens's hero "R. Wilfer " (blessed with a limited income) to have to pay the additional cost of railway fare before he can have the chance'of seeing any- thing worth while. It is computed that the average at- tendance at the London theatres nightly isabout 45,000, and they suppnrt a very large number of theatres and music halls, and it certainly would not be too much to expect from the inhabitants of a town like Warrington, with a population numbering over 50,000; that they would support liberally one good first-class theatre. In conclusion, I trust that some enterprising man willcome forward and supply this want in our toivn.—Yours truly,
"R. WILFER."

div.head: To-night Mr. Arthur Savage, of Runcorn, will be bidding his native land "Good-night,'
div.p: To-night Mr. Arthur Savage, of Runcorn, will be bidding his native land "Good-night,'
Adieu adieu! my native shore Fades o'er the waters blue.

Mr. Savage has given up farming in the old country, and on Tuesday night departed from Runcorn to London en route to Sidney in Australia, to search in a new land and amid a strange people for fame and fortune. About forty of his numerous friends and acquaintances assembled at the Station and gave him a hearty hand-shake and many heartfelt wishes for his future prosperity. "For he's a jolly good fellow" and "Auld lang syne "were sung with such vigour and power that the words were no mere parrot cry; and as the train moved out of the station a spontaneous cheer burst forth. I now add my little cry to the general chorus.
Dr. F. Hurter. of Widnes, has been appointed honorary foreign secretary to the Society of Chemical Industry.

About 20 years ago Mr. Thomas Snape, C.C. Liberal Candidate for the Heywood Division, who was then in business in Blackstock-st., Liverpool, was unable to meet his liabilities, but on payment of 2s. 6d. in the Xhe received. a discharge in full. Since then, however, prosperity has beamed its smiles upon him,and he has paid all his creditors in full with interest for the years that have passed. Such an action stamps Mr. Snape as an honourable and conscientious man.

div.head: BY AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: BY AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.

The annual election of Commissioners draws near, and still there is no word as to passing of the provisional order ghich will enable the voting to be carried on in the three districts of Newton, Earlestown and Wargrave. Everything and every- body seems to be hanging fire in full expectation of the news that the Bill has been passed at the last moment, but should it not arrive before Saturday next, it is pretty evident, the old system of voting at Newton Town Hall, will for this occasion have to be adopted.

I am writing now with the full impression that there will be a contest, necessitating the voters' presence at Newton. Even on this point however there is no certainty, at least so far as is known outside a certain quarter. We are now within measurable distance of the election, andit is known that three members of the Board will retire, yet nothing is being done publicly to secure candidates. There appears to be an air of mystery surrounding the actions of the self-elected representatives of the ratepayers, but why this should be so further in- tensifies the mystery. This is a great mistake, as 1 think the bone fide ratepayers should be consulted openly in the matter, that is always presuming that candidates have been chosen, as 1 am given to understand such is the case.

I hinted last week that steps were being taken to re-organise the Liberal voting list in the division. I am now assured that this is an actual fact, and that considerable progress has already been made. It appears the Liberal Federation. imbued with the idea that the Newton Division is to be won by a Liberal, if proper measures are adopted, have sent down an agent to .work up the voters lists, and place the Division in a fighting condition, prepared ror any emerge Y. I may say that with a popular candidate the Liberal party have great expectations of wresting the seat on the next occasion from the Conservatives.

These articles it appears are lent on hire for a nom- inal sum, but in really deserving cases, the hiring charge is waived and they are lent free of cost. div.head: JOURNALISTS' TRIP TO THE ISLE OF
div.p: JOURNALISTS' TRIP TO THE ISLE OF
MAN.

On Saturday last a large number of members of the Institute of Journalists (Liverpool District) by the invitation of their confreres connected with the Isle of Man press, paid a visit to Manxland, and during their stay there which terminated on Mon- daylwere most handsomely and hospitably enter- tained. Free passages were given by the isle of Man Steam Packet Company to the excursionists, 1 who numbered over 50, and included two repre- sentatives of this journal, and several from other local papers, and a sumptuous dinner was provided for them on board by the Company. Soon after the island was reached the quarterly district meeting of the Institute was held at the Courthouse, Mr. C. Wall, the president, in the chair. There was a large attendance. It was resolved to recom- mend that the annual conference of the Insti- tute in 1892 be held at Douglas. In the evening the members of the Institute were entertained to a banquet at the Castle Mena Hotel. Mr. J. A. Mylrea, a member of the House of Keys., presiding, in the absence of the speaker of that House, Major Stephen another member of the Manx legislature occupying the vice-chair. A number of toasts were proposed, including that of "The Institute of Journalists," and responded to. On Sunday morning the members drove to Ramsey, where they were entertained to dinner at Alma House the residence of Mr. W. L. Wild, newspaper pro- prietor. The journalists were also accorded the privileges of free admission to the Palace, Falcon Cliff, and the theatre during their stay. Most of them returned from the island by the boat leaving at one o'clock on Monday morning. About fifteen, however, remained till Monday afternoon, a few of these going, notwithstanding, wet weather, to wit- ness the promulgation of the Manx laws. from Tynwald Hill. seats being reserved for the accom- modation of the members of the Institute. The trip was for the most part a delightful one, being marred only by a continuous thin rain which detracted from the pleasure of the Sunday drive, during the morning.

A. new writ for the Wisbech division of Cambridgeshire was ordered in the House of Commons on Thursday evening, Captain Selwyn having resigned his seat. Three people were seriously injured at a sh op in Dumfermline on Thursday by a gas explosion, follow- ing a search for an escape with a naked light. The Sunderland magistrates on Thursday dismissed the charge of perjury brought against Mr. Storey, M.P., in connection with proceedings arising out of the Silks- worth strike. An equestrian statue of the late Lord Napier of Mag- dala, Field Marshall and Constable ot the Tower, was on Wednesday unveiled by the Prince of Wales in Waterloo- place, London. A ghastly discovery was made on Wednesday at the Dead Letter Office, Telegraph-St. London, a tin box being found to contain the decomposed body of a male child three or four -weeks old.

ephenson, the father of rail- ways, projected the line of the Midland Company through the valley country, from Derby to Norman- ton, and excluded from the great highway the towns of Sheffield, Barnsley and Wakefield, Mr. Leather was employed to enrvey the route from Chesterfield through -Sheffield, and his pupil ac- quired his first experience as a railway engineer in laying out the line which was subsequently adopted. On the completion of his professional edu- cation, Mr. Fowler became an assistant to Mr. Ras- trick in the construction of several lines of railways then in progress, and amongst others the London and Brighton railway. He was then appointed resident engineer of the Stock- ton and Hartlepool railway, and of other lines in the same district. It was at this period that he first came as a witness before a Parliamentary Committee, and exhibited those qualities of acutene,s, firmness, and soundness of judgment which constituted him one of the ablest and most valued.engineering witnesses in the Com- mittee rooms of both [louses of Parliament. At the age of twenty-seven, Mr. Fowler was selected as the engineer for constructing the largo group of railways known as the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire line, winch includes tunnels, viaducts, and bridges of considerable magnitude, in addition to a dock, a floatino, pier, large hydraulic works, and a steam ferry, of all which large and multifar- ious works he had the sole engineering charge. From this time the name of John Fowler was established in the first rank of practical engineers, and he be- came, after settling in London, continuously em- ployed at. home and abroad in the laying out of -railways, docks, and other large works requiring a high class of engineering ability. One of the latest and greatest works with which Sir John Fowler has been connected is that of the construction of the Forth Bridge. and at the banquet after the opening the Prince of Wales announced baronetcies for him and Mr. Thompson, and knighthoods for Mr. Baker and Mr. Arroll.

Harcourt,the Attorney General Lords Cross, Dufferin, and Spencer; Messrs. Chamberlain, Childers, Courtney, Smith, Ritchie, Goschen, and the Lord Chancellor were present at luncheon.

div.p: THE YACHT NORSEMAN IN THE EASTHAM LOCKS.

At 1-50 yesterday, the yacht Norseman, 320 tons, belonging to Mr. S. Platt, chairman of the Works Committee of the Manchester ship Canal, was ad- mitted into the locks at Eastham. This was the first steamer admitted into the canal, with the ex- ception of those engaged on business. Mr. Platt and Mr. Marshall Stevens were on board. The in- quest on the lad Mist, the first. victim of the canal water, was held yesterday afternoon. THE SWING BRIDGE AT MOORE LANE.

div.head: VISIT OF THE GERMAN EMPEROR.
div.p: VISIT OF THE GERMAN EMPEROR.

The German Emperor arrived at Port Victoria at noon on Saturday, amidst salvoes of artillery from the Chan- nel Squadron, which were anchored in the Medway. The Prince of Wales, the Duke of Edinburgh, the Duke of Connaught, and the Duke of Cla- rence and Avondale, all in German uniforms, and ac- companied by a brilliant staff, travelled from London, and met the Emperor and Empress at one o'clock on board the Imperial yacht Hohenzollern. Af- ter lunch the Royal and Imperial party en- tered a special 'rain and journeyed to Windsor. The stations en route were crowded with spectators, who cheered as tho train passed. At Windsor the Princess of Wales, the Princess Beatrice, the Duchess of Connaught, the Princess Louise, and the Duke of Cambridge received the Imperial visitors. A Royal procession of twelve carriages then started to drive to the Castle. The streets were crowded with spectators, who displayed the great- est enthusiasm. At the Guildhall a stoppage was made whilst, on behalf of the Corporation, an address of wel- come was presented to the Emperor. His Imperial Majesty having made a suitable reply, the procession re- formed, and proceeded to the Waterloo Chamber entrance of the Castle, where the Queen surrounded by the Court, received the Emperor and Empress with great affection. On Sunday the Emperor was variously occupied with military, religious, and musical engagements, inspecting the Guards at the Victoria Barracks in the morn- ing, afterwards attending a special service at Holy Trinity Church, and being present at a sacred concert at the Castle in the evening. On Monday morning the Emperor was at a review of the Eton College Vo!unteers, and at the close he delivered a short address to the boys. His Majesty said he was highly pleased with the way in which they had gone through their drill, and he expressed the hope that if they ever had to use their arms, it would be in a good cause, and that they would show the pluck and spirit which had always distinguished British soldiers. On Tuesday, his Majesty, visited Windsor Great Park and witnessed a" musical ride" performed by the Life Guards. His Majesty next proceeded to Cumberland Lodge, where he lunched with Prince and Princess Christian. In the evening the Queen gave a dinner party at Windsor, the guests including the Emperor, and numbering about one hundred and fifty. The German Emporer took breakfast with he Queen at Windsor, on Wednesday, and in the afternoon, with the Empress, attended the garden party given at Cum- berland Lodge, by Prince and Princess Christian. In the evening the Emperor and Empress made their entry into London driving from Paddington to Bunkingham Palace amid great enthusiam. At night they attended a State performance given at the Royal Italian Opera, amid surroundings of the greatest pomp and splendour. On Thursday evening the Emperor received a num- ber of depvitations at Buckingham Palace. An address which was presented to him by a deputation of Ger- mans expressed a hope that the Imperial visit to this country might cement the relationship existing between the reigning families of England and Germany. To the representations made to him by the British and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society about slave-trade cruelties in Africa, His Majesty replied that " something must be done" to put an end to this evil.

div.head: INSPECTION OF VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: INSPECTION OF VOLUNTEERS.

At eight o'clock yesterday morning the Emperor in- spected the Queen's Westminster Volunteers on a spa- cious lawn at the rear of Buckingham Palace. Colenel Howard Vincent, M.P., was in command. The Duke of Westminster, honorary colonel, led the men up to the saluting point. The Emperor was accompanied by the Duke of Connaught and a brilliant staff, including Lords Mount-Edgcumbe and De Ros. His Ma- jesty cordially shook hands with Colonel Howard Vincent and the Duke of Westminster, and keenly inpected the men and their accoutre- ments. He expressed approval of their bearing. Shortly after eleven o'clock the sun burst through the clouds and effectually dispersed any anticipations of un- favourable weather. After reviewing the Queen's (Westminster) Volunteers, the Emperor proceeded to the , Naval Exhibition in the undress uniform of a British ad- miral. It has been finally decided that the review at Wimbledon to-day shall consiA of 16,500 volunteers, 600 regulars, cavalry, artillery, Foot Guards, in two divisions the Duke of Connaught commanding one and Sir Evelyn Wood the other. The Royal party subsequently returned to Buckingham Palace, and shortly afterwards the State procession set out for the city, receiving a great ovation along the route, ladies waving pocket-handkerchiefs,and the crowd cheering vociferously, which the Emperor acknowledged by saluting with his right hand. The Emperor and Empress were accompanied by a large suite and the Prince of Walea robed in the carriage (aiming

New MAGISTEATE.—Notice has been received that Mr. John Dolby Dewhurst, of Oughtrington House, brother cf the late Mr. G. B. Dewhurst, has been appointed a justice of the peace by the Lord-Lieutenant of the county. Citikaaa AGAIEST CARTERS.—At the Altrincham Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. R. H. Joynson and other magistrates, William Owen and Martin Boyle, of Lymm„ were summoned for being in charge of two horses and carts asleep.—Oven denied the charge, and Boyle pleaded guilty.—Boyle was fined ss. and costs, 15s. 6d., and Owen was discharged. Tim REV. W. EVANS.—On Sunday evening the Rev. W. Evans preached his valedictory sermon to a good congre- gation in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Eagle-brow, Lymm. The Rev. gentleman, who is just recovering from an attack. of inflbenza, and who was far from welr,made feeling reference to the kind feelings expressed to him and his family,, and the many friendships he had.formed during his ministry at Lymm. GOOD TEMPLARY.—TheLymm Tower of Refuge Lodge held a meeting. on Tuesday, under the presidency of Bro. J. A: Jenkins, of Warrington. Mr. Halliday, missionary on the Ship Canal, was duly initiated, a brother. A sur- prise visit from the Crusaders Lodge, Altrincham, of four members, and six from Warrington,. was made. A long and enjoyable session was held, several of the brothers speaking of the progress of the Order, and others giving songs, recitations, &c. ' Cnorn Tu.—on Monday morning,, the members of the choirnf the Congregational Church departed by the 8.32 train for Chester. On their arrival, they took a wagonette to Hawarden, and visited the Castle and grounds. They afterwards returned. to Chester, where • they partook of a capital tea. The day was a most beautiful one,. and the trip was thoroughly enjoyed. They returned home by the 9.30 train. The arrange- ments, wkich were in charge of Mr. James Astley, the choirmaster, were most satisfactory. CRICKET. LYMM GRAMMAR SCHOOL 11. BROOK- , LANDS SCHOOL. Hartley not out 1, extras 10 ; total 46. THEFT OF TOOLS.—At the Lymm Police Court, on Tuesday, a youth named Walter Williams, aged 15, was brought up before Mr. C. Lister and Dr. Brabazon, charged with stealing a quantity of fjpiners' tools from the New-Station, Partington, on the • second of July, the property of Jos. Garner, of the value of £3. He was further charged with stealing at the same time and place tools of the value of 125., the property of Edward Hughes. The tools were found. The prisoner was or- dered to received 12 strokes with a birch rod. The punishment was administered to the prisoner in the pre- sence of the magistrates, and he was then liberated. The tools were returned to the owners.

TRICYCLE ACCIDENT AT LYMM.—On Saturday evening, a few minutes after six, a party of cyclists from Altrinc- ham were coming along'the Higher-lane,Lymm, amongst whom were Mr. John Stokoe, clerk to the Altrincham Local Board. On coming to the top of, Penny-hill, being unaware of its steepness, he took. his feet off the pedals of his tricycle, and having no brake the machine rapidly increased in speed. His friends called on him to turn to the right at the Church Inn, and reduce his speed, as the decline became more dangerous at the Rectory gate. This he was powerless to do, as he could not regain his pedals, and, as the least of two evils,he ran his machine against the rectory wall. Of course, the result was dis- astrous to the machine, which was of little importance, and Mr. Stokoe was thrown with great violence on the macadam road. His face was badly disfigured and his ear cut, but all things considered, he had a merciful es- cape. Mr. Stokoe was at businesson Monday morning, suffering little inconvenience, except from his swollen, discoloured, and disfigured face.

THE FUSTIAN CUTTE-RS' STRIKE.—The strike of fustian cutters at Lymm and other districts in Cheshire still continues. At Lymm meetings are being held Ire quently, and the determination to holg out is as strong as ever. Tuesday was the day on which it was stated that Oldham and Manchester merchants had agreed prac- tically to pay the wages according to the price list sub- mitted by the Fustian, Cutters' Association. Dissatis- faction prevails in Warrington. but there the system of apprenticeship is largely in operation. Cutters in many instances, when their apprenticeship has expired, re- new their employers for a sovereign or some other mone- tary consideration handed to them. They have thus no opportunity of taking the same independent stand as their neighbours A meeting of the cutters out on strike took place on MOnday afternoon, in the Bridgwater Room, Lymm, when, an address was given by a delegate from Macclesfield: It was expected that money would he brought brought by the delegate to pay the hands on strike, in accordance with the promise made by th offi- cials of the Federation, but none was forthcoming. Boxes were taken round by the hands to the tradesmen and gentlemen of Lvmm on Friday, and £l2 were collected, which gave about 2s. 611. each to the appli- cants.

PARR'S BANKING CO.

IMPORTANT REPORT. An extraordinary and general meeting of Parr's Banking Co., Limited, as will be seen from the advertisement in another column, will be held at the Bank premises in Warrington on Friday. the 24th inst. The report which will be submitted will

be as follows :--- " The directors have had before them the audited balance sheet of the Bank at the 30th June, 1891, and they beg to report that the profits of the half-year, after providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, have been satisfactory. The directors recommend that there be now declared', for the half-year ending 30th June, an interim dividend at the rate of 19 per cent. per annum, free of income tax, and payable on and after 28th July. After providing for this dividend, there remains a con- siderable balance; which is carried forward to the next account. The position and prospects, of the business continue to be in every way satisfactory. The General Manager, Mr. John Dun, baying since last meeting been elected by the Board to be a director of the company and a member of the Select Committee, without, however, vacating the office of general mana- ger, which he has held for upwards of 25 years, the shareholders will be asked to confirm his election as a director. _

As announced by circular on 13th June, the directors have concluded an arrangement to amalgamate the old- established banking business of Messrs. Fuller. Banbury, Nix and Co.' of 77, Lombard-st., London, with that of this bank. This arrangement, which has been effected on advantageous terms, has secured the admission of the bank to the London Clearing House, which will in- volve the transference of the registered office and the head office of the Bank of London,but care will be taken that the business in the country- shall continue to re- ceive the same attention from the directors and the general manager as heretofore. Mr. E. W. Nix and Mr. Edward Banhurv, two of the active partners of the firm of Fuller, Banbury. Nix and Co., have joined the Board of the Bank, and will give for some time to come all re- quisite services in the management of the London busi- ness. The shareholders will be requested to confirm their election as directors. _ _

In order to carry out this amalgamation, the share- holders will be asked to create 2,500 additional shares in the company, of which 1,400 shares with £2O per share paid thereon. shall be issued to the partners in the firm of Fuller, Banbury, Nix, and Co., or in such names as they may direct ; 1,000 shares shall be allotted to the shareholders of the company whose names shall appear on the register on the 24th July, 1891, at the price of £5O per share, and in the proportion of one new share to each 30 then held ; and 100 shares shall be placed at the dis- posal of the directors, to be sold at their discretion at the market price of the day—the premiums to be received on such 1,000 and 100 shares to be applied to the extent of £28,000 to make good the sum of £2O per share to be paid up on the 1,400 shares to be issued to Messrs Fuller, Banbury, Nix, and Co., the balance to be carried to the reserve fund of the Company. The result will be to raise the Nominal Capital of the Company to £3,250,000 and the Paid-up Capital to £650,000. and to add probably about £B,OOO to the Reserve Fund,besides giving to the existing shareholders a substantial bonus by the allotment of the 1,000 s' at a price so much below the market value." Resolutions will be submitted for carrying out the amalgamated agreement; for the purposes of increasing the capital of the company, and for making th 3 necessary alterations.

A Gibraltar telegram on Wednesday announces the raising of the Anchor line steamer Utopia, which was sunk by the warship Anson in March, on which occasion several hundred Italian emigrants were drowned. A Blackburn cotton operative named Eastwood, after a long drinking bout,went home on Thursday with a pint pot full of oxalic acid, and tried to compel his wife and child to drink it. A neighbour interfered,and prevented this, whereupon Eastwwd drank it up himself, exclaim- ing "Its oxalic acid," lie expired in a very short time in, great agony.

In connection with the finding of the body of a child in a box at the General Post Office, London, which hod come from Glasgow, a policeman, yesterday morning, found a child's right leg floating in the Clyde -at Pinnies- ton Ferry. The leg had been severed at the thigh, and appears to have been in the water seven or eight days. One leg was missing from the body found.

div.head: MR. SPURGEON'S CONDITION.
div.p: MR. SPURGEON'S CONDITION.

Thursday morning's bulletin stated that Mt. Spurgeon passed a restless night. At intervals the delirium ceased, and the congestion of the kidneys was not worse. His strength is maintained, as he takes abun- dance of nourishment. Mrs. and Miss Benson called on Wednesday at Mr. Spurgeon's residence, , and left their cards and that of the Archbishop of Canterbury. The following bulletin was issued on Thursday evening "The Rev. C. H. Spurgeon is no better, and be is very weak." The following bulletin was issued yesterday morning :—" Rev. C. H. Spurgeon has • lOst, strength during the night, from extreme restlessness. The im- perfect action of the kidneys is causing exhaustion of the brain."
_ Mr. Spurgeon last evening was in the same critical condition.
THE LABOUR COMMISSION: LANCASHIRE EVIDENCE..

Group C of the Labour Commission, which cqmprises the textile, clothing, chemical, building, and miscel laneous trades, held a sitting yesterday morning under the presidency of Mr. A. J. Mundella, M.P. Mr. Thoma s Birtwistle, secretary of the North-East Lancashire, a well as of the United Textile Factory Workers', Associa - tion, was the first witness examined. He said the per- centage of half timers in Lancashire was little over 9-, in Yorkshire a little over 10, and in Cheshire about 9: per cent. He would be quite willing to see a redaction of the working hours if foreign competition (principally Continental and Indian) were far less keen than what it was now. Mr. Wilkinson, secretary of the Northern Counties Weavers' Association, expressed his general agreement:with the evidende of the last wit.rte.‘ Mr. Barker, speaking on belialt of the Blackburn weavers generally said that the temperature in some of the weav- ing rooms was as high as 90 degrees, and to this he attributed the high rate of mortality between the agesof 15 and 25 from chest diseases.
YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four. Lord Delamore took the oath and his seat on his elevation. The report stage of the Irish Land Purchase Bill was considered. Several amendments were agreed to, and the bill passed through its report stage: The House adjourned at 7.35. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. PROI'OSED INVITATION TO PRESIDENT CA/RNOT.—Mr. PHILIP STANHOPE :• I beg to ask the first Lord of the Treasury whether her Majesty's Government will take steps to convey to the French Government the satisfac- tion which would be given to the people of this country if the President could be prevailed upon to • pay a visit to England. Mr. W. H. SMITH : Sir,—lt is not in ac- cordance with usage for her Majesty's Government to convey invitations of this kind, but the head of the French Republic or any other friendly nation would always receive a cordial welcome in this country. SUPPLY.—The House then went into Committee of Supply. SirJ. FERGUSSON said steps had beenaken by her Majesty's Government to obtain the release of the girl Kate Greenfield, now in the hands of the Kurds. The Turkish Government had withdrawn their opposition and the Persian Government had ordered an adequate force of troops to disperse the disorderly assembly, and to get the girl brought before the acting British Consul. The House afterwards proceeded to discuss the policy of the Government with regard to Portugal;: the North Sea Convention; diplomatic appointments; and the mis- government that prevails in Asiatic -Turkey.
A butcher named William Burke has been arrested at Morpeth on a chargeof having over nine years ago mur- dered a boy named Burns, whose body was found in Tweedmouth Dock, at Berwick-on-Tweed.
THE LIBERAL ASSOCIATION OS THE NEWTON DIVISION.

The re-organisation of the Liberal voters in the Newton division of South-West Lancashire, is now in active progress. Since the. retirement of Mr. P. Campbell, as registration agent, matters havo been allowed to lapse, but owingto the near approach of the general election, the Liberal Federation have decided to move in the matter, and have sent down an agent to put the affairs of the district Ili sae- thing like order.

PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that an extra- ordinary GENERAL MEETING of this Company will be held at the Bank Premises. Winwick-st., IVRrrington • on FRIDAY, the Twenty-fourth day of July, 1891, at Twelve o'clock noon, for the purpose of sanctioning the declaration of an Interim Dividend, to be payable on the 28th July, 1891. electing Directors, conducting the ordinary businesa of the Company, and considering, and if thought expedient passing Special Resolutions to the following purport or effect, viz. No. I.—To approve of the Agreement to acquire thebusi- ness of Messrs. Fuger, Banbury, Nix, and Co. No. lI.—To Increase the Capital of the Company. No. lII.—To provide for the removal of the Head Office and Registered Office to London. No. IV.—To alter the conditions for the Lodgment of Proxies. No. V.—To increase the number of the Select Corn- m MO. The Transfer Books will be closed from the 18th to the 24th July, both days being inclusive. By order, JOHN DUN, General Manager, Old Bank, Warrington, 10th July, 1891.

THE ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER AT ALTRINCHAM. On Thursday, Patrick Mongon. a gardener, was charged at Altrincham with causing the death of his infant child, Ellen Mongon.. On his wife, Mary, entering the court, sha was taken into custody, and both were charged with manslaughter. At the outset Patrick volunteered the statement that his wife fainted and fell on the child, and that he thought it struck against a chair. Prisoners were remanded for further inquiry, and bail was refused. A. LITTLE GIRL DROWNED AT SANKEY. On Tuesday afternoon, an inquest was held by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, at the Black Horse Inn, Sankey, concerning the death of Christina Mary Weaver, aged six years, daughter of Alfred Weaver, labourer, of 9, Wright-st.. off- Liverpool-road, who was drowned in the canal at Sankey. Mrs. Weaver the child's mother said the child went out on Satur- day afternoon,and half an hour later, half-past four, her body was brought home. The first she knew about what had occurred was when a little boy brought the girl's hat in and said she was drowned. —Ethel' Dendy said she was playing with the deceased, and she was trying to walk along the wood which was placed below the towing path. She shut her eyes and fell in.— Samuel Leigh, 278 Liverpool-rd., Sankey Bridges, sa;d he was on the canal bank on Saturday afternoon, and, notic- ing a clowd, went to see what was the matter. Then he learned there was a child in the water. A flat happened to be passing, and he got a woodhook from it. He grappled for about five minutes and then found the body, about threevards from the side. There was some wood put along the side of the bank to prevent boats crushing against the bank, and this was about ten or eleven inches wide and thechildren tried to walk along it.—The jury returned a verdict that the deceased was drowned through accident- al/yr falling into the canal.

Longworth under a w9.rrant, charging him with leaving his son, chargeable to the common fund a the Daventry Union, in. the county of Northampton. He was handed over to the Northampton police the next day.
